text.0_Title Page, 4_Paragraph: The book HaBachur was established anew, Better than the initial version: Its author expanded it with fuller substance, Altering its structure for improvement: He added further good material, And placed within it thoughtful corrections: In the first there was lentil grain, Now it is entirely choice wheat:
text.0_Title Page, 5_Paragraph: Printed in Isny the city in the year from the creation of the world 302 according to the small count in the month of Sivan [Note: This refers to the Hebrew year 5302, corresponding to 1542 CE. Isny was a German city where Hebrew books were printed in the 16th century.]
text.0_Title Page, 6_Paragraph: Praise to the Most High Name
text.1_Introductory Poem, 0_Paragraph: And this is the poem that I composed in Rome the capital:
text.1_Introductory Poem, 1_Paragraph: I cry out and also call to men — youths together with elders, and even the aged.
text.1_Introductory Poem, 2_Paragraph: Come to me and I will teach you the rules of the Holy Tongue, which have new aspects.
text.1_Introductory Poem, 3_Paragraph: The foundations of grammar are indeed examined in my book, for those versed in law and judgment, wise and incisive.
text.1_Introductory Poem, 4_Paragraph: Shall I not bring hidden matters to light within it, and disclose the treasured teachings of the commentators?
text.1_Introductory Poem, 5_Paragraph: And into four chief treatises I will divide it, to clarify the required subjects.
text.1_Introductory Poem, 6_Paragraph: Thirteen principles in each one — that is, fifty-two in total.
text.1_Introductory Poem, 7_Paragraph: May my book, called HaBachur, bring joy to God and to mankind.
text.2_Foreword to Mantua Edition, 0_Paragrap: Said Elijah the Levite the Ashkenazi:
text.2_Foreword to Mantua Edition, 1_Paragrap: At the age of forty I was, when time sent me forth from Venice and I came to Rome. There I was questioned concerning the composition of this book, and in it I responded to matters as my heart saw fit. And behold, the Lord has preserved my life since then for thirty years, and now I am as one of seventy years, yet even today I remain strong — as my strength was then, so is my strength now — to go forth and come back in the battle of grammar, Scripture, and tradition. For since that time, other views have arisen within me, and new understandings that I did not previously know. In addition to this, from that day onward I discovered that I had omitted certain matters that were worthy of being written, yet I did not write them; and I also wrote things that I wish I had not written — I regret having done so. This should not be wondered at, for we find the same among our Rabbis of blessed memory, who said something in their youth and later retracted it in their old age, as we find that Rava retracted his view in that matter, and likewise Rav Ashi retracted what he had said in the first edition, and the law follows the later edition, as stated at the end of the chapter ‘One Whose Dead Lies Before Him.’ And just as their thoughts were, so are my thoughts; and I am no better than my forefathers. Therefore I resolved with my heart to print this book a third time, to add to it and to remove from it. In this way I shall improve the latter kindness beyond the former, so as not to go after young students teaching them false premises, invalid proofs, and unsound rules — which the students who come after them would then learn, resulting, God forbid, in the desecration of the Divine Name. Therefore, in this version I shall correct what is distorted, straighten what is crooked, repair what is flawed, and remove stumbling blocks from the path of my people. Thus God will be with me. And so I shall begin this introduction as it stands.
text.3_Introduction, 0_Paragraph: And this is the introduction that I composed in Rome:
text.3_Introduction, 1_Paragraph: In the year five thousand two hundred and seventy-seven from creation, the Lord stirred the spirit of a wise and understanding man in all knowledge, noble, precious, glorious, Prince Aegidius of Viterbo, may his glory be exalted, who sought to find pleasant words and upright writing in the books of our holy language. And to me, I his servant, the youngest of the grammarians, Elijah the Ashkenazic Levite, he called and said to me: "What are you doing here, Elijah? Arise now and make a book that gives beautiful words in the grammar of the holy language. For all the grammar books that I have seen do not suffice to fulfill my desire or to quench my thirst for grammar, for there are some of them that are long, multiplying words without benefiting this wisdom, and there are some of them that are brief, leaving out things necessary for it. And you—gird your loins like a man and choose from between the two extremes the middle way. And tell the hidden things of wisdom in the grammar of the language, in matters that have not been written and yet deserve to be written. Compose from them a book so that the many may benefit from it, and it will stand as a banner for peoples, and to it nations will seek and find rest for their souls.
text.3_Introduction, 2_Paragraph: And it came to pass when I heard his words, for they were pleasing, that I rose to fulfill my desire and hastened to comply with him. I resolved to make this book small in size and rich in quality, with concise rules that are useful and necessary for anyone who comes to learn the ways of the Holy Tongue, without lengthening my discussion with matters already written by the grammarians before me, for all books of grammar are full of them. Rather, my main intent in composing this work is to write certain rules and matters in which no one preceded me, as well as some of the good things written by the distinguished grammarians, scattered in various places throughout their books — here a little and there a little. I shall gather them, explain them, and make from them rules and principles whose remembrance will be easy for students. And this shall be your sign: in every place where I explain or introduce something from my own mind, you will find the image of a hand touching its lip from the outside, pointing with a finger as if to say, “See here — something new is being introduced to you.”
text.3_Introduction, 3_Paragraph: And this rule shall be the law and practice of the book: I shall adhere to everything that proceeds according to the rule and law of grammar, and my words will not be merely statements of the rule in the abstract, saying, “the law is thus.” And if one or two words are found that alter the order of the rule and depart from the general principle, I shall not give them attention — especially those words which the grammarians have called irregular or compound. I have already begun to compose a small book, and before it has even come into being its name has been called the Book of Composition; there all matters of the irregular and the compound will be explained clearly and thoroughly, and I have no concern with them in this book. All this is in order not to enlarge its size, lest one who sees it become weary upon looking at its appearance and the height of its stature.
text.3_Introduction, 4_Paragraph: Therefore, when I bring an example from Scripture, I will not multiply citations for it, but will establish the matter by the testimony of one or two verses.
text.3_Introduction, 5_Paragraph: Nevertheless, for every single verse I will record in the margin the name of the book in which that verse appears.
text.3_Introduction, 6_Paragraph: And not only this will I do for you, but I will also record the chapter number in which that verse appears, according to the order of chapters arranged by the Christians in all twenty-four books, which they call in their language capitulos. For I have found in this a great need and benefit for anyone studying any book in which a verse is cited, since at times, even if a person knows in which of the twenty-four books that verse appears, he may stand for a day or two, wearying himself, trying to find the entrance to its place. The truth is that the masters of the Mesorah already divided each book, as is known, into sections, and they called each section a seder.
text.3_Introduction, 7_Paragraph: And besides their division of the Five Books of the Torah into fifty-two portions, they further divided them into sedarim, saying: the Book of Genesis has twelve portions and forty-three sedarim; the Book of Exodus has eleven portions and twenty-nine sedarim; and so with all of them.
text.3_Introduction, 8_Paragraph: And likewise they divided the other books of the twenty-four into sedarim.
text.3_Introduction, 9_Paragraph: For example, the Book of Joshua has thirty-four sedarim, Jeremiah has thirty-one sedarim, and so with all of them — the greater according to its greatness, and the smaller according to its smallness.
text.3_Introduction, 10_Paragraph: And ever since I came of age, I have wondered why they did not do the same in Israel — to mark at the beginning of each seder and seder, in the manner of א ב ג ד ה ו, and so on, just as the masters of the Mesorah arranged them.
text.3_Introduction, 11_Paragraph: And behold, you should surely know that the Christians divided the Book of Samuel, the Book of Kings, and the Book of Chronicles, each into two parts. Therefore, in every place where you find written in a reference “Samuel” with the letter bet above it, Samuel ב׳, it means Second Samuel, beginning from “And it came to pass after the death of Saul” and onward. Likewise, “Kings ב׳” means Second Kings, beginning from “And Moab rebelled” and onward. And similarly, “Chronicles ב׳” means Second Chronicles, beginning from “And Solomon strengthened himself” and onward.
text.3_Introduction, 12_Paragraph: And behold, I divided the substance of this book into four treatises — that is, two on verbs and two on nouns. I divided each treatise into thirteen principles, corresponding to the thirteen principles of our holy faith. Thus these four treatises contain fifty-two principles, whose sign is אליה״ו.
text.3_Introduction, 13_Paragraph: And further, I divided each principle into smaller parts and marked them in the manner of א ב ג ד ה ו, and so on; the benefit of this is well known and needs no explanation.
text.3_Introduction, 14_Paragraph: And behold, I called the name of this book:
text.3_Introduction, 15_Paragraph: The Book HaBachur. And this is for three reasons. The first: because this book is choice and good, wholly fine flour, with no refuse in it.
text.3_Introduction, 16_Paragraph: The second: because it is composed for every young man to study in the days of his youth, and his latter end will be good.
text.3_Introduction, 17_Paragraph: The third: because it is a distinctive appellative name, and is called by the name HaBachur.
text.3_Introduction, 18_Paragraph: And concerning this I said in my poem:
text.3_Introduction, 19_Paragraph: Brothers and also companions, hear my words with attention.
text.3_Introduction, 20_Paragraph: A very pleasant book — today I have given it birth.
text.3_Introduction, 21_Paragraph: Since for every young man it is good and also choice,
text.3_Introduction, 22_Paragraph: and I myself am named Bachur, therefore I called it HaBachur.”

text.5_First Treatise, 0_Subject, 0_Paragraph: On the elucidation of the root categories of verbs, and it is divided into thirteen principles:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 0_Par: The First Principle. On the division of the roots of the Holy Tongue into eight parts:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that all the roots of the Holy Tongue are divided into two kinds of verbs; and each verb into six root categories; and each root category into seven verb patterns; and each verb pattern into six tenses:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 2_Par: And each tense is divided into two genders, and each gender into two numbers, and each number into three persons, and each person has its own distinct form of expression. And now I shall explain each and every one:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 3_Par: 2. There are two kinds of verbs: one is intransitive, and the other is transitive.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 4_Par: The intransitive: such as halakh, amad, yashav, and the like — for the action remains within the subject performing it and does not pass from it to another.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 5_Par: The transitive: such as shamar, paqad, harag, and the like — for the action passes from the subject to another. In many respects the intransitive verbs differ from the transitive ones, as will be explained briefly in this work.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 6_Par: 3. And the six root categories are: complete, defective, and doubled.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 7_Par: And there are three kinds of weak verbs: those with a weak first letter, those with a weak second letter, and those with a weak third letter — making six root categories in all.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 8_Par: And there are also other root categories, such as those with weak extremities, those lacking extremities, quadriliteral forms, and the like; but all of them are compound and derive from these six, as will be explained.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 9_Par: 4. And there are seven verb patterns: three active ones, called “fathers,” and three passive ones, called “derivatives.”
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 10_Pa: And one of the verb patterns is both a father and a derivative — that is, from one perspective it is active, and from another perspective it is passive, as will be explained.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 13_Pa: And the pattern that is both active and passive is called Hitpa‘el.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 14_Pa: 5. And as for one who claims that there exists another verb pattern called “quadriliteral,” such as shofet, shofateta, and so on — I will respond to this under the category of verbs with a weak middle letter in the Second Treatise, the Eighth Principle. There I will demonstrate with clear and correct proofs that this is not fitting to be called a verb pattern in its own right.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 15_Pa: 6. And there are six tenses, which are six actions: past, participle, passive, infinitive, imperative, and future.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 16_Pa: And the two genders are the masculine and the feminine.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 17_Pa: And the two numbers are the singular and the plural.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 18_Pa: And there are three persons: the third person, the second person, and the first person speaking for himself.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 19_Pa: And the distinct form of expression for each one is conveyed either by its vowel pattern or by the addition of one or two letters to the three root letters, such as the letters t-h-i-m-u-n at the end of the past forms, and the letters e-i-t-n at the beginning of the future forms:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 0_Par: The Second Principle. On the elucidation of the differences between each and every one of the eight divisions mentioned:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that although I said that in every root category there are seven verb patterns, this applies only to the division of transitive verbs. But the class of intransitive verbs has only three active patterns, for the passive patterns are not needed for them, since they themselves are already passive, as I have already hinted in section 2. Only a few are found that appear in the Nif‘al and Hitpa‘el patterns, as will be explained in the Eighth Principle:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 2_Par: 2. And as for what I said, that every verb pattern has six tenses, this applies only to the three active patterns; for in the other four the passive does not apply, since they themselves are passive, and in some of them the imperative does not apply either, as will be explained with respect to each one:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 3_Par: 3. And as for what I said, that each tense has two genders, this is correct for all the tenses except for the makor, to which no gender applies at all, for it is the same for all. It is called the makor because from it all the actions derive, as will be further explained.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 4_Par: And as for what I said, that each gender has two numbers, this too is correct in all cases except for the makor.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 5_Par: 4. And as for what I said, that each number has three persons, this applies only in the past and in the future. But the other tenses have only one person, for the participle and the passive have only the third person.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 6_Par: And if you wish to use them with the other persons, it is necessary to add a pronominal word of the second person together with the second person.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 7_Par: And likewise a pronominal word of the first person with the first person, for example: atta poqed, ani poqed, attem poqedim, anachnu poqedim, att poqedet, atten poqedot; and so too in the passive.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 8_Par: And the imperative has only the second person, and it cannot be used in the other persons, for commands are given only to one who is addressed.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 9_Par: 5. And as for what I said, that each person has a distinct form of expression, this applies only to the second person and the third person. But the form of expression of the first person is the same for masculine and feminine in all verbs and in all suffixes, such as ani, anachnu, and likewise all ni and nu found among the suffixes.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 10_Pa: However, the form of the third person that is the same for masculine and feminine applies only in the past tense alone, such as paqdu.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 11_Pa: And the general rule is that all forms of speech are divided into four parts: singular masculine, plural masculine, singular feminine, and plural feminine.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 12_Pa: And for each of these there are three persons: second person, third person, and first person. Accordingly, in each tense there should have been three forms for the masculine plural, three for the feminine singular, and three for the feminine plural. But since in the past tense the three persons are the same for masculine and feminine, as will be explained, there remain in it nine forms of expression.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 13_Pa: 6. And likewise in the future tense there ought to have been twelve forms of expression; but since the two first-person forms are also the same in it, there remain only ten forms of expression. And although the forms of the feminine third person and the feminine second person come in the same form — for the word tifqadnah serves for both — nevertheless it is not considered identical, for two reasons:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 14_Pa: The first is that every instance of “identical” that I have mentioned means identical for masculine and feminine, and this is not the case here:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 15_Pa: And the second reason is that their meaning is not the same: for one applies to the third-person feminine plural, and the other to the second-person feminine plural. Likewise, even though two distinct forms are made from tifqod, they are not called identical, for one is for the second person and the other for the third person; and one is not substituted for the other. Therefore, they are not called identical.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 0_Par: The Third Principle. On the elucidation of the three terms applied to the three root letters, and on the definition of complete verbs and those that are not complete:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Until now I have spoken in general about the root categories, the verb patterns, and their actions:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 2_Par: And now I shall speak of them in detail. First of all, you must know that every verb in the Hebrew language — whether it is complete or not complete — has three root letters. The grammarians have already agreed to measure every root according to the pattern pa‘al, and they called the first letter of every root pe, the second ‘ayin, and the third lamed.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 3_Par: And any root in which one of its three root letters is missing or weak is called “defective in pe,” or “weak in pe,” or in ‘ayin, or in lamed.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 4_Par: And in the Second Treatise, in the Sixth Principle, section 6, I shall explain the difference between the defective roots and the weak roots:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 5_Par: 2. Therefore, remember this: wherever you find written “the pe of the verb,” or “the ‘ayin of the verb,” or “the lamed of the verb,” whether in verbs or in nouns, it means the first letter, the second letter, or the third letter respectively. I shall speak further about this in the discussion of noun patterns at the beginning of the Third Treatise.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 6_Par: 3. And know that every verb called “complete” is one in which none of the letters aleph, he, vav, or yod occurs, and which also has no nun at the beginning, and whose last two letters are not identical; for in such a case none of the three root letters will ever be missing. For this reason it is called “complete.”
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 7_Par: And a verb that has a nun at the beginning is called from the category of the defective roots, as will be explained in its category; and a verb that has one of the letters aleph, he, vav, or yod is called from the category of the weak roots. And I shall now explain the manner of their weakness.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 8_Par: 4. The aleph may be weak at the beginning or at the end of verbs. For example, at the beginning, from akhal one says okhal, yokhal, tokhal, and at the end, as in qara, qarata, and so on. However, it does not appear in the middle of a verb, as in sha’ag, sha’al, and other similar forms.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 9_Par: The he becomes weak only at the end of a verb, such as galah, asah, and the like. But at the beginning or in the middle it does not become weak, as in harag, bahal, and the like.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 10_Pa: The vav becomes weak only in the middle, such as kum, shuv, and the like; but at the beginning or at the end a root vav is not found.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 11_Pa: The yod becomes weak only at the beginning, such as from yada, one says eda, yeda; eshev, yeshev.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 12_Pa: The tsere vowel indicates the presence of a yod; and according to the opinion of some, a weak yod does not occur in the middle of verbs, and at the end it never occurs as a root letter according to everyone.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 13_Pa: 5. And a verb that has two identical root letters at the end is called from the category of doubled roots, such as sabab and tamam.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 14_Pa: And only a few are found in which the first two letters are identical, and these follow the pattern of the complete verbs. For example, from dedeh one says eddaddeh (Isaiah 38:15); and from shashah, “veshishitem et ha-eifah” (Ezekiel 45:13). There are almost no others among verbs, but they are found more frequently among nouns, such as “darakh kokhav mi-Ya‘akov” (Numbers 24:17), “u-mashoaḥ ba-basar” (Jeremiah 22:14), “be-vavat ‘eino” (Zechariah 2:12), and the like — though they are few.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 15_Pa: 6. And verbs in which the first and third root letters are identical are not found at all among the complete verbs. The word ye‘al‘u dam (Job 39:30) does not have the root ‘ala‘, as I shall explain in the book HaHarkavah. But among roots that are not complete, such cases are found, such as hayah and natan, and a few others. They are found more frequently among nouns, especially with the letter shin, such as shemesh, shoresh, shalosh.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 0_Par: The Fourth Principle. Here I shall begin to analyze the six tenses, which are called pe‘ulot (“actions”), and I shall explain them two by two, beginning with the past forms and the future forms:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that the past and the future are the foundations of all the actions, and by means of them a person can suffice and speak in their place for all the other actions. Thus it is the way of Scripture to use them in place of the participle, the infinitive, and the imperative, as will be explained.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 2_Par: 2. And the letters used in the past tense to indicate the grammatical persons are the letters t-h-i-m-u-n, and they always appear at the end.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 3_Par: And those used in the future tense are the letters e-i-t-n, and they always appear at the beginning. However, there is no need to elaborate on their usage here, for you will see it in the table of verb patterns that I shall compose, God willing.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 4_Par: 3. And know that there are also three letters that are used at the beginning of past tense, whose mnemonic is shaveh; and I shall speak about them further in the chapter on the shimusim (particles).
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 5_Par: And the principal one is the vav, and its usage is in two ways.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 6_Par: The first is called the vav of conjunction, and it joins a verb to a verb or a noun to a noun, and so forth, as will be explained in the chapter mentioned.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 7_Par: And the second is called the vav of conversion, and it converts past forms into future forms, and future forms into past forms, as I shall explain here.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 8_Par: 4. Know that when you wish to convert a past form into a future form, you place a vav with sheva at its beginning.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 9_Par: For example, from shamar: “ve-shamar Hashem” (Deuteronomy 7:12), which is equivalent to ve-yishmor. Likewise, “ve-shamru benei Yisrael” (Exodus 31:16) is equivalent to ve-yishmeru.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 10_Pa: 12. Be it well known to you that in the languages of the nations there are three kinds of past tense: the simple past, the imperfect past, and the pluperfect (past already completed).
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 11_Pa: 5. And if you ask: how shall I know whether it is the vav of conjunction or the vav of conversion?
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 12_Pa: Know that when there is no other past verb preceding it, it is a vav of conversion; but if there is, then it is a vav of conjunction. One verse serves as a sign: “mi pa‘al ve-‘asah” (Isaiah 41:4), and the discerning will understand. Likewise, the two vavs in “ve-qara zeh el zeh ve-amar” (Isaiah 6:3) are both vavs of conversion, since it is written before them “va-ereh et Hashem,” which is a past verb on account of the vav with qamats in va-ereh.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 13_Pa: 6. And if someone should ask: but behold, the verbs yekhasseh and yi‘ofef that precede them are future forms — we reply that it is the way of Scripture to place the future in the place of the past when speaking of something that regularly or continually occurs. For example: “ve-ed ya‘aleh” (Genesis 2:6), “‘al pi Hashem yaḥanu” (Numbers 9:20), and that entire passage.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 14_Pa: 7. And know that it is the way of Scripture to speak in the past tense in place of the future, and this occurs most often in prophetic speech, for the matter is clear before the Omnipresent as though it had already been done.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 15_Pa: But in Psalms, Proverbs, and Job it is the opposite, for most of the future forms found in them stand in place of past forms; likewise in the Song at the Sea and in the section of Ha’azinu. But in narrative accounts of deeds and events, such usages are found only very rarely.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 16_Pa: 8. And know that for the second person singular and the first person singular there is one sign by which to distinguish the vav of conjunction from the vav of conversion. This is as follows: when they occur with the vav of conjunction, they are generally accented on the penultimate syllable, just as they normally are even without a vav. For example: “ve-akhaltí ḥattat ha-yom” (Leviticus 10:19), “ve-dibbartí ‘al ha-nevi’im” (Hosea 12:11). These are past forms with penultimate stress. But when they occur with the vav of conversion, they generally shift to final stress, as in: “ve-shamartá et kol ḥuqqav” (Exodus 15:26), “ve-dibbartá mishpatai” (Jeremiah 1:16). And this applies in all verb patterns and in all root categories, except for verbs with a weak final lamed–aleph or he, which always retain penultimate stress, whether with the vav or without it, such as ve-qarata, u-matsata, u-vanita, u-fanita, and the like.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 17_Pa: And I shall give you one general rule for all nine forms of the past tense, by which you may know which is accented on the penultimate syllable and which on the final syllable:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 18_Pa: 9. Know that five of them are always accented on the final syllable, whether with the vav or without it, namely: paqad, paqdu, paqedah, paqadtem, peqadten. And two are always accented on the penultimate syllable, whether with the vav or without it, namely: paqadnu and u-paqadt. And two of them, without the vav, are always accented on the penultimate syllable, but with the vav are sometimes accented on the penultimate syllable and sometimes on the final syllable, namely: paqadta and paqadti, as I have written.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 19_Pa: And this rule applies to all the verb patterns of the category of complete verbs, except for the third-person masculine and feminine forms of the Hif‘il pattern, which are for the most part accented on the penultimate syllable, as will be explained.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 20_Pa: 10. And know that the three third-person forms — paqad, paqdu, and paqedah — have a special rule: when they are joined to a short word, or to a word that is accented on the penultimate syllable, they themselves also shift to penultimate stress. For example: “qara laylah” (Genesis 1:5), “ve-sha’al lo” (Numbers 27:21), “ve-qare’u lo” (Deuteronomy 25:8), “bagdu bah” (Lamentations 1:2), and the like.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 21_Pa: 11. And know that in the future tense there is another sign by which to distinguish the vav of conjunction from the vav of conversion. This is that the vav of conjunction is pointed with a sheva, as I hinted above in section 4; but the vav of conversion is governed to be pointed with a pataḥ and followed by a dagesh, such as va-yomer, va-tomer, va-nomer. And since the aleph does not accept a dagesh, the vav before it is pointed with a qamats. All of this will be explained well in the chapter mentioned above, God willing.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 22_Pa: 12. Be it well known to you that in the languages of the nations there are three kinds of past tense: the simple past, the imperfect past, and the pluperfect (past already completed).
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 23_Pa: However, in the Holy Tongue all three appear in a different manner, and according to the context each one is explained in one of these three ways. I shall now give you an example from the word paqad as it appears in Scripture in all three senses. “paqad ‘avonekh bat Edom” (Lamentations 4:22) — this is a completed past. In the Ashkenazic tongue it is expressed as er hot gedokht, and in the vernacular tongue as visito.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 24_Pa: “And Hashem paqad et Sarah” (Genesis 21:1) is an imperfect past — that is, it is like “was attending to.” In the Ashkenazic tongue it is expressed as er rakhte, and in the vernacular tongue as visitava. But according to the explanation of Rashi, of blessed memory, it is a past already completed; see there.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 25_Pa: “For ki paqad Hashem et ammo” (Ruth 1:6) is a past already completed, for it is as though it said “had already attended to.” In the Ashkenazic tongue it is expressed as er hatte gedokht, and in the vernacular tongue as avia visitamo.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 26_Pa: And likewise the vav that converts the future into the past generally converts it into an imperfect past, such as va-yomer and va-yedabber, which are explained as “was saying” and “was speaking.” In the Ashkenazic tongue: er zogte, er redite. Except in certain cases, when a completed past precedes it, in which case it too takes that sense. For example: “ki me‘at asher hayah lekha lefanai va-yifrotz la-rov va-yevarekh Hashem otkha” (Genesis 30:30). Here they are equivalent to paratz and berakh, on account of the word hayah that precedes them.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 27_Pa: 13. Nevertheless, know that the vav does not have the power to convert the future into a past already completed, except in very few places. For example: “va-yishlaḥ Yitzḥaq et Ya‘aqov [va-yishma‘ Ya‘aqov el aviv ve-el immo] va-yelekh Paddanah Aram” (Genesis 28:7). These are equivalent to “had already sent,” “[had already heard],” and “had already gone,” as Rashi of blessed memory explains there; see there.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 0_Par: The Fifth Principle. On the explanation of the participles and the passive forms:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that an action being performed now, in the present time, is called the action of the participle, and it is composed of the past and the future. For example, when you say “Reuben is okhel,” it implies that he has already begun to eat and will still eat. Now, the Holy Tongue has no special verb that indicates this present time, for what we call the participle is in truth called the shem ha-po‘el (the active noun), and it is in the form of an adjective.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 2_Par: 2. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between them. The shem ha-po‘el, which is the participle, can be applied only to a person at the time he is performing that action; whereas an adjectival noun can be applied to a person who possesses that quality even at a time when he is not performing the action. For example, from gonev (“stealing”) and gannav (“thief”): gonev is said of a man at the moment he is stealing, but gannav is an adjective describing a man whose way it is to steal; and even at a time when he is sleeping, he is called a gannav. This is what Rashi of blessed memory explains regarding “ve-im ma’en attah le-shalleaḥ” (Exodus 9:2); see there.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 3_Par: 3. And the passive form is also called a participle, for its action has been effected in the present time, and it is composed of the past and the participle. For example, when you say “the house is banui,” it implies that it has already been built and is still standing. This is the difference between it and the past passive, for when you say “the house was nivne,” it is possible that it has since been destroyed or burned. Thus, the passive form too is like an adjective; and the difference between it and a true adjective is the same as the difference between the participle and the adjective, as I have written.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 4_Par: 9. Know that five of them are always accented on the final syllable, whether with the vav or without it, namely: paqad, paqdu, paqedah, paqadtem, peqadten. And two are always accented on the penultimate syllable, whether with the vav or without it, namely: paqadnu and u-paqadt. And two of them, without the vav, are always accented on the penultimate syllable, but with the vav are sometimes accented on the penultimate syllable and sometimes on the final syllable, namely: paqadta and paqadti, as I have written.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 5_Par: And since the participles and the passive forms are in the nature of nouns, the letters mesheh and kholav, which are used with nouns, are also used with them, as will be explained in the chapter on the particles.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 6_Par: 5. [Printer’s error: And now I shall give you a few rules by which you may recognize when these forms stand in place of a participle (in the Ashkenazic tongue: di gegenwertige leit), or in place of an adjective (in the Ashkenazic tongue: dat itel vort). This is as follows: when you find in them one of the letters of bekholam, then they are adjectives and not participles, such as “Ahitofel ba-qoshrim” (II Samuel 15:31), “ka-nosheh ka-asher nashah bo” (Isaiah 24:2), “le-‘oseh orim” (Psalms 136:7), “mi-shomerim la-boqer” (Psalms 130:6), and the like. All of these are adjectives, for these four letters are not used with verbs but only with the infinitive, since it too is in the nature of a noun; and for this reason some grammarians call it the shem ha-po‘el (verbal noun). But when the letters shoheh, which are also used in past and future forms, are used with participles, then it is possible that they are either participles or adjectives.]
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 7_Par: And indeed, according to the intent of the context, a person can understand in which place they function as a participle and in which place as an adjective. For example: “ha-shomer aḥi anokhi” (Genesis 4:9) is an adjective — in the Ashkenazic tongue: er hiter. “ha-shomer emet le-‘olam” (Psalms 146:6) — in the Ashkenazic tongue: der da hot; and so in all such cases.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 8_Par: Printer’s error: You may also recognize them somewhat by other signs that I shall now give you. You must know that verbal actions do not enter into construct, nor does a construct form attach to them. Therefore, when you find participles and passive forms in construct, such as ro‘eh tson (Genesis 4:2), shomrei mishmeret (Numbers 3:28), ge’ulei Hashem (Psalms 107:2), and the like, they are adjectives and not participles. Another sign: know that every participle after which comes the word et is certainly a participle and not an adjective, such as “koh amar Hashem … ‘al ha-ro‘im ha-ro‘im et ‘ammi” (Jeremiah 23:2). The first is an adjective, for it is not in construct, and the second is a participle. And included in this rule are oto, otakh, oti, otam, and all pronominal forms that indicate the object. Likewise, when they are joined with first- or second-person pronouns, such as anokhi holekh (Genesis 25:32), asher attah ‘oseh la-‘am (Exodus 18:14), anachnu ‘osim (II Kings 7:9), attem ‘osim (Jeremiah 44:7) — all of these are participles and not adjectives. For just as you cannot say attah paqad or anokhi paqad, so too you cannot say attah poqed or anokhi poqed as adjectives, but only as participles. There are additional good signs, but these that we have written suffice for now.]
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 0_Par: The Sixth Principle. On the elucidation of the infinitive and the imperative:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that the letters used with infinitives are b-k-l-m; and it goes without saying that the vav is also used with them, for such is its usage with all verbs, nouns, and particles — except with the word o (“or”), and with the word aval (“but”), and with the word asher when its beginning is the interrogative he, as I shall explain in my book HaHarkavah in the discussion of the word ve-he’ezniḥu.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 2_Par: 2. And know that, for the most part, the infinitive does not appear except with b-k-l-m, except when it is adjacent to a past or a future tense, such as halokh halakhta (Genesis 31:30), amor amarti (I Samuel 2:30), shamor tishmerun (Deuteronomy 11:22), abbed te’abbedun (Deuteronomy 12:2), and the like. In such cases it comes to indicate the intensification of the action, and it is usually placed before the verb, though in a few places it comes after it, such as vayevarekh barukh (Joshua 24:10), and similar cases. But when it is used with the imperative, it always comes after it, as in shim‘u shamoa‘ (Isaiah 6:9) and the like — and this is to indicate an even greater strengthening of the command.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 3_Par: 3. Know that the letter most commonly used with the infinitive is the lamed, as in lishmor, lizkor, and the like. And even when the infinitive appears without b-k-l-m, its meaning is usually as though it were with the lamed, such as hiskalta ‘asoh (Genesis 31:28), re’oh faneikha (Genesis 48:11), which are equivalent to la‘asot, lir’ot. And every infinitive that appears in place of an imperative, such as zakhor et yom ha-shabbat (Exodus 20:8), shamor et ḥodesh ha-aviv (Deuteronomy 16:1), and the like, should be interpreted as though it were lizkor, lishmor. In that case they function exactly like true imperatives, such as zekhor, shemor. And in the other stems, aside from the qal stem, there is no difference in writing or in reading between the infinitive when it appears without b-k-l-m and the singular imperative; and this will be explained to you further in the thirteenth principle of the second treatise.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 4_Par: 4. And as I have already said, the infinitive has no inherent tense; nevertheless, when it appears with b-k-l-m it does carry some indication of time. For with the bet and the kaf it most often indicates past time, as in binsōa‘ ha-aron (Numbers 10:35), kishmoa‘ ‘Esav (Genesis 27:34), which mean “when it traveled,” “when he heard.” And with the lamed and the mem it most often indicates future time, as in lishmor et derekh (Genesis 3:24), middabber ‘im Ya‘aqov (Genesis 31:29), which refer to the future. Thus far I have spoken concerning the infinitive; and now I shall speak concerning the imperative.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 5_Par: 5. Know, that no prefixed particle ever comes at the beginning of the imperative, except for the vav alone. And although I have already said that the imperative applies only to the second person, I now say that one may also issue a command to the third person — but in the form of the future tense, such as ya‘aseh Par‘oh ve-yafqed peqidim (Genesis 41:34), and many similar cases.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 6_Par: 6. And likewise, the command to the second person may appear in the language of the future, as in most positive commandments, such as tispor lakh (Leviticus 25), ta‘aseh li (ibid. 26), and the like. It also appears in the language of the past with the vav of conversion, such as ve-ahavta et Hashem (Deuteronomy 6), ve-‘anita ve-amarta (ibid. 26), and similar cases. Those that appear in the true imperative form are few, such as kabbed et avikha (Exodus 20:12), shema‘ Yisrael (Deuteronomy 6). But negative commandments never appear except in the language of the future, such as lo tirtsaḥ, lo tinaf, lo tignov (Exodus 20:13). One does not say lo retsaḥ, lo ne’af, lo gnov, because the imperative never follows any of these words: al, lo, pen, asher, et, lema‘an, ba‘avur, and the like.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 7_Par: 7. And with regard to the speaker speaking about himself, the imperative does not apply at all, for a person does not command himself. Yet sometimes the imperative appears in the language of request and supplication, especially when directed toward the Exalted Name, as is frequently found in the Book of Psalms. And sometimes the words na or anna are added to indicate entreaty, such as selaḥ na (Amos 6), anna Hashem hoshi‘a na (Psalms 118). The imperative is also sometimes found in the language of irony or sharp exhortation, such as semaḥ baḥur be-yaldutekha (Ecclesiastes 11:9), bo’u Beit-El (Amos 4:4), and the like — though such cases are few.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 0_Par: The Seventh Principle. In this I shall begin to explain the meanings of the seven stems, and in it the meaning of the qal stem alone will be explained:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 1_Par: 1. The first stem is the parent stem qal, so called because of its lightness, for it has neither a dagesh nor any added letter as its identifying sign. For all the other stems—both the parent stems and their derivatives—each has a distinct sign, whether a dagesh, or the addition of one or two letters together with a dagesh, as you will see in the table of stems, God willing.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 2_Par: 2. And the essential function of this qal stem is to indicate one who performs an action upon another. In the Ashkenazic tongue: di tetige gatung. That is to say, most of the verbs in this stem are transitive verbs. And we may say that for this reason the language assigned to every verb three root letters: two of them are required for the action itself—for no verb consists of fewer than two letters—and the third letter indicates the one to whom the action is directed. Therefore, verbs of the class with a quiescent middle letter are indeed intransitive verbs, since they have only two active letters, such as qam, shav, sar, rats, ram. And thus most complete verbs are transitive, though a few are found that are intransitive, such as halakh, yashav, ‘amad, shakhan, yashen, shakhav, saḥaq, ka‘as, bakhah. And there are signs by which these may be recognized: namely, that neither the passive form nor the nif‘al stem applies to them; likewise, none of the words that indicate a direct object can follow them, such as et, oto, oti, otkha, and the like. Nor do they combine with pronominal suffixes, such as yeshiveni, ‘amadeni, ‘amadahu, and similar forms. Yet the truth is that in all these signs there are exceptions to the rule.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 3_Par: Therefore I shall give a sign by which one may easily distinguish them, and it is this: for every verb before which the word mah (“what”) can properly be placed is a transitive verb, such as mah shamar, mah akhal, mah shatah, and the like. But with intransitive verbs it is not appropriate to say mah, for it is not possible to say mah yashav, mah ‘amad, mah yashen, mah bakhah.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 4_Par: 3. And know that there are roots which are sometimes transitive and sometimes intransitive. For example: “hafakh libbam lisno ‘ammo” (Psalms 105:25) is transitive, for its meaning is that the Holy One, blessed be He, turned their heart. But “ve-ish Yisrael hafakh” (Judges 20:41) is intransitive. Likewise, “asher ḥalaq Elohekha la-‘ammim” (Deuteronomy 4:19) is transitive, whereas “ḥalaq libbam” (Hosea 7) is intransitive — and there are others besides these.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 0_Par: The Eighth Principle. On the meaning of the nif‘al stem:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 1_Par: The second stem is called the nif‘al stem, and it is of three kinds:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 2_Par: 1. The first kind is a derivative of the transitive qal stem; that is to say, it receives the action directly from its parent, the qal. For example, if you say of the parent akhal (“he ate”), you say of the derivative ne’ekhal (“it was eaten”). Likewise: nilkad, nisraf, nishbar, or nishbah, as in “im ganov yigganev” (Exodus 22:9), “sarof yissarfu” (II Samuel 23), and many similar cases. All of these are passives effected by another. The meaning of this kind is exactly the same as that of the pu‘al stem, for there is no difference between “ve-gunnav mi-beit ha-ish” (Exodus 22:6) and ve-nignav, nor between “ve-hinneh shoraf” (Leviticus 10:16), which is from the pu‘al stem, and nisraf.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 3_Par: And you should know that imperatives never occur in this kind, for we cannot say hissaref, higganev, hillaked, or hishaver. Rather, they occur in the second kind, and the reason for this will be explained to you in the discussion of the pi‘el stem (Principle 10, section 2).
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 4_Par: 2. And the second kind consists of nif‘al forms that are acted upon by themselves; this is the largest category within nif‘al. In this respect its meaning is truly like that of the hitpa‘el stem. Thus we find that the Scripture uses them interchangeably, as in “al tittam’u be-khol elleh” (Leviticus 11), which is equivalent to tit-tetamm’u; and afterward it says, “ki be-khol elleh nitme’u ha-goyim” (Leviticus 11), which is from the nif‘al stem. Likewise, Onkelos translates every expression of nif‘al in the language of hitpa‘el, and so too Rashi, as he explains on “va-titkas” (Genesis 24:44). And similarly, “sheteh gam attah ve-he‘arel” (Habakkuk 2:16). Imperatives also occur in nif‘al of this kind, and their meaning is like that of hitpa‘el, such as “hishamer lekha” (Genesis 31:24), “hippared na me-‘alai” (Genesis 13:9), which are equivalent to hishtamer and hitpared.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 5_Par: And the general rule is that for all nif‘al forms of this kind there is no difference between them and the hitpa‘el stem. For example: “yiqqavu ha-mayim ve-tera’eh ha-yabbashah” (Genesis 1:9); likewise “va-yera Hashem” (Genesis 18), “va-yinnaḥem Hashem” (Genesis 6), “shavat va-yinnafash” (Exodus 31:17–18), “el beito va-yeḥanak” (II Samuel 17:23). All of these are to be understood as though they were from the hitpa‘el stem.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 6_Par: And there are nif‘al forms that are not found in the qal stem, such as nishba‘, nilḥam, nish‘an, nizhar, nikhna‘, and the like. These are explained as deriving from qal, as will be clarified at the end of the thirteenth principle.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 7_Par: 3. And know that just as there are verbs in the qal stem that are sometimes transitive and sometimes intransitive, as I have written, so too in this stem there are nif‘al forms that are sometimes transitive and sometimes intransitive. For example: “u-ve-navi nishmar” (Hosea 13) is transitive, whereas “ve-‘Amassa lo nishmar” (II Samuel 14) is intransitive, its meaning being that he did not guard himself. Likewise, “ve-nimkar bi-gneivato” (Exodus 22:2) is transitive, meaning that the court sold him, whereas “ve-nimkar lakh” (Leviticus 25:39) is intransitive, as the Sages of blessed memory explained—that he sells himself because of his distress.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 8_Par: And there are nif‘al forms that are derived from intransitive verbs, and these are very rare, such as “ve-niggash Mosheh” (Exodus 24:2), “ve-niqrav ba‘al ha-bayit” (Exodus 22:7), “ke-tsel kintoto nehelakhti” (Psalms 109:23), “erets noshavet” (Exodus 17), and the like — only a few.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 0_Par: The Ninth Principle. On the meaning of the pi‘el stem with dagesh:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 1_Par: Know that this third stem is also a parent stem and is called pi‘el ha-dagush, for the middle root letter (‘ayin ha-po‘el) is always geminated in it; and it is of four kinds:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 2_Par: 1. The first kind consists of verbs that are exclusive to this stem alone and do not occur in the qal stem. Their meaning corresponds to that of a transitive qal verb acting upon another, such as dibber, miher, tsivvah, and the like.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 3_Par: 2. The second kind consists of verbs that occur in both stems, but in the qal stem they are intransitive, such as shakhan, halakh, and the like.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 4_Par: And when they enter the pi‘el stem, they become transitive toward a second object, as in ohel shikken (Psalms 78), ‘arom hilləkhu beli levush (Job 24). Their meaning then corresponds to that of the hif‘il stem acting upon a second object, as I shall explain in its proper place.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 5_Par: 3. The third kind consists of verbs that likewise occur in both stems and are transitive in both of them. The only difference between them is that in the pi‘el stem they indicate greater force and continuity of the action than in the qal stem, such as shalakh and shillaḥ, shavar and shibber, and the like.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 6_Par: 4. The fourth kind consists of verbs that likewise occur in both stems and are intransitive in both of them; and even here the pi‘el form indicates greater intensity of the action than the qal, such as “u-se‘areikh tsimmeaḥ” (Ezekiel 16), “pittaḥ ha-semadar” (Song of Songs 7:13), which are equivalent to a pataḥ and a tsamaḥ. However, the leading grammarians do not concede that intransitive verbs exist in the pi‘el ha-dagush stem, for this stem was established only for transitive verbs. They therefore say that tsimmeaḥ and pittaḥ belong to the pa‘al stem, with the ḥiriq in place of a qibbuts, and that they are like tsummeaḥ and puttaḥ, just as “va-yisem ba-aron be-Mitsrayim” is like va-yussam.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 7_Par: Behold, there are found in this stem verbs that have no parallel in any of the other stems, namely verbs that indicate the reversal of an action. For example, “ve-dishnu et ha-mizbe’aḥ” (Numbers 4), which means the removal of the ashes; likewise, “tevu’ati tesharresh” (Job 30), meaning the uprooting of the roots; and “mesa‘ef pu’arah be-ma‘aratsah” (Isaiah 10), meaning the removal of the branches — and the like.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 8_Par: 5. And know that this occurs only with verbs that are derived from nouns, such as those I have mentioned, and as I shall further explain in the chapter on the categories. Moreover, you are not permitted to form such verbs from every noun-derived verb at will, but only from those that are found in Scripture. And this stem as well produced a derivative, which is called the pu‘al stem.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 0_Par: The Tenth Principle. On the elucidation of the meaning of the pu‘al stem:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 1_Par: 1. The fourth stem is called the pu‘al stem. It is a derivative of pi‘el and has only one meaning: it is always passive, effected by another—namely, its parent, the pi‘el stem, from which it receives its form. For this reason it too is geminated like its parent. For example, if you say of the parent sipper, kipper, you say of the derivative suppar, kuppar. And note that the agent—the one who tells or the one who makes atonement—is not mentioned; that is, it is not specified whether the doer is male or female, singular or plural. Therefore it is called a stem in which the name of the agent is not mentioned.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 2_Par: 2. And likewise with the hof‘al stem, which is derived from the hif‘il stem, for the law governing both of them is the same: they always receive their action from another. For this reason, neither of them has an imperative, for how could one command another in a passive form derived from transitive verbs, as I have written in this treatise in the eighth principle? And all the more so, they have no active form. Even the participle does not occur in pu‘al except in a few places where it functions as an adjective, such as “ve-ha-seneh einennu ukkal” (Exodus 3:2), “la-na‘ar ha-yullad” (Judges 13:8). These are adjectival forms, as is evident from the qamats vowel; and one cannot say that they are past tense forms with a qamats because of the end of the verse, for if that were so it would have had to say “ve-ha-seneh lo ukkal,” since the word ein is used only with nouns and not with verbs. Likewise, the he of the definite article in the word ha-yullad proves that it is not a past tense verb, for the definite article is never used with verbs. Therefore we must say that these are adjectival participles. In the hof‘al stem, however, neither participle nor adjective is ever found. The infinitive too is found in neither of them except in a few places, and never with the letters bekholam, as will be explained to you in the second treatise, principle two. Thus there remain in them only the past and the future.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 3_Par: 3. And some grammarians say that even in the future tense one should not use the pu‘al and hof‘al stems except in two persons, since the first-person forms are lacking from them. They say this because only one such form is found in Scripture, namely “mi-beten la-qever uval” (Job 10:19), which is a future form from the hof‘al stem of a verb with a quiescent initial yod. But it seems to me that for this reason one should not refrain from using them. For how many words do we use by way of reasoning even though they are not found explicitly in Scripture—and all the more so in cases like these, where at least one instance is found in Scripture. Why, then, should we not use them?
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 0_Pa: The Eleventh Principle. On the elucidation of the meaning of the hif‘il stem:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 1_Pa: The fifth stem is also a parent stem and is called hif‘il, and it too is of four kinds:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 2_Pa: 1. The first kind consists of verbs that are intransitive in the qal stem, and this stem renders them transitive toward a second object. For example: qam (“he rose”) becomes heqim (“he caused [someone] to rise”); yarad (“he went down”) becomes horid (“he brought down”). For this reason this stem was established. Accordingly, it appears most often in the class of verbs with a quiescent middle letter, which is the usual domain of intransitive verbs, as I wrote in the sixth principle. It also appears, though less frequently, with complete verbs, such as from shakhav and rakhav, yielding hishkiv and hirkiv—all of which are transitive toward a second object.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 3_Pa: 2. The second kind is when the qal stem is transitive toward a second object, and this stem makes it transitive toward a third. Thus, from the root akhal, which is transitive toward a second object, we say he’ekhīl, which is transitive toward a third. For example, “ha-ma’akhilkha man”: here there are three participants—the Holy One, blessed be He, who causes to eat; Israel, who eats; and the manna, which is eaten.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 4_Pa: 3. The third kind consists of verbs that are not found in the qal stem at all, such as hishkim, hishlikh, and the like. Their meaning nevertheless corresponds to that of this stem, as will be explained at the end of the thirteenth principle.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 5_Pa: 4. The fourth kind consists of verbs that are intransitive in the qal stem and also in this stem, such as “u-Far‘oh hiqriv” (Exodus 14:10), and “va-ya‘teq mi-sham” (Genesis 12:8), which are equivalent to qarav and ‘ataq. Ibn Ezra said that the object is omitted in these cases: in “u-Far‘oh hiqriv” the object maḥanehu (“his camp”) is lacking; and likewise in “va-ya‘teq mi-sham” the object oholoh (“his tent”) is lacking; and so too in other places. And there are verbs in this stem that in one context are intransitive and in another are transitive, such as “heḥepir Levanon qamal” (Isaiah 33:9), which is intransitive, but “yav’ish ve-yaḥpir” (Proverbs 10:22; 23:5), which is transitive; likewise “ve-khen et ha-‘ir lo hirḥiqu” (Genesis 44:4) is intransitive, whereas “hirḥiq mimennu et pesha‘einu” (Psalms 103) is transitive. Similarly, “ki ya‘ashir ish” (Psalms 49:17) is intransitive, while “birkat Hashem hi ta‘ashir” >(Proverbs 10) is transitive. And behold, this stem too produced a derivative, which is called the hof‘al stem.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 0_Pa: The Twelfth Principle. On the elucidation of the meaning of the hof‘al stem:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 1_Pa: The sixth stem is called the hof‘al stem, and it is a derivative of hif‘il; therefore it too has the prefixed he like it, and it is of two kinds:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 2_Pa: 1. The first kind is when the corresponding qal stem is intransitive, as in qam, from which comes huqam. Its meaning is the same as that of the pu‘al stem—namely, that it indicates an action performed upon it by another.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 3_Pa: 2. The second kind is when the corresponding qal stem is transitive; in that case this stem receives the action by means of an intermediary. For example, “hokhrat minḥah va-neseḵ” (Joel 2:14). Here there are three participants: the locust, the vine, and the offering. The locust is the one that cuts off; the vine is cut off; and as a result the offering is cut off. And all the remaining rules governing the hof‘al stem are the same as those governing its counterpart, the geminated pu‘al, as I have explained in its proper place.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 0_Pa: The Thirteenth Principle. On the elucidation of the meaning of the hitpa‘el stem:
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. [Printer’s error: The seventh stem is called the hitpa‘el stem.] I have already said that it is both a parent and a derivative—that is, both active and passive—because its actions are performed by the subject upon himself and not upon another, as in “ve-hitqaddishtem ve-hiyitem qedoshim” (Leviticus 20:7), meaning: you shall make yourselves holy. This is its essential meaning, and so too is the meaning of the nif‘al stem in its second kind, as I wrote in its proper place; see there.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Furthermore, I have another observation: sometimes this stem appears as though it were receiving an action, though in truth it is not so. For example, “ve-hitbarekh bilvavo” (Deuteronomy 29:18)—that is, he thinks in his heart that he is blessed, though he is not so. Likewise, “yesh mit‘asher ve-ein kol, mitroshesh ve-hon rav” (Proverbs 13:7)—that is, one presents himself as rich or as poor, though he is not so. And there are many similar cases.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. And know that this occurs only with intransitive verbs. In some of these you are permitted to form such usages even if they are not found explicitly in Scripture; however, take care not to do so with transitive verbs. The general rule is that this stem never acts upon another. Pay no heed to false claims that it is found in places where it is transitive, such as “ve-khol keli ‘ets titḥatta’u” (Numbers 31:20), “ve-hitnaḥaltem et ha-’arets” (Numbers 33:54), and the like; for these can readily be interpreted in a manner in which the subject acts upon itself, and there is no need here to elaborate further.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 4_Pa: 4. Moreover, there are verbs that occur only in the hitpa‘el stem, such as hitpallel, hitḥannen, and the like. These are to be interpreted as though they belonged to the qal stem. This is a major principle: any verb that is found only in one of the stems other than qal is to be explained as though it were from the qal stem. Thus nishba‘ (“swore”) and nilḥam (“fought”) in the nif‘al, and hishkim (“rose early”) and hishlikh (“cast”) in the hif‘il, are all to be understood in this manner, as I have explained in each of those cases.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 5_Pa: The First Treatise is concluded, in the Name of God, the First and the Last.
text.5_First Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 6_Pa: And in the Name of Him who is One, and none beside Him, I begin the Second Treatise.
text.6_Second Treatise, 0_Subject, 0_Paragrap: On the elucidation of the differences between each binyan and the others, with respect to the vowel patterns and the additional letters unique to each, which serve as identifying signs by which one may distinguish them from one another—whether complete or incomplete—and it, too, is divided into thirteen principles.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 0_Pa: The First Principle. On the vowel patterns of the Qal and Nif‘al binyanim in the complete verbs, and their identifying signs.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. The Qal conjugation is so called because it has no additional letter as a distinguishing sign beyond the three root letters, and it also contains no dagesh.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 2_Pa: The Perfect (Past) — throughout it, the first root letter (peh) is vowelled with qamats, except in the forms of the masculine and feminine plural, in which the qamats changes to a sheva because of the mem and nun at the end, and the accent is on the final syllable (milra‘), as in paqadtem, paqadten. This is the rule for every word whose first vowel is a qamats: when it is lengthened by an added syllable and the accent falls on the final syllable (milra‘), the qamats reverts to a sheva. The middle root letter (‘ayin) is vowelled with pataḥ in all forms, except in the masculine and feminine singular third person, where it has a sheva na‘, as in paqdu, paqedah. The reason is that if it were vowelled with pataḥ, it would have to be followed either by a sheva naḥ or by a dagesh, as is the rule after every short vowel. But here a sheva naḥ is impossible: for the plural requires a following vav with shuruq, and for the feminine singular an he with preceding qamats. Nor is a dagesh possible, for one cannot say paqdu or paqedah with a dagesh, since this conjugation is called qal, meaning “light,” that is, without dagesh.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 3_Pa: 2. Know that the third-person masculine singular (the “hidden” form) is found in three patterns: pa‘al, pa‘el, and pa‘ul. All three occur together in a single verse: “And Moses lo yakhól entered the Tent of Meeting, for the cloud shakhán was upon it, and the glory of the Lord malé the Tabernacle” (Exodus 40:35). In all the other forms of the perfect tense, the conjugations follow the regular paradigms. Thus, just as from shamar one says shamárti, shamárta, shamárnu, and so forth, so from khafáts one says khafátsa, khafátsi, and the like. The only exception is the masculine and feminine third-person forms: when they occur in pause, they return to their original vowel with a tsere, as in khafétsu and khafétsa. However, roots whose final letter is an alef retain a tsere in all forms of the perfect, as I shall mention later. The pattern pa‘ul has ḥolam in all forms of the perfect, except for the masculine and feminine third-person forms, where it has a sheva, as in yakhlu and yakhla. When these forms occur in pause, they return to a ḥolam, as in: “to bring forth the lice, but they lo yakhólu” (Exodus 8:14).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 4_Pa: 3. Know that the patterns pa‘al and pa‘ul generally occur only with **intransitive verbs**, such as zaqén (“was old”), malé (“was full”), ḥadélu (“they ceased”), and qamélu (“they withered”). From malé, however, transitive forms are also found. Likewise, all verbs whose roots are from the class naḥei lamed–alef and are intransitive appear in the pattern pa‘al, such as tamé (“was impure”) and yaré (“feared”). The root yatsa (“went out”) is an exception. The vowel sheva under a qamats is characteristic here, and only a few complete roots that are transitive appear in this pattern, such as ḥafáts, aháv, and akhál. The pattern pa‘ul, by contrast, is always derived from **intransitive verbs**, such as yakhól, yagór, and qatón, as in the verse: “Qatón have I become from all the kindnesses” (Genesis 32:10). Therefore, these verbs have neither a participle nor a passive form, as I explained in the First Treatise, Principle Five, Section Four. Instead, the **adjectival form** appears in place of both, using the perfect-tense pattern. Thus: “And Abraham was zaqén, advanced in days” (Genesis 24:1) — this is an adjective. “But it came to pass when Isaac had zaqén, and his eyes were dim” (Genesis 27:1) — here it is a perfect verb. “And Moses lo yakhól” — this too is a perfect verb. No adjectival form of yakhól is found in Scripture, yet our Rabbis of blessed memory used it adjectivally, saying eno yakhól (“he is unable”), enam yekholím (“they are unable”). All other verbal forms in this category follow a single consistent pattern, and there is no distinction among the three patterns.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 5_Pa: 4. The Participle (in Ashkenazic language: di gegen-vertige layt; in Latin: praesens). The first radical (peʾ) takes a ḥolam in all three persons, and the second radical (ʿayin) takes a tsere only in the singular, as in poqed. In the other forms it changes to a sheva (vocalized sheva: naʿ), according to its regular rule, as in poqedim, poqedah, poqedot. Know that the feminine form generally comes with a final tav and two segolim before it, as in poqedet. More rarely, it appears with a final heʾ, as in: halekhah hi (Jeremiah 3:6), hi shafṭah et Yisraʾel (Judges 4:4). I shall speak further about this in the Third Treatise, Principle Five, Section Two.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 6_Pa: 5. The Passive Participle The first radical (peʾ) takes a qamats in the singular, as in paqud. In the other forms it changes to a sheva, according to its rule, as I explained above with the past tense. In all of them the second radical (ʿayin) takes a shuruq, as in pequdim, pequdah, pequdot.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 7_Pa: The Infinitive (in Ashkenazic language: azn-bet-tiyete art; in German: Infinitiv) The first root letter (peʾ) takes a qamats, as in paqod. This occurs when the infinitive is in construct with the past or future, as in shamor tishmeron and halokh halakhta. When it is used in place of a command, the same rules apply (see my discussion in the first treatise, Sixth Principle). With prepositions, the qamats changes to a sheva, and sometimes this occurs even without prepositions, as in: "et avod ha-nisharim" (Deuteronomy 7:20) "et sefod ve-et raqod" (Ecclesiastes 3:4) The middle root letter (‘ayin) is vowelled with a cholem, and with prepositions it is pronounced with a chirik. The letter immediately following the preposition is soft, as in: ba-paqod and la-paqod. After a mem, a dagesh is added, as in mi-paqod. This rule compensates for the absence of the final nun in certain forms, as will be explained further in the chapter on poetry, Song 5.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 8_Pa: 6. The Imperative. (In Ashkenazic: di gebitende art; Latin: imperativus) In the singular, the first radical (peʾ) takes a sheva, and the second radical (ʿayin) takes a ḥolam, following the pattern of the infinitive when used with b-k-l-m. In the plural—and also in certain singular forms—the peʾ takes a ḥiriq, because the ʿayin takes a sheva, as will be explained in the Third Treatise, the Tenth Principle, section twenty. Likewise, when the singular imperative appears with an added heʾ at the end, the peʾ takes a ḥiriq, as in shikhvah ʿimmi (Genesis 39:12), shilḥah ha-naʿar (Genesis 43:8). This applies when the ʿayin has a pataḥ, as in shalaḥ, shakhav. But when the ʿayin has ḥolam, the peʾ takes a ḥataf-qamats, as in zekhorah li (Nehemiah 6:14). There are exceptions to these patterns, but I have no concern with them here.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 9_Pa: 7. The Future. (In Ashkenazic: di mit-künftige layt) You already know that its identifying sign is ʾe-i-t-n at the beginning, and that the vowel-patterns of the future follow those of the imperative. Take this rule firmly in hand for all the verb-forms, in all the root categories (gizrot): add the letters ʾe-i-t-n to the imperative, and you will obtain the future form. In this conjugation, the letters of ʾe-i-t-n always take ḥiriq. [First edition: And there is always a sheva naḥ after the ʾe-i-t-n, except for alef, which takes a segol, as in ʾefqod, because it is a guttural.]
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 10_P: 8. Know that the first-person forms (medabber baʿado), singular and plural, sometimes appear with an added heʾ at the end, as in ʾazkerah ʾElohim (Psalms 77:4), nishleḥah ʾanashim (Deuteronomy 1:22). The third-person forms (nistarim and nimtzaʾim) sometimes appear with an added nun at the end, as in lemaʿan yilmadun, shamor tishmerun. The rule governing this heʾ and nun applies to all the conjugations (binyanim) and to all the root-categories (gizrot), [First edition: and to all the gizrot except those of naḥei lamed-heʾ, in which an additional heʾ does not occur, unless the root heʾ is replaced by yod, as in va-ʾehemiyah (Psalms 77:4).]
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 11_P: 7. The Future. (In Ashkenazic: di mit-künftige layt) You already know that its identifying sign is ʾe-i-t-n at the beginning, and that the vowel-patterns of the future follow those of the imperative. Take this rule firmly in hand for all the verb-forms, in all the root categories (gizrot): add the letters e-i-t-n to the imperative, and you will obtain the future form. In this conjugation, the letters of ʾe-i-t-n always take ḥiriq. [First edition: And there is always a sheva naḥ after the ʾe-i-t-n, except for alef, which takes a segol, as in ʾefqod, because it is a guttural.]
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 12_P: 9. Know that there are verbs whose future forms sometimes appear with a ḥolam at the end and sometimes with a pataḥ, as in va-yishbot ha-man with a ḥolam (Joshua 5:12), and lamah tishbot ha-melakhah with a pataḥ (Nehemiah 6:3). There are also verbs that are always open with a pataḥ, and most of these are intransitive verbs (peʿalim ʿomdim), such as yishkav, yirkav, yishman, yeshurun va-yivʿat (Deuteronomy 32:15). But those that take a ḥolam are for the most part transitive verbs (peʿalim yotzʾim), except when the ʿayin of the root is an ʿayin or a ḥet, in which case they are always open with a pataḥ, whether they are transitive or intransitive, such as yishmaʿ, yishlaḥ. Likewise, when the ʿayin of the root is an ʿayin or a ḥet, as in tishḥaq lamo, tilʿag le-khol ha-goyim (Psalms 59:9), they are exceptions, even though they are intransitive verbs. Also among the exceptions are va-yinahem ʿalav (Isaiah 5:30), and mah ʾezʿam lo zaʿam Hashem (Numbers 23:8). All of these rules apply equally to the imperative, for the future and the imperative share the same vowel-patterns, as I wrote above in section 7.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 13_P: 10. The Nifʿal Conjugation It has an additional nun prefixed at the beginning, and it is light like its parent (qal), in that it has no dagesh as its identifying sign.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 14_P: The Past. Throughout, the prefixed nun takes ḥiriq at the beginning and a following sheva naḥ, and the second radical (ʿayin) is open with pataḥ, as in nifqad, nifqadet. All of its vocalization follows the patterns of its parent, the qal conjugation.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 15_P: 11. The Participle. It too has an additional prefixed nun, like the past tense, but the second radical (ʿayin) takes a qamats in all forms, as in nifqad, nifqadim, nifqadah, as in ruaḥ nishberah (Psalms 51:19). It is always accented milraʿ. But the form ʾaḥat me-henah lo nishberah (Psalms 34:21), which is accented milʿel, is a past tense feminine form, and it occurs in this way only in a pause (hefseq). Outside of a pause it takes a sheva, as in nishberah qiryat tohu and similar forms (Isaiah 24:10)
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 16_P: The Passive. It does not exist here, as you already know.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 17_P: (First edition: 12.) The Infinitive It appears with the loss of the nun of the conjugation, and the first radical (peʾ) is always dageshed to indicate the missing nun. For this reason it was necessary to place an additional heʾ before the peʾ, as in aḥarei hipared Lot (Genesis 13:14). This is in order to strengthen the dagesh, since a strong dagesh cannot occur at the beginning of a word, as will be explained in the chapter “Shirah,” in the fifth song.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 18_P: And even with the prefix letters b-k-l-m, the additional heʾ appears, as in be-haqhel ha-ʿedah (Numbers 17:7). Only in a few places is the heʾ lacking, such as be-ʿatef ʿolel (Lamentations 2:11), le-ʿanot mipnei (Exodus 10:3), and u-ve-khashlo ʾal yagel libbekha (Proverbs 24:17).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 19_P: 12 (First edition: 13). The Imperative It always appears with an added heʾ, as in hippared naʾ me-ʿalay (Genesis 13:9). But the future does not require the heʾ, because the ʾe-i-t-n letters at the beginning produce a strong dagesh. The general rule is that in this conjugation the nun, the heʾ, and the letters of ʾe-i-t-n all take a ḥiriq, even the alef of ʾe-i-t-n (for the most part), as in ʾanokhi ʾishavaʿ (Genesis 21:24). This is not the case in qal, as I explained earlier. And the first radical (peʾ) always has a dagesh with a qamats, except when the peʾ is one of the guttural letters ʾalef–ḥet–ʿayin–resh, in which case the heʾ and the letters of ʾe-i-t-n take a tsere, as in heʾasef, yeʿavor, and the like, as will be explained in the chapter “Shirah,” in the ninth song.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 0_Pa: The Second Principle. On the elucidation and vocalization of the conjugation Piʿel ha-dagush and of Piʿel from the complete roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 1_Pa: The Piʿel conjugation is identified by a dagesh in the ʿayin of the root throughout the entire conjugation.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 2_Pa: 1. The entire past tense has the first radical (peʾ) with a ḥiriq, and the second radical (ʿayin) open with a pataḥ, except for the third-person masculine singular, in which the ʿayin is for the most part with a tsere, as in ʾizzen, ḥiqer, tiqqen. It is also found with a pataḥ, as in va-ʾibbed ve-shibber beriḥeha (Lamentations 2:9), and similar cases are few. The third-person masculine plural and the feminine singular have a sheva naʿ, as is its rule under a letter with a dagesh, as in piqqedu, piqqedah.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 3_Pa: (First edition: 2) The Participle and the Passive They always appear with an added prefixed mem with a sheva at the beginning. In the participle there is a pataḥ after it, as in mefaqed. In the passive there are three vowels after it, as in mefuqqad. Your mnemonic for this is MPMʾP. The second radical (ʿayin) of the root, in the singular participle, takes a tsere, and in the other forms it takes a sheva naʿ, as in mefaqed, mefaqedim, and so forth. In the passive, in all forms, the ʿayin takes a qamats, as in mefuqqad, mefuqqadim, and so forth.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 4_Pa: 2 (First edition: 3). The Infinitive The first radical (peʾ) has a pataḥ, and the second radical (ʿayin) has a tsere, as in paqed [as in gaddel peraʿ (Numbers 6:25)]. The prefix letters b-k-l-m take a sheva, except for mem, which always takes a ḥiriq, as in be-feqed, ke-feqed, li-feqed, mi-feqed.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 5_Pa: 12 (First edition: 13). The Imperative It always appears with an added heʾ, as in hippared naʾ me-ʿalay (Genesis 13:9). But the future does not require the heʾ, because the e-i-t-n letters at the beginning produce a strong dagesh. The general rule is that in this conjugation the nun, the heʾ, and the letters of ʾe-i-t-n all take a ḥiriq, even the alef of ʾe-i-t-n (for the most part), as in ʾanokhi ʾishavaʿ (Genesis 21:24). This is not the case in qal, as I explained earlier.
