And the first radical (peʾ) always has a dagesh with a qamats, except when the peʾ is one of the guttural letters ʾalef–ḥet–ʿayin–resh, in which case the heʾ and the letters of ʾe-i-t-n take a tsere, as in heʾasef, yeʿavor, and the like, as will be explained in the chapter “Shirah,” in the ninth song.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 6_Pa: 3. And take this rule firmly in hand for every verbal pattern in which the participle appears with the addition of a mem: the letters e-i-t-n are vocalized as in Hif‘il, with a reduced vowel under the middle root letter; and there I will reveal to you the reason.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 7_Pa: 4. And if the middle root letter is one of the letters RaʿA, then in most cases the dagesh is removed, and the vowel is transferred to the letter before it. If that vowel is a hiriq, it is changed to a tsere; and if it is a pataḥ, it is changed to a qamats, as I will explain in the chapter on poetry, in the ninth poem.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 8_Pa: But the letters he and ḥet, although they generally do not receive a dagesh, do not have the power to cause the dagesh to drop into the preceding letter, as in shaher, kḥer, maher. Instead, they appear with tsere, as in nahalta ve‘ozekha (Exodus 15:13), and similar cases are few. Likewise, in the pattern Hitpa‘el, as in mityahadim, mitlaḥashim, they appear with a pataḥ.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 9_Pa: The Pattern Paʿal Its identifying sign is a dagesh in the middle root letter throughout the entire pattern, like its prototype.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 10_P: The Past Throughout, the first root letter has three dots, as in pakad, pakadta, and so on; in all other vowels it follows the pattern of its prototype.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 11_P: The Participle For the singular, it is like the past tense, except that the middle root letter takes a qamats, as in pakad. The plural is pekadim, and so on, as I explained in the First Treatise, in the Tenth Principle.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 12_P: The Passive and the imperative do not exist in this pattern. The infinitive, which is found only rarely in it, likewise has three dots under the first root letter, as in ganav, ganavti. And in forms where the final root letter is quiescent, it bears all its affliction, as in et kol ‘anvato; and there is no more. Moreover, forms with the prefixed letters bekholam are not found in it.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 13_P: The Future In this pattern, the e-i-t-n letters appear with a sheva, like its prototype, and the first root letter has three dots, as in the past tense, as in efkod, yifkod, and so on. But when the middle root letter is a guttural or a resh, the kubuts changes to a ḥolam throughout the entire pattern, as in ki lo forash (Numbers 15:34), and umarak ve-shataf (Leviticus 6:21), as will be explained in the chapter on poetry, in the ninth poem.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 0_Pa: The Third Principle: On the elucidation of the vowels of the patterns Hif‘il and Paʿal for strong roots, and their identifying signs.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. The Pattern Hif‘il The past tense throughout has a he with a hiriq at the beginning, as in hifkid, with stress on the final syllable. [But hifkidu and hifkidah are both stressed on the penultimate syllable.] (The hiriq under the middle root letter occurs only in the masculine singular, the masculine plural, and the feminine plural, as in hifkid, hifkidu, hifkidah, and they are penultimately stressed; but hifkidu and hifkidah are both penultimately stressed.)
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 2_Pa: And in the other persons, a pataḥ appears in place of the hiriq to lighten the vocalization, because of the multiplicity of vowels, as in hifkadta, hifkadti, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 3_Pa: The Participle It is formed with the addition of a mem with a pataḥ at the beginning; and the passive with a kubuts; and after both of them there is a quiescent sheva, as in mafqid, mufqad. Its mnemonic sign is mefaʿal–mefuʿal. And in every participle the middle root letter has a long hiriq, and in every passive it has a long qamats.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 4_Pa: 2. The Infinitive It has a he with a pataḥ at the beginning, in order to distinguish it from the past tense, and the middle root letter is usually with a tsere, as in ve-hakhbed et libbo. But with the prefixed letters bekholam, it takes a hiriq, as in lehakṭin eifah and ulehagdl sheqel.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 5_Pa: 3. The Imperative For the singular, the middle root letter has a tsere, as in hafqed et ha-Levi’im (Numbers 1:50). But when it appears with the addition of a he at the end, the middle root letter takes a hiriq, as in ha’azinah, haqshivah. And the plural and the feminine singular always take a hiriq, as in hifkidu, hifkidi. And for the feminine plural, hafqednah; and this is said by way of reasoning, for it is not found in Scripture.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 6_Pa: 3. The Future You already know that the letters e-i-t-n are placed upon the imperative, as in afqid, yafqid. And know that it would properly have been ha’afqid, ha-yafqid, with the he of Hif‘il; but they dropped it in order to lighten the vowels, and placed a pataḥ under the e-i-t-n letter. Likewise in the participle they dropped the he, saying mafqid, whereas it should properly have been mehfaqid; and similarly the passive mufqad, whereas it should have been mehfuqad, just as in le-arba‘tam mehaqtsu‘ot (Ezekiel 46:22). And for the most part, the middle root letter with e-i-t-n takes a hiriq, except in a few cases where it comes with tsere, following the pattern of the imperative, as in yikhret Hashem (Psalms 12:4). And with the conversive vav, it is always with a tsere, as in va-yavdel Elohim (Genesis 1:4).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 7_Pa: The Pattern Hif‘al Its identifying sign is the addition of a he, like its prototype.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 8_Pa: The Past Throughout, the he appears with a ḥataf-qamats, as in hakkēret minḥah; or with three dots, as in ve-hishlikh mekhon miqdasho (Daniel 8:11). In forms where the first root letter is quiescent and where the middle root letter is quiescent, the he comes with a shuruq, as in va-Yosef hurad (Genesis 39:1). For these three vowels are siblings, and they frequently replace one another, especially in the patterns Paʿal and Hif‘al.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 9_Pa: (In the first edition: vav) The Participle, the Passive, and the Imperative do not occur in it. And the small amount of Infinitive found in it is likewise with a ḥataf-qamats, and the middle root letter (the ʿayin ha-poʿal) in a tsere, as in: ve-ha-melaḥ lo himlaḥt (Ezekiel 16:4), ve-ha-ḥotel lo ḥittalt (ibid.). And with an added he: redah and hashkēvah (ibid. 32:19). And with the prefix letters be-kholam it is not found at all.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 10_P: The Future The letters e-i-t-n appear with a ḥataf-qamats, to indicate the identifying sign of the pattern, as in kalil tuqṭar (Leviticus 6:15). And if the first root letter is a guttural, the first root letter is vocalized with a qamats and the middle root letter with a ḥataf-qamats, as in ya‘amod ḥai (Leviticus 16:10), yeḥoram kol rekhusho (Ezra 10:8).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 0_Pa: The Fourth Principle: On the elucidation of the vowels of the pattern Hitpa‘el for strong roots, and its identifying signs.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 1_Pa: The Pattern Hitpa‘el Its identifying signs are a he, a tav, and a dagesh in the middle root letter — thus there are three identifying signs.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 2_Pa: 1. The Past Throughout, it has a he with a hiriq, followed by a tav with a quiescent sheva, and after it three root letters. The first root letter has a pataḥ throughout the entire pattern, and the middle root letter takes a dagesh, as in hitpaqed. But when it is one of the guttural letters or a resh, it takes a qamats, as in hitpa’er ‘alai (Exodus 8:5), and hitbarekh bilvavo (Deuteronomy 29:18), and similar cases. And all its reading and vocalization follow the pattern Paʿal with a dagesh.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 3_Pa: The Participle It is formed with the addition of a mem with a hiriq at the beginning, followed by a tav with a quiescent sheva. Here too they dropped the he, for it would properly have been mehitpaqed, just as I wrote regarding the e-i-t-n letters in the pattern Hif‘il.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 4_Pa: The Passive It does not occur in this pattern.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 5_Pa: 2. The Infinitive It is like the past tense, and the he does not drop, even when combined with the prefixed letters bekholam.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 6_Pa: And likewise the Imperative It always appears with the he; but in the future tense the he drops, as in the participle, and the letters e-i-t-n are vocalized with a hiriq, as in the pattern Qal and in the pattern Nif‘al. And for the most part the middle root letter has a tsere, as in ethalekh lifnei Hashem (Psalms 116:9); and in a few cases with a pataḥ, as in al tit’hader lifnei melekh (Proverbs 25:6).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 7_Pa: 3. It is known that in this entire pattern the tav of Hitpa‘el normally comes before the first root letter, as I have written. But when the first root letter is one of the letters zayin, samekh, shin, or tsadi, it has other rules. With a samekh and a shin, the tav comes after the first root letter, as in va-yishtamer ḥuqqot ‘Omri (Micah 6:16), and va-yistabbel he-ḥagav (Ecclesiastes 12:5). With a tsadi, it changes into a tet, as in u-ma nitzṭaddaq (Genesis 44:16). And with a zayin, it changes into a dalet, as in hizdamaneton le-me’amar (Daniel 2:9).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 8_Pa: 4. And it seems to me that no proof should be brought from hizdamaneton, for two reasons. First, because it is an Aramaic word. Second, because in the Masoretic tradition it is found as: written hizdamaneton, read hizdamaneton; and it is one of the two words that are read with a dalet but not written with it. It thus appears that they were in doubt whether the dalet ought to be written or not. And although we find that the masters of the Talmud were accustomed to do so, saying nizdaman lo tsevi, nizdaqen ha-din, this is not done in the Hebrew language, for thus our Rabbis of blessed memory said: the language of Scripture is one thing, and the language of the Mishnah is another (Avodah Zarah 58b).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 9_Pa: 5. Moreover, when I searched throughout all of Scripture, I did not find any root whose first root letter is zayin from which the pattern Nif‘al is built with its second meaning, as explained in the First Treatise, in the Eighth Principle, section two. And the word raḥatsu hizakku (Isaiah 1:16) you will find in the Book of Composition; likewise ve-hitshotatnah ba-gederot (Jeremiah 49:3) you will find there as well.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 10_P: And now I shall turn to explain the defective roots, and afterward the quiescent roots, and afterward the doubled roots, briefly.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 0_Pa: The Fifth Principle: On the elucidation of the class of roots deficient in the first root letter, such as nigash.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. The Pattern Qal The past tense, the participle, and the passive appear in full form, and the infinitive as well, for the most part, as in nafol tipol lefanav (Esther 6:13), halokh ve-naso‘a. Likewise, the imperative for the most part appears in full form, as in natsor banai, and lifnei hitgalla‘ ha-riv netosh (Proverbs 17:14), and nidru ve-shallemu (Psalms 76:12), naflu ‘alenu (Hosea 9:8). But there are a few roots in which the nun is missing in the infinitive, and in its place an additional tav appears at the end; these are nagash, naga‘, nata‘, nafaḥ, and there are almost no others, as in be-gishat Yisra’el (Numbers 8:19), laga‘at bakh (2 Samuel 14:10), lifḥot ‘alav (Ezekiel 22:20), ‘et lita‘at (Ecclesiastes 3:2). But know that these forms occur only with the prefixed letters bekholam; without bekholam they never occur with the loss of the nun and the addition of a final tav. And likewise in the imperative, the nun is missing in some of these, as in gash hal’ah (Genesis 19:9), ve-ga‘ el ‘atsmo (Job 2:5), u-feḥi ba-harugim (Ezekiel 37:9). And from nashal: shal na‘alekha. But from nata‘ it is not said ta‘.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. However, the future tense for the most part comes with the loss of the nun and a dagesh in the middle root letter to indicate it, as in anash yigash; and all of them are with a pataḥ or with a ḥolam, as in epol, yipol. A few are found that come in full form, as in ve-torotav yintseru (Psalms 105:45), ha-yintor le-‘olam (Jeremiah 3:5). But when the middle root letter is a guttural, it always comes like the strong roots, as in lo tina’af, and ve-leḥem setarim yin‘am (Proverbs 9:17), ha-yinaq pere (Job 6:5). Except for a few that come with the e-i-t-n letters in tsere in place of the nun, as in mi yiḥet ‘alenu (Jeremiah 21:13), and va-tehom kol ha-‘ir (Ruth 1:19), whose roots are naḥat and naham.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. The Pattern Nif‘al I shall include it within the pattern Paʿal with dagesh.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 4_Pa: The Patterns Paʿal and Puʿal With roots deficient in the first letter nun, know that because these two patterns always have a dagesh in the middle root letter, as you already know, they therefore come in this class only in full form. For there is no way to drop the nun and place a dagesh in the middle root letter in its stead, since it is already dageshed; and two dageshim cannot occur in a single letter. Nor can one dagesh indicate two things. Therefore, they always appear in full form.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 5_Pa: 4. And know that in this class there is no difference between verbs that belong to the pattern Nif‘al and those that belong to the pattern Paʿal, for both of them have a dagesh in the middle root letter: in Nif‘al because of the loss of the root nun, and in Paʿal as the identifying sign of the pattern. As in ve-lo nikar shoa‘ lifnei dal (Job 34:19), which is a past tense of Nif‘al; and nikar elidam ito (1 Samuel 23:7), which is a past tense of the pattern Paʿal. And so in every place you will recognize, according to the sense of the context, which form is Nif‘al and which is Paʿal.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 6_Pa: 5. The Patterns Hif‘il and Hif‘al With roots deficient in the first letter nun, both patterns are identical in their vocalization to the strong roots, except that the root nun is missing and a dagesh appears in the middle root letter in its place throughout the entire pattern.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 7_Pa: The Past higgish, which properly would have been haniggish; and likewise the participle magish, the passive mugash, and the infinitive and the imperative hagish with a tsere; higgishu, higgishi with hiriq. Likewise with the prefixed letters bekholam, it is with a hiriq, as in behaggish, kehaggish, and so on. The e-i-t-n forms are agish, yagish.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 8_Pa: The Pattern Hif‘al Throughout, the he appears with a ḥataf-qamats, for the dagesh is more clearly perceived after a kubuts than after a ḥataf-qamats.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 9_Pa: The Past huggash, huggashta, and so on. It has no participle, passive, or imperative. The infinitive is huggash, as in haggēd haggēd li (Ruth 2:11), and with the prefixed letters bekholam it is not found. The future tense is uggash, yuggash, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 10_P: 6. The Pattern Hitpa‘el It too appears in full form, for the reason I wrote regarding the pattern Paʿal.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 11_P: 6. And know that there are roots whose first root letter is yod that behave according to the class of roots deficient in the first letter nun; and they are called roots deficient in the first letter yod, and not quiescent first-letter yod roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 12_P: I say that this applies only when the middle root letter has a tsere, as in yatsag, yatsaq, yatsa‘, yatsar, yatsat. Thus you say yatsag gevulot ‘amim (Deuteronomy 32:8), atsigah na ‘immekh min ha-‘am asher (Genesis 33:15), ki atsokh mayim ‘al tsame (Isaiah 44:3), ve-’atsi‘ah She’ol hinnekh (Psalms 139:8), be-terem etzorkha ba-beten yeda‘tikh (Jeremiah 1:5), and va-yatsat esh be-Tsiyon (Lamentations 4:11). In all of these, the tsere is dageshed in place of the yod of the first root letter. But the root yatsa is an exception. Therefore I say hiqifu yemei ha-mishteh (Job 1:5), and likewise lo heniyaḥ adam (Psalms 105:14), for these are dageshed, their roots being naqaf and nuaḥ, and not yaqaf or yanuḥ. I will speak further about this among the quiescent first-letter yod roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 13_P: 7. And there is one root whose first root letter is lamed whose infinitive, imperative, and future tense for the most part follow the pattern of roots deficient in the first letter nun. This is the root laqach. From it you say the infinitive qaḥat, be-qaḥat, laqaḥat; and the imperative qaḥ, qḥu, qḥi, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 14_P: And in the future tense it comes with a dagesh, as in eqach, yiqach, tiqach; the dagesh stands in place of the lamed of the first root letter. No other lamed is found to drop except this one, and this is because of the frequent use of this root. And sometimes even the dagesh itself is dropped, and this occurs only when the middle root letter has a sheva, as in va-yiqḥu elekha (Numbers 19:2), and ve-eqḥah pat leḥem (Genesis 18:5). In both of these the qof is soft, just as from the root nasa‘ it is said va-yis‘u and va-yaḥanu (Numbers 33:6), and va-yis’u oto banav (Genesis 50:13), where the samekh and the shin are soft because of their frequent use. And there are those who say that the language of “taking” has two roots, laqach and naqach: the past tenses and participles come from laqach and naqach, and the future tenses from naqach, just as the language of “going” likewise has two roots, halakh and yalakh: the past tenses and participles come from halakh, and the future tenses from yalakh, as in elekh, yelekh, and so on. But the first explanation is the more correct.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 0_Pa: The Sixth Principle: On the elucidation of the class of roots quiescent in the first letter, aleph and yod, such as amar and yashav.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. The Pattern Qal It appears in full form up through the future tense; and in the future tense the root aleph becomes quiescent, as in yomar, tomar, nomar. But in first-person singular, the aleph is dropped and a quiescent vav comes in its place, as in omar el Eloah; this is so that two alephs should not come together, that is, to avoid saying a’omar. And when yomar, tomar, nomar come with the conversive vav, the pataḥ returns to a segol and the stress shifts to the penultimate, as in va-yomer, va-tomer, va-nomer. And when they come again without it, they return to their original rule with a pataḥ and final stress, as in yomar, tomar; except for va-ya‘an Iyov va-yomer and similar cases, all of which are penultimately stressed.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. And know that all the other patterns come according to the manner of the strong roots, and the aleph does not become quiescent in them; only that the vowels change in some of them because of the aleph, which is guttural. And likewise with the other guttural letters aleph, ḥet, he, ‘ayin, the hiriq of the nun of Nif‘al and of the he of Hif‘il changes to segol (and the letter following the nun or the he takes a ḥataf-segol), as in ne’ekhal, he’ekhil, as will be explained in the chapter on poetry, in the thirteenth poem. And there are also roots whose first letter is aleph that come in full form even in the pattern Qal, such as from asaf and asar, where one says e’esof and e’esor. The reason is that since these are not used frequently, they were not strict about them.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. The Classes of Roots Quiescent in the First Letter Yod such as yashav.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 4_Pa: The Pattern Qal It comes in full form up through the infinitive, the infinitive included, when it is joined to verbal forms, as in yarad, yaradnu, yashuv, eshav. But when it is not joined to verbal forms, it appears with the loss of the yod and with the addition of a final tav, as in shevet, redet, da‘at, and similar forms; and this occurs even without the prefixed letters bekholam, as I wrote above.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 5_Pa: 4. The Imperative It too appears with the loss of the yod, as in shev, shevu, and so on. (In the first edition: and with the addition of a final he, shevah; and in pause with a tsere, redah; and when joined by maqqef or adjacent to a short word, with a segol and penultimate stress, as in lekh na.) There is no difference between this imperative and the imperative of roots deficient in the first letter nun; therefore be careful not to confuse them. But the e-i-t-n letters distinguish between the two classes: for in roots deficient in the first letter nun, the e-i-t-n letters are vocalized with a hiriq and a dagesh follows, as in yigash, tigash, and so on; whereas in this class they take a tsere, which is a full vowel indicating the quiescent yod that is not written, as in eshav, yeshav, and so on. And there are cases where the yod is written with a tsere, as in eilekh sholel (Micah 1:8), [ha-smol ve-eimanah (Genesis 13:9)], and similar cases are few.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 6_Pa: 5. And for the most part, when the yod is written, the e-i-t-n letters take a hiriq and the middle root letter has a pataḥ, as in einaq, yinaq; e’irash, yirash; eitav, yitav; eishan, yishan. And there are cases that come with a dagesh in place of the quiescent yod, as from yatsaq: atsokh ruḥi ‘al zar‘ekha; and from yatsar: be-terem etzorkha. And they called these “roots deficient in the first letter yod” and not “roots quiescent in the first letter yod”, for in the future tense they proceed according to the manner of roots deficient in the first letter nun, as I explained regarding roots deficient in the first letter nun. And although I have searched throughout all my books of grammar to find a reason for this, I did not find one.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 7_Pa: 6. And to me the reason appears to be this: because the letters tsadi and samekh are close to one another in point of articulation and pronunciation, especially when the tsadi is not dageshed, so much so that many people do not distinguish between them, and especially all the people of France. For if we were to say from yatsav, yatsaq, and yatsag: etsav, etsaq, tetsag, according to the rule of roots quiescent in the first letter yod, it would sound as though it were esav, yesag, tesag. Therefore the tsere was dageshed in order to strengthen its pronunciation. And this is a great rule in grammar: when a dagesh comes in place of a missing letter, that word is called one of the deficient roots; but when one of the full vowels comes in its place, that word is called one of the quiescent roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 8_Pa: 7. The Pattern Nif‘al The Past Throughout, the nun appears with a quiescent vav as a ḥolam in place of the root yod, as in noda‘, noda‘at, noda‘ti, and so on. Likewise in the participle: noda‘, noda‘im, and so on. But in the rest of the pattern the vav is mobile, and all its vocalization is like that of the strong roots, as from yada‘: hoda‘. And the e-i-t-n forms are oda‘, yoda‘. And the aleph is always with a hiriq, contrary to the usual rule, for its normal vowel is generally segol; yet this form never comes with a segol, and I do not know the reason for this. And the yod was changed to a vav because the dagesh is perceived more clearly in a vav than in a yod.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 9_Pa: 8. The Pattern Hif‘il — The Past Throughout, the he appears with a ḥolam in place of the root yod, as in hoshiv, hoshavta, and so on. And likewise throughout the entire pattern, the prefixed letters at the beginning take a ḥolam: in the participle moshiv, in the infinitive and the imperative hoshiv, and in the future oshiv, yoshiv, toshiv. Except in the passive, where the mem is always with a shuruq or a kubuts in every passive form, whether of strong roots or of those not strong (as in mufqad, mushav). And a few cases are found where the mem has a ḥataf-qamats, as in shesh mashzar (Exodus 26:1), zoveaḥ mashḥit (Malachi 1:14). And the vocalization of the middle root letter in this entire pattern is the same as in the strong roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 10_P: 9. Nevertheless, know that those future forms which I wrote about in the pattern Qal, in which the e-i-t-n letters sometimes take hiriq with the root yod written, likewise for the most part occur in this pattern as well with the yod written, but with a tsere before it. Thus from yatav it is said va-le-Avram heitiv ba‘avurah (Genesis 12:16); from yanaq: ve-tinaq lakh et ha-yeled (Exodus 2:7); from yaman: im ha-smol ve-eimanah (Genesis 13:9); and from yalal: espedah ve-eililah (Micah 1:8).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 11_P: 10. And the Participle: the mem has a tsere in all forms, as in metiv, metivim, metivah. But not so in roots quiescent in the middle letter, where only the singular has a tsere and the rest have a sheva, as in mevin, mevinim, and so on. And likewise the imperative, the infinitive, and the e-i-t-n forms have a quiescent yod after the tsere.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 12_P: 11. The Pattern Pu‘al The he appears with shuruq, as in va-Yosef hurad; and likewise with roots quiescent in the middle letter, as in huqam; and with doubled roots, as in hutav. In all three, the he has shuruq, and there is no difference between them in vocalization. However, in the other persons of the past tense there is a difference between the doubled roots and the roots quiescent in the first letter yod and those quiescent in the middle letter vav.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 13_P: And this difference lies in the dagesh, as will be explained in this treatise, in the Twelfth Principle, section eight.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 14_P: 12. The Pattern Hitpa‘el This entire pattern appears in full form, as from yalad: va-yityaldu (Numbers 1:18), and from ya‘ats: va-yitya‘atsu (Psalms 83:4). And sometimes the yod is changed into a mobile vav, as from yada‘: be-hitvada‘ Yosef (Genesis 45:1), and from yada: ve-hitvada ‘alav (Leviticus 16:21).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 0_Pa: The Seventh Principle: On the elucidation of the class of roots quiescent in the middle letter vav.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 1_Pa: Know that every root whose middle letter is a vav is quiescent in all patterns, as from qum one says qam, qamta, and so on. Except when the final root letter is he, in which case the vav is mobile in all patterns, as from avah: otah nafshi (Micah 7:1); from qavah: qiviti Hashem (Psalms 130:5); from ravah: harveh et ha-aretz (Isaiah 55:10); from tsavah: tsiviti otkha (Exodus 29:35); and from ‘avah: ‘ivvatah veshti (Esther 1:16). In these, the vav never becomes quiescent. And there are five roots whose final letter is not he in which the vav never becomes quiescent, and they are: gava‘, shava‘, ‘avat, ‘aval, ‘avar. However, gava‘ appears only in the pattern Qal, as in ki gava‘ Aharon (Numbers 20:29), and va-yigva‘ va-yamot (Genesis 25:17). And shava‘ is found only in the pattern Paʿal with a dagesh: shava‘, shava‘ta, shava‘ti. And ‘avat is found in Paʿal, Nif‘al, and Hitpa‘el, as in le-‘avvet adam (Lamentations 3:36), ben na‘avot ha-mardut (1 Samuel 20:30), and ve-hit‘u oto anshei ha-ḥayil (Ecclesiastes 12:3). And ‘aval and ‘avar are found only in Paʿal, as in mi-kaf me‘avel ve-ḥometz (Psalms 71:4), ha-shoḥad ye‘aver ‘einei ḥakhamim (Exodus 23:8). All the rest are quiescent vav roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 2_Pa: 1. The Pattern Qal In the past tense, the first root letter has a qamats, as in qam, to indicate the quiescent vav, even though it is not the usual function of qamats to indicate a vav (that role properly belongs to a ḥolam). Here it was changed to a qamats in order to make this Qal form conform to the other Qal past tenses, in all of which the first root letter has a qamats, except for doubled roots, as will be explained in the Twelfth Principle of this treatise. And an aleph is found written after the qamats in the word ve-qa’am sha’on (Hosea 10:14), where it is quiescent. And it appears as mobile in the word ve-ra’amah ve-yashvah (Zechariah 14:10), and these two alephs stand in place of a vav. Likewise in the third-person plural and feminine, the first root letter has a qamats and the stress is penultimate, to indicate the quiescent vav, as in qamu, qamah. But in the other persons, the first root letter has a pataḥ, as in qamta, qamti, and so on. This is because of the quiescent sheva that belongs to every Qal past tense: if the first root letter were with a qamats, the sheva would not be quiescent but mobile, as will be explained in the chapter on poetry, in the eighth poem. And the past tense also comes with a tsere according to the pattern Paʿal, as in ka’asher met Aharon (Deuteronomy 32:50), ki metu kol ha-anashim (Exodus 4:19), and likewise kenim anakhnu (Genesis 42:11), madua‘ atem lanim neged ha-ḥomah (Nehemiah 13:21). And according to the pattern Pu‘al: ha-boker or (Genesis 44:3), ki oru ‘einai (1 Samuel 14:29), and similar cases are few.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 3_Pa: 2. The Participle Throughout, the first root letter has a qamats, and there is no difference between the participle and the past tense in the masculine singular, as in ba aḥikha be-mirmah (Genesis 27:35), which is past tense, and anokhi ba elekha be-‘av he-‘anan (Exodus 19:9), which is a participle. But in the feminine there is a difference: the past tense has penultimate stress, as in ve-Raḥel ba’ah (Genesis 29:9), whereas the participle has final stress, as in ve-hinneh Raḥel bito ba’ah (ibid., v. 6). And it also comes with a tsere according to the pattern Paʿal, as in met atah; and according to the pattern Pu‘al, as in tov tovim.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 4_Pa: 3. The Passive And the infinitive and the imperative: for the most part the middle root letter has a shuruq.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 6_Pa: The Imperative qum, qera; and likewise the passive. But we cannot form it from qum, for it is an intransitive verb; rather, we form it from sum, which is a transitive verb, and we say sum, sumim, as in ‘al pi Avshalom haytah shumah, shumah, shumot. And thus the infinitive and the imperative are found with a ḥolam following the manner of doubled roots, as in qum yaqumu devarai, por hitporerah erets, mot hitmotetah erets. And the imperative likewise, as in ve-shuv elai ne’um Hashem, mol et benei Yisra’el.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 7_Pa: 4. The Future The e-i-t-n letters take a qamats to indicate the vav of the middle root letter, as in aqum, yaqum, and so on. And the vav with a shuruq is not the middle root letter, but rather a connective vav, as in efqod, yifqod, and so on. And there are those who say that it is a root letter, and their proof is from yaqumu, taqumu; for if the vav were not a root letter, we would say yaqmu, taqmu, following the pattern of yifqedu, tifqedu, which have no vav.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 8_Pa: 5. There are also cases that come with a ḥolam, as in ve-al taqots. And likewise in the Masoretic tradition: bal yaḥus, taḥum with ḥolam, except for one case with a shuruq, lo taḥus ‘einam; and every aḥus like it is with a shuruq. And in pause, the future tense always comes with a ḥolam, as in yeḥi Re’uven ve-al yamut, and u-sheloshim shanah va-yamot. But when they are not in pause, the ḥolam returns to a ḥataf-qamats, especially with the conversive vav, as in va-yaqam Avraham va-yishtaḥu le-‘am ha-aretz, and va-yiqots Mo’av. And likewise without the conversive vav, when joined to a short word, as in yeshev na appekha ve-ḥamatkha, teshev na nefesh ha-yeled. And the second qamats in all these cases is called a ḥataf-qamats; this will be explained to you in the chapter on poetry, in the eleventh poem.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 9_Pa: 6. The Pattern Nif‘al — The Past In the third-person forms, the nun has a qamats, in the three forms of the concealed persons, as in navon, navonu, navonah. But in the other persons, the qamats changes to a sheva, as is its rule, and the ḥolam changes to a shuruq, as in ki nivniti, nifuneti, nidkheti. This is in order that two ḥolam vowels should not occur together.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 10_P: 7. The Participle In the singular it is like the past tense; but in the other forms the qamats changes to a sheva, as in navon, nevonim, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 11_P: The Infinitive and the imperative come with a he with a hiriq at the beginning and a dagesh following it, as with the strong roots, as in hakhon. And likewise akhon, yakhon, takhon, nakhon, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 0_Pa: The Eighth Principle: A discussion to prove that the pattern Paʿal in this class is the pattern that some grammarians have called “quadriliteral.”
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 1_Pa: The Patterns Paʿal and Puʿal Behold, I have now reached the place where I said at the beginning of the First Treatise that I would prove that the so-called quadriliteral pattern does not exist at all. Know that some grammarians have said concerning the words to’khelehu esh (Job 20:26), meloshni ba-seter (Psalms 101:5), le-mishpati etḥannan (Job 9:15), that they belong to a quadriliteral pattern, because of the ḥataf-qamats on the first root letter, which they take to stand in place of a ḥolam to indicate a quiescent vav after the first root letter.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 2_Pa: 1. The Past okhel, okhelet; loshen, loshenet; shofet, shofetet — thus, according to them, there are four root letters. So far is their claim. But I say that no proof should be brought from these three, for they are found only in these instances alone, and one does not establish a verbal pattern on their account. Rather, they belong to the class of anomalous or compound forms, as will be explained in the Book of Composition, each one in its proper place.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 3_Pa: And what they further said is that there are found in this class true quadriliteral forms, such as from bun one says bonen: the quiescent vav is the middle root letter, and afterward there are two nuns, which they take to be the two final root letters. Thus there are, according to them, four root letters, and therefore they are called true quadriliterals. So far is their claim.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 4_Pa: 2. To this I reply and say that it is true that konen, qomem, and shovev have a doubled final root letter; but they belong to the pattern Paʿal with dagesh. And since the vav is quiescent, it is impossible to place a dagesh in it, for a dagesh never occurs in a quiescent letter. Therefore they doubled the final root letter in place of the dagesh, and said konen instead of kon. The proof of this is that even in Hitpa‘el in this class they doubled the final root letter in place of the dagesh, and said hitkonen instead of hitkon. Likewise in Paʿal, which also requires a dagesh, they said be-ein tehomot ḥullalti (Proverbs 8:24) instead of ḥullalti; and me-Hashem mitz‘adei gever konanu (Psalms 37:23), which is from the pattern Paʿal in this class, instead of konu; and likewise yimolal ve-yavesh (Psalms 90:6), from the pattern Paʿal of this class. And those who say that these are formed on the pattern yaqomem, yashovev, from a quadriliteral pattern, would need to say that they are intransitive verbs. But this is not my view, for the law of this entire pattern is that it is transitive. And this too supports my position, for it stands in place of Paʿal, which is always transitive, as I wrote in its principle.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 5_Pa: And there is yet another proof that this pattern stands in place of Paʿal: for its participle and its passive are formed with a mem with sheva at the beginning, and likewise the prefixed letters bekholam and the letters e-i-t-n are all with a sheva, in accordance with the rule of every Paʿal pattern. And the difference between the participle and the passive is that the participle has a tsere, as in meshovev netivot (Isaiah 58:12).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 6_Pa: And the passive has a qamats, as in ve-hu meḥullal mi-pesha‘einu (Isaiah 53:5).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 7_Pa: 3. And the general rule is this: the pattern Paʿal in this class has the first root letter vocalized with a ḥolam to indicate the quiescent vav, which is the middle root letter; and the final root letter is doubled in place of the dagesh, and it is vocalized with a tsere, as in bonen, qomem. And all the additional prefixed letters at the beginning are with a sheva, following the rule of the pattern Paʿal. In this manner the pattern Paʿal appears, and there is no difference among these forms except according to the sense of the context. Thus konenu ḥitzam (Psalms 11:2) is from the pattern that I call Paʿal; mitz‘adei gever konanu (Psalms 37:23) is from the pattern Paʿal; ḥillalah yado (Job 26:13) is from the pattern Paʿal; and lifnei gva‘ot ḥullalti (Proverbs 8:25) is from the pattern Paʿal, as I wrote above.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 8_Pa: 4. The Pattern Hif‘il In the past tense throughout, the first root letter has a tsere at the beginning; and in the three concealed persons the first root letter has a hiriq, as in heqim, heqimu, heqimah. But in the other persons it has a pataḥ, as in haqemta, haqemti, and so on. Sometimes even in these the first root letter has a hiriq, but the he has a ḥataf-pataḥ or a ḥataf-segol, as in heqimot, heqimoti, heqitsoti, as in ki Hashem yismekheni (Psalms 3:6).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 9_Pa: The Participle The mem has a tsere, like the he of the past tense; but in the other forms the tsere changes to a sheva, as is its rule, as in meqim, meqimim.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 10_P: The Passive The mem has a shuruq, as is its rule, as in muqam, muqamim, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 11_P: The Infinitive It has a he with a qamats in order to distinguish it from the past tense, and the first root letter has a tsere, as in haqem. But with the prefixed letters bekholam it takes a hiriq, as in behakim, kehakim, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 12_P: 5. And likewise the Imperative For the singular and the plural it has a tsere; and in the other forms with a hiriq, as in haqem, haqimu, haqimi, haqemnah. And sometimes they drop the he of the pattern from the infinitive and the imperative, as in nitsav la-riv Hashem (Isaiah 3:13), and ‘omed la-din ‘amim (ibid.), which correspond to le-hariv, le-hadin. And in the imperative likewise, as sim koh (Genesis 31:37), lin poh (Judges 19:9). And with the addition of a final he, as in binah hagiye, therefore the word has penultimate stress. And for the plural, they are most often found with the loss of the he, as in simu, sikhu, shiru, sithu, gilu, linu, all of them with penultimate stress. And likewise for the feminine, as in shiti libbekh (Jeremiah 31:20), lini ha-laylah (Ruth 3:13). And the dropped he is also found in the past tense, as in binoti ba-sefarim (Daniel 9:2), in place of hevinoti. And likewise in digum rabim and digum (Jeremiah 16:16), which they say is like ve-ha-digum; see the Book of Composition.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 13_P: But know that this loss occurs only in verbs for which no imperative is found in the pattern Qal, such as those I mentioned; for we cannot say sumu, shukhu, shotu, golu, lonu. Likewise, in most of them the future tense is not found in Qal, so that one does not say avon, ashor, ashot, ashum, ashush, agol. And the other actions of the pattern Qal are not found in them either, except for a few cases, such as asher shar la-Hashem (Psalms 7:1), ki shet li Elohim (Genesis 4:25), binah le-re‘i (Psalms 139:2), and similar cases, which are few. But verbs in which both Qal and Hif‘il are found, for the most part—such as qam, shav, sar, ba, from which are found heqim, heshiv, hevi— the imperative never comes with the loss of the he, for we cannot say qemu, shevu, sirru, bi’u, and the like.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 14_P: And remember this rule and treasure it, for it is good, and no one has preceded me in it.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 15_P: 6. The Future Here too the letters e-i-t-n come with a qamats, as in avin, yavin, and so on. And it would have been proper for them to be with a tsere, like the mem of the participle, according to the rule I gave for the pattern Paʿal of strong roots (in this treatise, in the Second Principle, section four). But they come with a qamats in order to distinguish them from the future tense of Qal in roots quiescent in the first letter yod, which are with a tsere, as in eshav, yeshav, and so on. Therefore they vocalized the e-i-t-n here with a qamats, like the e-i-t-n of Qal in this class. But there the first root letter has a shuruq, as in aqum, yaqum, whereas here it has a hiriq, as in aqim, yaqim, and so on, or sometimes a tsere, as in yaqem. And when the conversive vav comes with them, the tsere returns to segol, as in va-yaqem, va-yeshev, and this is because they are penultimately stressed.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 16_P: The Pattern Hif‘al I have already written about it among the roots quiescent in the first letter yod in this treatise, in the Sixth Principle, section eleven.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 17_P: 7. The Pattern Hitpa‘el I have already written above, under the pattern Paʿal in this principle, section two, that its rule is to appear with a doubled final root letter in place of the dagesh, as in hitbonen, hitbonanta, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 18_P: The Participle mitkonen. The infinitive and the imperative are hitbonen, like the past tense. The future tense is etbonen, yitbonen, titbonen, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 0_Pa: The Ninth Principle: On the elucidation of the class of roots quiescent in the final letter aleph, such as qara.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. The Pattern Qal Throughout, it comes with a quiescent aleph and a qamats before it, except in the third-person plural and feminine, where the aleph is mobile, as in qar’u, qar’ah. And in the participle and the passive, the aleph is quiescent only in the singular; in the other forms it is mobile, as in qore, qor’im, [qaru, qeru’im], and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 2_Pa: The Infinitive qera; and with the prefixed letters bekholam: be-qera, ke-qera, le-qera, mi-qra. And it sometimes comes with an added tav, following the manner of roots quiescent in the final letter he, as I will explain in the next principle, as in le-vilti qerot lanu (Judges 8:1), and le-fi melot le-Bavel (Jeremiah 29:10).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 3_Pa: 2. And likewise, this class is interchanged in many places with roots quiescent in the final letter he; and I have no need to elaborate further.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 4_Pa: The Imperative qera, with the aleph quiescent; but in the other forms it is mobile, as in qer’u, qer’i, qer’na. And it also comes with the loss of the he, as in qer’an lo va-yokhal laḥem (Exodus 2:20); and the aleph is quiescent in the word qer’an li Mara (Ruth 1:20).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 5_Pa: 3. And the letters e-i-t-n are vocalized as in the strong roots, and the aleph is quiescent when it stands at the end of the word, as in eqra, yiqra, and so on. But when another letter follows it, it is mobile, as in yiqre’u, tiqre’u, tiqre’i. Yet in the feminine plural it is quiescent, as in tiqre’na milḥamah (Exodus 1:10).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 6_Pa: 4. And all the other patterns proceed in this same manner, except that in them a tsere most often appears before the quiescent aleph in the past tense, when it occurs, and likewise in the first-person forms, as in niqre’ta, niqre’ti, malle’ta, malle’ti, himtza’ta, himtza’ti. And I have already written to you that many roots quiescent in the first letter aleph come according to the pattern with a tsere, and all of them are intransitive verbs, such as male, sane, yare, and the like; see there.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 0_Pa: The Tenth Principle: On the elucidation of the vocalization of the class of roots quiescent in the final letter he, such as galah.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. The Pattern Qal The he is divided into four forms. The first is that it appears quiescent at the end, as in galah. The second is that it disappears, as in galu. The third is that it is changed into a yod, as in galiti, and so on. And with the prefixed letters bekholam, the first root letter is vocalized as in the strong roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 2_Pa: And know that in the third-person masculine and feminine, the he sometimes changes into a mobile yod, as from ḥasah: tsur ḥasyo bo (Deuteronomy 32:37), bakh ḥasyah nafshi (Psalms 57:2), following the pattern of paqdu, paqedah.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 3_Pa: 2. The Participle In the singular, the he is quiescent, and it is usually preceded by a segol, as in goleh, in order to distinguish it from roots quiescent in aleph, which take a tsere, as in qore, as I wrote in its principle. And when it is joined to a short word or to a word with penultimate stress, it too takes a tsere [and then it has penultimate stress], as in va-yehi boneh ‘ir (Genesis 4:17), ‘oseh fele (Exodus 15:11), and many similar cases, which are counted according to the Masoretic tradition. And the feminine singular has a qamats before the he, as in Ester ‘asah (Esther 2:18). And in the masculine and feminine plural, the he disappears, as in golim, golot.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 4_Pa: 3. The Passive In it the he is changed into a mobile yod in all forms, and its vocalization is like that of the strong roots, as in galuy, geluyim, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 5_Pa: The Infinitive The first root letter has a qamats, and the middle root letter has a ḥolam, with a quiescent he at the end when the infinitive is not joined to a prefixed letter (bekholam) and when it is attached to verbs, as in ra’ah, ra’inu, ‘asah, ya‘aseh lo. When it is not attached to a verb, the final he takes a sheva, as in ra’oh fanekha lo filalti (Genesis 48:11), ‘asoh tsedaqah u-mishpat (Proverbs 21:3). Likewise, after verbs, as in hiskalta ‘asu (Genesis 31:28). When the infinitive is joined to a prefixed letter (bekholam), the he changes to a quiescent vav, with an added tav at the end, as in be-galot, ke-galot, and so on. It is also found without any prefix, as in galot ha-aretz (Judges 18:30), and similar forms, which are rare. One instance is found joined to a verb with the added tav, as in heyot ehyeh kamokha (Psalms 50:21), and it has no parallel.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 6_Pa: 4. The Imperative In the singular it has a sheva, and the he is quiescent at the end, with a tsere before it, as in geleh. In the masculine plural and the feminine singular, the he disappears, as in gelu, geli. In the feminine plural, it is changed into a quiescent yod with a segol before it, as in ‘al Sha’ul be-khinah (2 Samuel 1:24), or sometimes without a yod, as in tse’ena u-re’ena (Song of Songs 3:11). Although tse’ena has the root yatsa, it comes according to the pattern of re’ena, in order to pair the words.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 7_Pa: The Future You place the e-i-t-n letters upon the imperative, and you will obtain it; and its vocalization is like that of the strong roots. And behold, all the rules that I have mentioned in this pattern— the changing of the he into a yod or into a tav, or its complete disappearance— apply to all seven verbal patterns. And the vocalization of the first root letter and of the prefixed letters, such as the mem of the participles and passives, and the letters bekholam and e-i-t-n of all the patterns, are vocalized as in the strong roots. Therefore there is no need to explain each one individually.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 8_Pa: 5. And know that the middle root letter in the past tense, in the third-person masculine singular, is qamats in all of them, as in galah, niglah, gullah, higlah—all alike. And in the future it is with segol, as in egleh, yigleh, tigleh, yugleh, hugleh, and so on. Likewise, the participle in the masculine singular has a segol, and in the feminine singular it has a qamats. And so too in the passives, except for the passive of the Qal pattern, as I wrote above in section three. And all the infinitives, when they appear with the prefixed letters bekholam, have a final tav and a ḥolam before it. And all the imperatives are with a tsere, as in geleh, higleh, galleh, hugleh, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 9_Pa: It is also important to know that most future forms in this class sometimes appear with the loss of the root he. In Qal: egal, yegal, tegal, negal, with a ḥiriq or segol on the middle radical and penultimate stress (mil‘el). There are also forms with the letters of e-i-t-n in a tsere, as in al tifan (Numbers 16:15) and va-teta‘ ba-midbar Be’er Sheva‘ (Genesis 21:14). In Nif‘al: egal, yegal, tegal, negal, with a sheva on the middle radical and a pataḥ elsewhere. In the patterns Pa‘al and Pu‘al, the loss of the he does not occur. In Hif‘il: egal, yegal, tegal, negal, with a segol on the middle radical. In Hitpa‘el: etgal, yitgal, titgal, nitgal.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 10_P: 6. And know that, for the most part, this loss occurs only with the conversive vav, as in Qal: va-yiven Elohim (Genesis 2:22); in Nif‘al: va-yiqar Elohim (Numbers 23:4); in Paʿal: va-yetsav Elohim (Genesis 2:16); in Hif‘il: va-yifen zanav el zanav (Judges 15:4); and in Hitpa‘el: va-yitgal betokh aholoh (Genesis 9:21). And your mnemonic sign is: ha-nissah davar elekha tila’eh (Job 4:2) with the he, and immediately after it is written tavo elekha ve-til’eh (ibid. 4:5) with the loss of the he. And only a few are found without the conversive vav, such as al tifen el minḥatam (Numbers 16:15), sod aḥer al tegal (Proverbs 25:9), ya‘as Hashem ‘immakhem (Ruth 1:8), and the like.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 11_P: 7. The Imperative In the singular it sometimes comes with the loss of the root he, as in Paʿal: tsav et benei Yisra’el (Numbers 28:2), gal me-‘alai (Psalms 119:22). In Hif‘il: heref mimmeni (Deuteronomy 9:14), harbeh kavseni (Psalms 51:4), shekhav ‘al mishkavkha ve-hitḥal (2 Samuel 13:5). But in Qal and in Nif‘al, the imperative never comes with the loss of the he.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 12_P: 8. And know that there are four roots whose final letter is he that never becomes quiescent. Your mnemonic for them is taganakh, that is: tamah (to be astonished), gavah (to be high), ganah (to reproach), kamah (to yearn). Therefore they are vocalized with a qamats and a pataḥ like the strong roots, and not like roots quiescent in he, which always have two qamats. Accordingly, the open forms take a mappiq to indicate their completeness. Thus, from gavah: va-yigbah Hashem Tseva’ot (Isaiah 5:16), ya‘an ki gavhu benot Tsiyon (Isaiah 3:16). From kamah: kamah lekha vesari (Psalms 63:2); and one may say kamahte, kamahati, even though such forms are not attested. From nogah: lo yigah sheviv esho (Job 18:5). From tamāh: hemah ra’u ken tamahu (Psalms 48:6), al titmah ‘al ha-ḥefets (Ecclesiastes 5:7), with a mappiq. But va-yitmahmehah (Genesis 19:16), and likewise hitmahmehu and tamahu (Isaiah 29:9), belong to the root mahmah, which is quadriliteral; therefore they are not included among the four mentioned above. And there is a dispute concerning va-telah erets Mitsrayim (Genesis 47:13), whether its root is la’ah or lahah; from it comes ke-mithlahleh ha-yoreh (Proverbs 26:18). But this controversy does not concern me, for I do not engage in hidden matters.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 0_P: The Eleventh Principle: On the elucidation of the vocalization of the patterns Qal and Nif‘al in the class of doubled roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 1_P: These are those roots in which the last two letters are identical, such as sabab, shalal, gazaz, and the like. And the other kinds of doubling I have already discussed in the First Treatise, in the Third Principle, section six.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 2_P: 1. And now know that there are doubled roots which sometimes appear as if they were strong roots, such as sabab, shalal, gazaz, sabbavta, shallalta, gazzazta, and the like, and there is no need to explain them. But for the most part they appear with the loss of one of the doubled letters, and the remaining one is doubled with a dagesh to indicate it, as in sabbot, sabboti. And we must say that the letter that is lost is the middle root letter, and the one that is doubled is the final root letter; for if it were the reverse, the dagesh would have no power to indicate it, since a dagesh always indicates what is missing before it, not what comes after it. Understand this and remember it, for it is a great principle in grammar.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 3_P: 2. The Past sav: the first root letter has a pataḥ, in order to distinguish it from roots quiescent in the middle letter, in which it is a qamats; and also because of the dagesh that follows it in the other forms, as in sabbot, sabboti, and so on. For if the samekh were with a qamats, the dagesh could not occur afterward, since a dagesh does not come after a qamats.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 4_P: 3. And likewise the Participle It is with a pataḥ for this same reason, as in sav, sovavim, and so on. Even those that are with a qamats according to the Mesorah, such as tam ve-yashar (Job 1:1), from which we say yihyu temimim (Exodus 20:24); but tsaddiq tamim (Genesis 6:9), which has a qamats, is singular, while its plural is temimim, following the pattern of ḥasid, ḥasidim. Thus there is no difference between the past tense and the participle in the masculine singular except according to the sense of the context, as in tam ha-kesef (Genesis 47:18), which is past tense, and bar levav (Psalms 24:4), which is a descriptive participle. But in the feminine there is a difference: the past tense has penultimate stress, as in ha-misgav ve-ḥattah (Jeremiah 48:1), whereas the participle has final stress, as in ve-lashon rakkah (Proverbs 25:15).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 5_P: The Passive It occurs only in complete form, as in ve-at shadud (Jeremiah 4:30), and ve-shallaḥ retsutsim (Isaiah 58:6), and the like.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 6_P: The Infinitive and the Imperative They come with a ḥolam in order to distinguish them from roots quiescent in the middle letter, which have a shuruq. The infinitive: sov et ha-har ha-zeh (Deuteronomy 2:3). The imperative: sov demeh lakh (Song of Songs 2:17), sovu Tsiyon (Psalms 48:13), sovi ‘ir (Isaiah 23:16), with penultimate stress. (And therefore a dagesh comes after the ḥolam, even though it does not normally follow a long vowel. This will be explained to you further in the chapter on poetry.)
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 7_P: The Future The e-i-t-n letters take a qamats, as with roots quiescent in the middle letter; but the difference between them is that in these the first root letter most often has a ḥolam, as in ve-ḥannoti et asher aḥon (Exodus 33:19). Likewise in the plural: teshalu lah (Ruth 2:16), yeronnu yoshvei sela‘ (Isaiah 42:11). And likewise yesovu, tesovu, tesovi; and in the feminine plural tesovnah, because of the many vowels the quiescent letter drops. And likewise in the imperative sovnah, as in ve-hineh tesovnah alumoteikhem (Genesis 37:7), and u-farashav lo yedakkenu (Isaiah 28:28). But roots quiescent in the middle letter most often have a shuruq, as I wrote there. And there are those who say that the e-i-t-n letters come with a dagesh, as in yatom and the like; I will speak of these in the discussion of the Nif‘al pattern that follows.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 8_P: 4. The Pattern Nif‘al In the past tense, in the three concealed persons, the vowel is a qamats, and the first root letter is vocalized in one of three ways, just as the Qal pattern of strong roots appears as Pa‘al, Pe‘al, or Pu‘al, as I explained there. The open forms are, for example: ve-naqal (2 Kings 3:18), ve-nasav ha-gevul (Numbers 34:4), ve-ḥam ha-shemesh ve-namas (Exodus 16:21). And it would have been proper for them to have two qamats because of the pause, but instead they take what is called pataḥ de-sifra; the rule of pataḥ de-sifra will be explained in the Book of Mesorah of the Mesorah, in the tenth treatise, with God’s help. The other persons are doubled, as in nasovu ‘al ha-bayit (Genesis 19:4), nesavotem, nesavunu, and so on. Those with a tsere are, for example: namas betokh me‘ai (Psalms 22:15), nesavah elai (Ezekiel 26:2). Those with a ḥolam are found only in the plural, as in ve-nagolu ke-sefer ha-shamayim (Isaiah 34:4), nagozu ve-‘avar (Nahum 1:12). And we may posit the singular forms nagol, nagoz, following the pattern of namukh, which is found in the words of our Sages, whose root is makhakh, as in va-yimokhu ba-‘avonam (Psalms 106:43). All three patterns appear in the other past forms according to one rule: nesavot, neqalot, niglot, all with a doubled final root letter to indicate the doubling. And a few are found in a lightened form, such as ve-navkah ruaḥ Mitsrayim (Isaiah 19:3), ve-raḥavah ve-nesavah (Ezekiel 41:7), naqtah nafshi ba-ḥayyai (Job 10:1), where the expected forms would be navkah, nesavah, naqtah.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 9_P: 5. The Participle In the masculine singular it appears with a qamats, as in ‘im navar titbar (2 Samuel 22:27), and with a tsere, as in lev namas (Nahum 2:11), naqal me-hyotekha li (Isaiah 49:6). In the other forms it follows these two patterns with a dagesh, as in anaḥnu nimmaqim (Ezekiel 33:10); and likewise one should say nimasim with a dagesh, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 10_: The Infinitive It comes with a ḥolam above, following the manner of roots quiescent in the middle letter, as in boq tavoq (Isaiah 24:3), or with a tsere, as in ha-mas yimas (2 Samuel 17:10). And likewise the imperative is with a ḥolam, following the pattern of the infinitive. It may also come with a pataḥ, just as the future tense may come so, as I shall explain, for the rule of the imperative is to follow the e-i-t-n letters, as I have written more than once. And the other forms of the imperative have a doubled middle root letter, as in boqu, boqi, or masu, masi.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 11_: The Future It too follows the manner of roots quiescent in the middle letter, as in asham va-esha’af (Isaiah 42:14), yitom peryo (Ezekiel 47:12), va-yidom Aharon (Leviticus 10:3). Now there is a great dispute concerning these dageshim, for some say that they belong to Qal, bringing proof from va-ekhatt etto taḥon (Deuteronomy 9:21), which is certainly from Qal, as shown by otto; and others say that they belong to Nif‘al, on account of the dagesh which indicates the nun of Nif‘al. But I say that some of them are from Qal and some of them are from Nif‘al, and according to the context and the intent you should determine them. I have no need to elaborate further.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 12_: However, the true rule is that the e-i-t-n letters of this pattern ought always to come with a pataḥ, as in lo yimmad (Hosea 2:1), yiddal kevod Ya‘aqov (Isaiah 17:4). And when the middle root letter is vocalized, it is doubled, as in yitammu ḥatta’im (Psalms 104:35), nishessu ha-batim (Zechariah 14:2). And when the first root letter is guttural, the e-i-t-n letters take a tsere, as in ve-al taḥat (Deuteronomy 1:21), ve-al aḥateh ani (Jeremiah 17:18). And sometimes this occurs even without a guttural, as in va-eqal be-‘eineha (Genesis 16:5), va-tiq‘a kaf yarekh (Genesis 32:25). There are also lightened forms, such as yidmu ka-even (Exodus 15:16), va-yitammu yemei bekhi (Deuteronomy 34:8), where the expected forms would be yidmu, yitammu. And there are those who say that these are from Qal, from forms like va-yidom and va-tetom, as I wrote above.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 0_P: The Twelfth Principle: On the elucidation of the five remaining verbal patterns in the class of doubled roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 1_P: 1. The Pattern Paʿal This pattern for the most part follows the manner of the strong roots, as in qillel, qillalta, and the like, and there is no need to explain it. But sometimes it follows the manner of the Paʿal pattern of roots quiescent in the middle letter, in which the final root letter is doubled in place of the dagesh; only that in these cases the vowels are with pataḥ, as in ve-romem taḥat le-shoni (Psalms 66:17), asher ‘olal li (Lamentations 1:12). But roots quiescent in the middle letter take a tsere, as I wrote above, and thus we say from ramam: romemu Hashem Eloheinu (Psalms 99:9), aromem, yeromem, and so on. And likewise from bun: bonen, bonenu. The reason is that since the last two letters are identical, it was difficult in their view to place a dagesh in one of the doubled letters, for it would appear as though there were three identical letters in succession, since the dagesh indicates a doubled letter, as I explained. Therefore they sometimes dropped the dagesh and placed in its stead a quiescent vav. As a result, doubt arises in some of these verbs whether they belong to the class of roots quiescent in the middle letter or to the class of doubled roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 2_P: 2. But the participle and the passive occur only in complete form, as in mesovev, mehallel. Therefore, everything that you find in the pattern mefu‘al with a tsere, or mefu‘al with qamats, such as meshovev netivot (Isaiah 58:12), me‘onen u-menachesh (Deuteronomy 18:10), ve-hu meḥullal mi-pesha‘einu (Isaiah 53:5), u-meromam ‘al kol berakhah (Nehemiah 9:5), belong to the class of roots quiescent in the middle letter, and not to the doubled roots. This is also the view of R. Abraham ibn Ezra in his book Ṣaḥut.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 3_P: But I find difficulty with u-meḥonnen ‘anavim (Proverbs 14:21), for it is certainly from the doubled roots, its root being ḥanan. And Rabbi David Kimḥi has brought some such forms both among the roots quiescent in the middle letter and among the doubled roots; see his discussion under that root.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 4_P: The Hitpa‘el For the most part it comes in complete form, as in hitpallel, hitḥannen, and the like. But sometimes it comes according to the manner of roots quiescent in the middle letter, as from madad: va-yitmoded ‘al ha-yeled (1 Kings 17:21); and from galal: mitgalel ba-dam (2 Samuel 20:12), and similar cases.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 5_P: 3. The Pattern Hif‘il — The Past It comes in two forms, and in both the prefixed he has a tsere. In the first, the first root letter also has a tsere, as in ve-hesav lev melekh Ashur (Ezra 6:22), heḥel ha-negef (Numbers 17:11), he‘ez ish rasha‘ (Proverbs 21:29). In the second, the first root letter comes with a pataḥ, as in he-mar Shaddai li me’od (Ruth 1:20), he-qel artsah Zevulun (Isaiah 8:23). Likewise, the third-person masculine and feminine appear in these two patterns with a tsere, as in hesebu elai et ha-aron (1 Samuel 5:10), ve-ha-massa’ah heḥelah (Judges 20:40); and with a pataḥ, as in hemakku, hemakkah. But all the other past forms follow the manner of roots quiescent in the middle letter, except that here they are doubled, as in hesivota et libbam (1 Kings 18:37), ve-hizkita bor kappi (Job 9:30), whereas roots quiescent in the middle letter are light, as in ve-heshivota, ve-heshivoti, and so on. And if the first root letter is guttural, the prefixed he is vocalized with a pataḥ, as in heḥeloti Sha’ul lo (1 Samuel 22:15).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 6_P: 4. The Participle Here too it is with a tsere, as in roots quiescent in the middle letter. But whereas there the first root letter has a ḥiriq, as in meqim, meshiv, in these it has a tsere, as in meseb kele milḥamah (Jeremiah 21:4), meḥel le-hara‘ (Jeremiah 25:29). And the remaining forms are with a dagesh, as in mesibbim, mesibbah, whereas roots quiescent in the middle letter are light, as in meshivim, meshivah.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 7_P: The Passive With a mem with a shuruq or a qubbuts, as is always its rule, as in musav. The remaining forms are with a dagesh, as in musabbim, musabbah, musabbot; some are written in full and some defectively, according to the Masoretic tradition. But roots quiescent in the middle letter are light, as in moshavin, moshavah, moshavot.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 8_P: 5. The Infinitive It has a he with a qamats and a tsere, as in ha-meq basaro (Zechariah 14:12). And it comes with a tsere even with the prefixed letters bekholam, as in le-ḥal, le-hadeq; but katat le-hadeq (2 Chronicles 34:7) has a pataḥ in place of a tsere on the first root letter. This is not so with roots quiescent in the middle letter, which have a ḥiriq, as in le-haqim, le-hashiv.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 9_P: 6. And likewise the Imperative It is with a tsere, as in haḥel rash (Deuteronomy 2:24). The other forms are doubled, as in hassevu, hassevi ‘einekh (Song of Songs 6:5), all with penultimate stress, for otherwise the dagesh could not occur. And in the feminine plural: hassevnah.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 10_: 7. The Future The e-i-t-n letters come with a qamats, as with roots quiescent in the middle letter, yet they are distinguished from them, for in these the first root letter has a tsere, as in aḥel gadlekha (Joshua 3:7), yaqel et yado (1 Samuel 6:5), whereas in those it has a ḥiriq, as in aqim, yaqim. And when they come with the conversive vav, the tsere returns to a segol, because the stress shifts to the penultimate, as in va-yigal et ha-even (Genesis 29:10), va-yideq le-‘afar (2 Kings 23:6). In this respect they resemble roots quiescent in the middle letter, as I wrote there.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 11_: And there is also a pattern in which the e-i-t-n letter has a pataḥ and a dagesh follows it, as in va-yasev Elohim (Exodus 13:18), ki titammu derakhekha (Job 22:3). And one also finds va-yasovu penehem (Judges 18:23), va-yasovu et ha-aron (1 Samuel 5:8), where the samekh and the bet are doubled, contrary to the usual practice, in order to absorb one letter; the expected form would have been va-yasovu. And the feminine plural forms are with a sheva, as in va-teḥilnah sheva shenei ha-ra‘av (Genesis 41:54).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 12_: 8. The Pattern Huf‘al In the past tense, the prefixed he has a shuruq, as in husav, as I wrote above concerning roots quiescent in the middle letter. The remaining forms have a doubled middle root letter, as in husavot, husavoti, and so on. But roots quiescent in the middle letter are light, as in hushavta, hushavtem levadkhem (Isaiah 5:8).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 13_: The Future It comes in two forms. The first, which is the more common, has the e-i-t-n letters with a shuruq and a following light consonant, as in leḥem yuddaq (Isaiah 28:28), ‘al kamots yusav, u-mivtsarekha yushad (Hosea 10:14), ke-hitmokh shoded tushad (Isaiah 33:1). These have a dagesh together with a quiescent vowel, contrary to the normal rule. The second form has three dots (qibbuts) together with a dagesh, as in yukkat sha‘ar (Isaiah 24:12), mi-boqer la-‘erev yukkatu (Job 4:20).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 14_: The Pattern Hitpa‘el I have already included it within the discussion of the pattern Paʿal, and there is no need to repeat it.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 0_P: The Thirteenth Principle: On the elucidation of some of the rules concerning the compound classes of roots.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 1_P: 1. Behold, I have already written at the beginning of the First Treatise that the fundamental classes of roots are six, and these are the ones I have explained up to this point. Now I shall explain the remaining classes, which are compound formations derived from those six. There is no need to elaborate at length, for each of them proceeds according to the rules of the two classes from which it is composed. For example, the root natah is composed of roots deficient in the first letter and roots quiescent in the final letter. Thus, its nun follows the rule of the nun of nagash, and its he follows the rule of the he of galah. That is to say: in every place where the nun of nagash drops, or the he of galah becomes quiescent, so too the nun and the he of natah drop or become quiescent. The exception is the imperative: from nagash one says gash, geshu, with the loss of the nun; but from natah one cannot say teh or tu, rather one must say natah, netu. Likewise, from galah one may form the imperative in the pattern Paʿal as gal, tsav, with the loss of the he; but from natah one cannot say nat. And similarly with nasa: in every place where the aleph of qara is quiescent, the aleph of nasa is likewise quiescent, except in the infinitive, where the aleph moves with a sheva, as in set, beset, and so on.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 2_P: 2. And the class of roots quiescent at both ends is of three kinds. The first is where the first root letter is aleph and the final root letter is he, such as avah, afah. In these, the aleph follows the rule of roots quiescent in initial aleph, like akhal, and the he follows the rule of roots quiescent in final he, as in tifneh. The second is where the first root letter is yod and the final root letter is aleph, such as yare, yirat. These take a tsere according to the Paʿal pattern. The infinitive is yare or yera, and with the prefixed letters bekholam: bi-yero, ke-yero, le-yero, mi-yero. The imperative is yera, as in yir’u et Hashem, with the aleph quiescent, for the shuruq of the vav belongs to the resh, and the aleph is quiescent to distinguish it from the verb of seeing, as it is written: ki lo yir’ani ha-adam va-ḥai. The future is ira, yira, tira, with quiescent yod; and in the feminine plural tir’ena, with quiescent aleph. In Nif‘al, the aleph changes to a vav, as in nora, ora. The third is where the first root letter is yod and the final root letter is he, such as yarah, yarita. Here the yod follows the rule of roots quiescent in initial yod, like yashav, and the he follows the rule of roots quiescent in final he, like galah, galita. The infinitive is yaroh, yiroh, and with the prefixed letters bekholam: lirot, as in lirot be-mo ofel (Psalms 11:2). The imperative is yereh, yeru, and so on. The future is ireh, yireh; and with the loss of the he: ir, yir, tir, following the pattern of va-yif be-gadlo (Ezekiel 31:7) and va-tifi me’od (Ezekiel 16:13), whose root is yafah.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 3_P: 2. And the class of roots quiescent at both ends is of three kinds. The first is where the first root letter is aleph and the final root letter is he, such as avah, afah. Here the aleph follows the rule of roots quiescent in initial aleph, and the he follows the rule of roots quiescent in final he. The second is where the first root letter is yod and the final root letter is aleph, such as yatsa, yatsata, and the like. These take a tsere according to the Paʿal pattern.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 4_P: The third is where the first root letter is yod and the final root letter is he, such as yarah, yarita, and the like. In these, the yod follows the rule of roots quiescent in initial yod, like yashav, and the he follows the rule of roots quiescent in final he, like galah, galita, except for the infinitive and the imperative, which come in full form with the first root letter expressed.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 5_P: The Infinitive It is yira or yero; and with the prefixed letters bekholam: bi-yero, ke-yero, le-yero, as in mi-penei David (1 Samuel 18:29).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 6_P: The Imperative As in yir’u et Hashem qedoshav (Psalms 34:10), with the aleph quiescent; for the shuruq of the vav belongs to the resh, and the aleph is quiescent in order to distinguish it from the verb of seeing, since it is said: ki lo yir’ani ha-adam va-ḥai (Exodus 33:20). And from yarah one says yereh or yorah; and with the prefixed letters bekholam: lirot be-mo ofel.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 7_P: 3. And the general rule is this: all types of compound roots whose first letter is yod never come with the loss of the first root letter, neither in the infinitive nor in the imperative, except for the roots yatsa and nasa, which do come with the loss of the first letter. Thus, from yatsa: tset, be-tset, ke-tset, and so on. And from nasa: set, ke-set, be-set, and so on; sa, se’u, and the like. And the future forms of yare are: ira, yira, with a quiescent yod; and from yarah: ireh, yireh, and so on. And with the loss of the he: ir, yir, and the like, following the pattern of va-yif be-gadlo (Ezekiel 31:7).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 8_P: 4. And the class of roots deficient at both ends is found only in the root natan. In the past tense, the final nun is dropped, as in natata, natati. In the imperative and in the future, the initial nun is dropped, as in ten, etten, yitten, and so on. In the infinitive, sometimes both ends are dropped, as in aḥel tet (Deuteronomy 2:25), be-tet Hashem (Numbers 5:21), where the expected form would have been be-tent, on the pattern of be-gashet. And the past tense is also found with the loss of both ends in the expression va-oyevai titta li ‘oref (2 Samuel 22:41).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 9_P: 5. And the class of quadriliteral roots—that is, roots of four letters, such as ve-sha‘asha‘ yonek (Isaiah 11:8)— is a compound of roots quiescent in the final letter and of doubled roots. The final he of the root has fallen away, and the first and middle root letters have been doubled, for its root is sha‘ah. Likewise toratekha sha‘asha‘ti (Psalms 119:70): both are from the pattern Paʿal. And in Paʿal, in the plural, tasha‘asha‘u (Isaiah 66:12); and in Hitpa‘el, be-ḥuqotekha eshta‘asha‘ (Psalms 119:16). There are also two roots of four letters that are distinct, meaning that no letter in them is doubled, namely karbel and karsam, as in yekharsmenah ḥazir mi-ya‘ar (Psalms 80:14), and ve-David mekharbel (1 Chronicles 15:27). As for the forms ratpesh and parshu, our Rabbis of blessed memory said that they are compound words: ratpesh = ratov + pash; parshu = perush + ziv.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 10_: 6. Moreover, many forms derived from the class of doubled roots are also found following this same pattern, with the first root letter doubled after the middle root letter, for example: From galal: ve-gilgaltikha min ha-sela‘im (Jeremiah 51:25). From qalal: ve-hu lo fanim qilqel (Ecclesiastes 10:10). From salal: salselah ve-teromemekha (Proverbs 4:8). All of these are found only in the pattern Paʿal. Likewise, from the class quiescent in the middle letter: hinneh Hashem metaltelkha taltelah gaver (Isaiah 22:17), whose root is tul, as in va-yatilu et ha-kelim (Jonah 1:5). And those forms which the grammarians call “quadriliteral” because of the doubling of the final root letter, such as from shuv: meshovev, and from qum: mekomem, I have already demonstrated to be from the pattern Paʿal; there is no need to elaborate further here.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 11_: 7. A verb of five letters is found only in a single instance, namely ḥamarmar, as in: panai ḥamarmaru bekhi (Job 16:16), and in pause: me‘ai ḥamarmaru. In this form both the middle and final root letters are doubled after the three original root letters, for its root is ḥmr. However, forms such as libbi saḥarḥar (Psalms 38:11) and hafakhpakh darko (Proverbs 21:8) are adjectival nouns, not verbs, like yeraqraq (“greenish”) or admadam (“reddish”).
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 12_: 8. There is also found a single five-letter form from the class of verbs with a final ה (lamed-he), namely: yefifita mibnei adam (Psalms 45:3), whose root is y-p-h (“beautiful”). In it, both the first and the second radicals are doubled, and it belongs to the qal stem. By contrast, ḥamarmar belongs to the pa‘el stem. Nevertheless, it is also possible to derive from it its corresponding parent stem, and to say: ḥamarmar, ḥamarmarta, ḥamarmarti, for the grammarians have stated that from every root for which a derived stem exists, one may construct its parent stem — and likewise the reverse. Thus, from: yiqqaḥ na me‘at mayim (Genesis 18:4) and yitten mayim ‘al zera‘ (Leviticus 11:38), both of which are in the pa‘el stem, we may derive their parent hif‘il forms and say: ha-leqiḥa, ha-netina.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 13_: 9. Likewise, on the basis of a single attested form, one may construct the entire verbal paradigm. For example, from the word: hissamtaḥta kol ’oyevav (Psalms 89:43), we may also construct: • the participle: mesammiḥ, • the passive: mesummaḥ, • the infinitive and imperative: sameaḥ, • the imperfect (with prefix letters): ’esammeaḥ, yesammeaḥ. “May the LORD our God gladden us through His anointed servant.” Amen, selah.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 14_: Be strong, and let us be strengthened. May the scribe not be harmed.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 15_: The first part has been completed, namely the section on the verbs.
text.6_Second Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 16_: Now I shall begin the section on nouns, and I will explain all the patterns.
text.7_Third Treatise, 0_Subject, 0_Paragraph: On the elucidation of the noun patterns, divided into thirteen principles:
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 0_Par: The First Principle: On explaining what is meant by the term “pattern” and how nouns are measured.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 1_Par: Behold, I have already written in Treatise One, Principle Three, that all grammarians agreed to measure all verbs according to the pattern paʿal.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 2_Par: 1. And just as they did with verbs, so they did with nouns.
