For example, they measured ʾereṣ (“land”) according to the pattern paʿal, and ḥakham (“wise”) according to the pattern paʿal. Likewise, nouns that have an additional letter at the beginning or at the end, such as mishmar (“guard”), are measured according to the pattern mifʿal; zikaron (“remembrance”) according to the pattern paʿalon; and tifʾeret (“glory”) according to the pattern tifʿelet.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 3_Par: 2. Likewise, for nouns that come from defective or quiescent root classes, they assigned them the pattern paʿal as well. That is to say: whenever a letter of the noun is missing or quiescent, they likewise remove or quiet a corresponding letter from the pattern paʿal. For example, maṭṭaʿ (“planting”) and massaʾ (“burden”): since the root nun is missing in them, and since they have an added mem at the beginning, they said that they belong to the pattern maʿal. Likewise maṭṭarah (“purpose”) and mattanah (“gift”), in which the first radical of the pattern paʿal drops when prefixed by one of the letters b-k-l-m, and which have an added mem at the beginning and the feminine he at the end. Thus mattanah is measured according to the pattern maʿalah.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 4_Par: 3. Likewise, nouns from roots whose first radical is a quiescent yod, such as shanah (“year”), deʿah (“knowledge”), and ʿeṣah (“counsel”), in all of which the initial yod of the root drops, and which have the feminine he at the end, are measured according to the pattern ʿalah. Similarly, nouns from roots with a quiescent middle radical, such as ʾor (“light”) and yom (“day”), are measured according to the pattern pul; and sir (“pot”) and qir (“wall”) according to the pattern pil; and zar (“stranger”) and ṣar (“narrow / enemy”) according to the pattern pal.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 5_Par: 4. Likewise, when these quiescent forms appear with an added letter, such as maqom (“place”) and malon (“lodging”), they are measured according to the pattern mepul. Similarly, tavnit (“form”) and tarmit (“deceit”) are measured according to the pattern tifʿit. So it is with all nouns from all root classes. But be very careful when assigning a pattern, to know which letter is a root letter and which is a functional (servile) letter, lest it become a snare to you, as it is written, “for it will be a snare to you” (Exod. 23:33). This is especially important with verbs. For example, in “And I find more bitter than death” (Eccl. 7:26), the word moṣeʾ is measured according to the pattern poʿel, for it is a participle of the qal stem from the root maṣaʾ (“to find”). But in “He brings forth the wind from His treasuries” (Ps. 135:7), the word moṣiʾ comes from the root yaṣaʾ (“to go out”), and it is a participle of the hifʿil stem, and its pattern is moʿal.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 6_Par: 5. Likewise with nouns such as mapel in “making the ephah small” (Amos 8:6), which is measured according to the same pattern as makel (“staff”) in “a staff in the hand” (Ezek. 39:9). For mapel comes from a root defective in the first radical nun, with the mem added as a prefix, whereas makel comes from a complete root and the mem is a root letter. Similarly, maqom (“place”) is measured according to the pattern of shalom (“peace”): maqom belongs to the class of roots with a quiescent middle radical, while shalom comes from a complete root. Yet in the construct state and in the plural there is no distinction between them, and their vowel patterns change in the same way. I will explain each of these individually, according to its pattern and its principle.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 0_Par: The Second Principle: On elucidation of the causes for the change of vowel-points in nouns, which vowels are subject to change, and into which vowels they change.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that there are four causes that bring about changes in the vowel-points of nouns, and their mnemonic is SRNK: construct state, pluralization, femininity, and pronominal suffixes. The vowel-points that change in nouns are four: qamats, tsere, segol, and ḥolam, and the mnemonic for them is QTS–Ḥ. The sheva also changes in one of these cases, but it is not counted among them, since it is not considered a vowel, as will be explained in the chapter on prosody, in Song Six.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 2_Par: 2. The fundamental change of a tsere and a qamats is into a sheva, especially when they occur in the first letter of the word. But when they occur in the second letter, they revert to a pataḥ, as in davar → dvar-Hashem (“the word of the LORD,” Jer. 1:2), and from zaqen → zaqan beto (“the elder of his house,” Gen. 24:2). Likewise, in some singular pronominal suffixes they remain unchanged, as in devarekha, devarakh; but they change to a sheva in some plural suffixes and in the construct state, as in devarai, devarakhem, devarakhen, as you will see later in Principle Seven.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 3_Par: 3. The general rule is this: any noun from a complete root whose first vowel is a qamats will change to a sheva in all four of the changes mentioned above. The same rule applies when the first vowel is a tsere. The only difference between them is this: a qamats changes to a sheva in every noun, regardless of what the second vowel may be; but a tsere changes only when the second vowel is a qamats.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 4_Par: 4. For example, when the first vowel is a qamats, as in davar (“word”), gadol (“great”), qaṣir (“harvest”), and zaqen (“elder”): in the singular construct state you say dvar, gdal, qṣir, zqan; with singular pronominal suffixes: dvaro, gdalo, qṣiro, zqano; in the plural: dvarim, gdolim, qṣirim, zqenim; and with plural pronominal suffixes: dvarav, gdolav, qṣirav, zqenav. But in the plural construct state they appear with a ḥiriq, as in dvare, gdale, qṣire, zqene. I will reveal the reason for this later in this treatise, in Principle Six.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 5_Par: And there are four roots on the pattern paʿal that, in the construct state, remain on the pattern paʿal. They are: yerekh (“thigh”), katef (“shoulder”), gader (“wall”), and gazel (“robbery”). For example: yerekh Yaʿaqov (“the thigh of Jacob,” Gen. 32:25), katef ha-mizbeaḥ (“the shoulder of the altar”), gader avnav (“the wall of its stones,” Prov. 24:31), and gazel aḥ (“the robbery of a brother,” Ezek. 18:18).
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 6_Par: 5. As for those nouns whose first vowel is a tsere and whose second vowel is a qamats, such as levav (“heart”), ʿenav (“grape”), and shaʿar (“gate”), and the like: the tsere changes to a sheva in all four of the changes, and the qamats changes to a pataḥ in the singular construct only. Thus: levav, ʿenav, shaʿar; levavo, ʿenavo, shaʿaro; levavot, ʿenavim, shaʿarot. But when the second vowel is not a qamats, the initial tsere does not change, as in ʾefod bad (“a linen ephod,” 2 Sam. 6:14) and ʾevus bar (“a manger of grain,” Prov. 14:4); ʾefodo, ʾevuso. Likewise, in all four of the changes, it does not change.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 7_Par: 6. As for those nouns whose second vowel is a segol, such as sefer (“book”), ʿegel (“calf”), ʿesev (“grass”), and the like, they will be explained in the next principle. They are found with four vowel-points, that is, with two tseres, as in Helel ben Shaḥar (“O morning star, son of the dawn,” Isa. 14:12) and tevel ve-yoshveha (“the world and those who dwell in it,” Ps. 24:1), and they do not pluralize and do not take pronominal suffixes. But tevel hu (“it is a perversion,” Lev. 18:23), where tevel is used in the sense of abomination, is pointed with six vowel-points. And the mnemonic is: “Four things are small upon the earth” (Prov. 30:24), “Six things the LORD hates” (Prov. 6:16), and the discerning will understand. (Another sign is that every tevel meaning “earth” is accented on the final syllable.) A few nouns are found where the first vowel is qamats and the second is segol, such as ʾaven (“iniquity”), mavet (“death”), and ʿavel (“injustice”). In all of these the middle radical is vav, and therefore they should be counted among roots with a quiescent middle vav, as I will explain in the fourth treatise, Principle Four, Section Five.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 8_Par: 7. Know that the second vowel never changes except when it is a qamats, tsere, or segol. Qamats and tsere change to a pataḥ in the singular construct, as I wrote above; and all three change to a sheva in the plural construct and in some plural pronominal suffixes, as I will explain in Principle Six. But in the other types of change they do not change at all, except for a segol, as I will explain in Principle Three.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 0_Par: The Third Principle: On the elucidation of nouns that are vocalized with a segol.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that you will not find a noun whose first vowel is a segol unless the second vowel is also segol, such as beged (“garment”), qever (“grave”), ḥesed (“kindness”), ʿeved (“servant”), and the like. These constitute the greater part of nouns and are called “nouns of six vowel-points.” They are always accented on the penultimate syllable and do not change at all in the singular construct state, as in beged pishtim (“a linen garment,” Lev. 13:47) and ḥesed ʾEl (“the kindness of God,” Ps. 52:3). With a singular pronominal suffix, the first segol changes to a ḥiriq and the second to a sheva, as in bigdo (“his garment”) and qivro (“his grave”). But ḥasdo (“his kindness”) and ʿavdo (“his servant”) take a pataḥ, because of the gutturals ḥet and ʿayin.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 2_Par: 2. Many are also found with a pataḥ even without the presence of a guttural, such as from regel (“foot”) → raglo (“his foot”), and from gefen (“vine”) → gafno (“his vine”), and the like. However, in all the other types of change, they all follow the pattern of nouns with two qamats vowels. That is, just as you say from davar: dvarim, dvare, dvarav, so you say from beged: bgadim, bgade, bgadav; and from ḥesed: ḥasadim, ḥasde, ḥasdav.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 3_Par: 3. Know that there are some of these “six-vowel” nouns that at times appear with only five vowel-points. For example, neder (“vow”): five of its forms occur with five vowel-points, and the rest with six. Likewise sekhel (“understanding”): five of its forms occur with six vowel-points, and the remaining forms with five. Many others of this kind exist, and they are known on the basis of the tradition. I will present all of these in my larger work, which I have not yet begun, though thirty years ago—before it was even born— I already called it by name: Sefer ha-Zikhronot (“The Book of Remembrances”).
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 4_Par: 4. There are also nouns that always appear with five vowel-points, such as sefer (“book”), ʿegel (“calf”), ʿesev (“grass”), ḥelev (“fat”), and ḥeleq (“portion”). Most of these contain ḥet or ʿayin. But a noun whose first vowel is segol and whose second vowel is tsere is never found at all, as I hinted at the beginning of this principle.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 5_Par: 5. Know that nouns with six vowel-points differ from those that sometimes or always have five vowel-points in two respects. The first is this: when those with six vowel-points occur at a pause— that is, at etnaḥta or at the end of a verse— the first segol changes to qamats, as in af lekha ʾareṣ (“to you also belongs the land,” Ps. 89:12), and ʿarum yekhasseh ke-veged (“he covers the naked with a garment,” Ezek. 18:7). Some even change at zaqef, as in yihyeh li ʿeved (“he shall be my servant,” Gen. 44:17), and likewise mitḥareh ba-ʾerez (“competing with the cedar,” Jer. 22:15). Yet there are some that do not change at all, even at etnaḥta or at the end of a verse, such as melekh (“king”), teven (“straw”), and the like. Thus ʾareṣ is found unchanged in four places, and so on, in Proverbs and Psalms; and likewise kesef (“silver”) always changes, except in naḥpah ba-kesef (Ps. 68:14), where it remains with segol at etnaḥta. The general rule is that the accents of Job, Proverbs, and Psalms have different laws, as you will see in the book Tov Taʿam. But those nouns with five vowel-points never change to a qamats at a pause.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 6_Par: 6. The second difference is this: those nouns with six vowel-points sometimes take a ḥiriq and sometimes a pataḥ with a singular pronominal suffix, as I wrote above. But those with five vowel-points always take a ḥiriq, and even with guttural letters the ḥiriq usually does not change, as in: from ʿesev (“grass”) → ʿisvot harim (“the grass of the mountains,” Prov. 27:25), and from ʿeqev (“heel”) → ʿiqvot meshikhekha (“the footsteps of Your anointed,” Ps. 89:52). Some, however, change to a segol, as in ḥelqo, ʿeglo, ḥelvo; and in the plural construct: ḥelqe, ʿegle, ḥelve, and the like. By this method you can distinguish these from those.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 7_Par: 7. Know that for all of these nouns with six vowel-points, when the third radical is ḥet or ʿayin, the second segol changes to a pataḥ, as in ṣemaḥ (“plant”), peraḥ (“flower”), shevaḥ (“praise”), shevaʿ (“seven”), revaʿ (“quarter”). But if the second radical is ḥet or ʿayin, then both segol vowels change to pataḥ, as in shaḥal (“lion”), naʿar (“youth”), baʿar (“brutish”), naḥal (“stream”), shaḥar (“dawn”), and the like. However, paḥam (“coal”), gaḥal (“ember”), and kaḥash (“deceit”) belong to the class of doubled patterns. That is to say, if the ḥet were not present, they would follow the pattern of ganav (“thief”) or shabbat (“Sabbath”). The proof is that they do not change in the plural, for we say geḥalim, banim, keḥashim, since doubled nouns do not undergo change, as I showed in Principle Five.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 8_Par: 8. Furthermore, all of these are accented on the final syllable (milraʿ), whereas all the forms with pataḥ are always accented on the penultimate (milʿel), like those with six and five vowel-points. By this as well they are distinguished from those with two qamats vowels, for those are always accented milraʿ, such as zahav (“gold”), davar (“word”), and ʿashan (“smoke”), though there are a few exceptional cases.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 0_Par: The Fourth Principle: On the elucidation of the noun patterns whose first vowel is ḥolam.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that when the first vowel is ḥolam, it changes to a ḥatef qamats with singular pronominal suffixes, in the plural, in the construct state, and with pronominal suffixes— but only on the condition that the second vowel is a segol and not some other vowel. Thus with nouns such as ʾozen (“ear”), qodesh (“holiness”), and ḥodesh (“month”), and the like, one says: ʾozno, qodsho, ḥodsho; ʾoznayim; ʾozne; ʾoznav, and so forth. But in the singular construct state they do not change, as in ʾozen Aharon (“the ear of Aaron,” Exod. 29:20), and qodesh Hashem (“holy to the LORD,” Lev. 19:8), and similar cases.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 2_Par: 2. But when the second vowel is not segol, as in ʾotsar (“treasury”), kokhav (“star”), ʿolel (“child”), and the like, the initial ḥolam does not change at all. As for the qamats or tsere at the end, I have already written the manner of their change in the Second Principle, Section Two. Now, I wrote concerning nouns of six vowel-points, in the Third Principle, Section Seven, that because of ḥet or ʿayin the final segol changes to pataḥ; know that the same rule applies here as well, as in ʾoraḥ (“path”) and kovaʿ (“helmet”), so one says ʾorḥo, kivʿo, and so forth. But when the middle radical is one of the gutturals, the ḥatef qamats moves under the middle radical, and the first radical takes a qamats, as from ʾohel (“tent”): va-yeṭ ʾaholah (“and he pitched his tent,” Gen. 35:21); and from toʾar (“appearance”): mah toʾaro (“what is his appearance?” 1 Sam. 28:14). Yet sometimes the first radical remains with a ḥolam, as in toʾaro mi-benei ʾadam (“his appearance more than that of men,” Isa. 52:14).
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 0_Par: The Fifth Principle: On the elucidation of the noun patterns of the remaining vowel classes in general.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that nouns whose first vowel is shuruq are few, such as minnim and ʿugav (“strings and pipe,” Ps. 150:4), ʿagil and kumaz (Num. 31:50). With ḥatef qamats there is only a single example, namely maʿaseh yedei ʾoman (“the work of the hands of a craftsman,” Song 7:2). Thus there remains for me to explain only pataḥ, ḥiriq, and the “three-point” patterns. I will give you one general rule sufficient for all of them, namely: since these three are small vowels, it is proper that a dagesh follow them, as will be explained to you in the chapter on prosody, Song Five. Therefore, nouns with a doubled consonant do not change, such as ʾabbir (“mighty”), kabbir (“great”), gannav (“thief”), and sullam (“ladder”). Thus in the construct state one says ʾabbir ha-roʿim (“the mighty of the shepherds,” 1 Sam. 21:8), kabbir koaḥ (“great in power,” Job 36:5), and with pronominal suffixes ʾabbiro, kabiro. There are, however, a few exceptional cases that do undergo change.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 2_Par: 2. Know that nouns whose first vowel is sheva never have that sheva change, such as devash (“honey”), gevir (“lord”), zeʾev (“wolf”), ḥamor (“donkey”), and gevul (“boundary”). As for what is found in “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey” (Song of Songs 5:1), they say that it belongs to a different pattern, just as there are found, in all noun patterns, forms that depart from their general class. I will speak further about these in my introduction to the book Sefer ha-Harkavah.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 3_Par: 3. Know also that the vowel following an initial sheva does not change except when it is a qamats, as in ketav (“writing”), yaqar (“precious”), and the like. I have already explained, in the Second Principle, Section Two, the manner in which qamats changes. And when these forms come into the plural construct state, the initial sheva changes to a ḥiriq, as in kitvei and yiqrei. The reason for this I will explain in the next principle.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 0_Par: The Sixth Principle: On the elucidation of a preliminary rule concerning pronominal suffixes of nouns.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Here it is necessary for me to set before you a great rule concerning the law of sheva, for it is a principle and foundation in the use of pronominal suffixes, especially with complete roots. You already know that two shevas can never occur one after the other at the beginning of a word. And I have already informed you, in the Second Principle, Section Two, that qamats and tsere change to a sheva at the beginning of every noun.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 2_Par: 2. The same rule sometimes applies in the middle of a word as well. Therefore, whenever a noun begins with a sheva, or when a sheva arises because of one of the four changes that I explained at the beginning of the Second Principle, and that sheva is followed by a qamats or a tsere, and then another cause occurs that requires the qamats or tsere to change into a sheva, so that two shevas would come to stand at the beginning of the word— which is impossible— the first sheva therefore changes into a ḥiriq. For example, from dvarim (“words”) and zqenim (“elders”): when they come into the construct state, the final mem drops, as will be explained in this treatise in Principle Eleven. It then becomes necessary to lighten the vowels and to change the qamats or tsere into a sheva, as is their rule. This would result in two shevas at the beginning of the word, which is impossible. Therefore the first sheva is changed to a ḥiriq, and one says divrei and ziqnei.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 3_Par: 3. Likewise, with plural pronominal suffixes, all of the suffix forms are pronounced with a sheva at the beginning, such as devarav, ziqnav, devarekha, ziqnekha, except for those whose suffix ends with a mem or a nun. In those cases it is necessary to lighten the vowels and to change the qamats or tsere into a sheva; this would then result in two shevas, as in *dvarhem*, *zqenhem*—which is impossible. Therefore the first sheva is changed to a ḥiriq, and one says divreihem, ziqneihem, and the like.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 0_Par: The Seventh Principle: On the elucidation of pronominal suffixes.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that every noun has ten pronominal suffixes, and the letters used for them are six, whose mnemonic is “the suffixes.” Here are the ten suffixes in order, using davar (“word”) as the example: dvaro (“his word”), devarkha (“your [m.sg.] word”), devari (“my word”), dvaram (“their [m.] word”), devarkhem (“your [m.pl.] word”), dvarenu (“our word”), dvarah (“her word”), devarakh (“your [f.sg.] word”), dvaran (“their [f.] word”), devarkhen (“your [f.pl.] word”).
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 2_Par: 2. You can see that the first letter in all of them has a sheva, and the second has a qamats, except for those whose suffix ends with a mem or nun, in which the qamats of the middle radical changes to a sheva. This is because of the greater number of vowels they contain in comparison with the others. Here are the plural suffix forms from dvarim (“words”): dvarav, devarekha, dvarai, dvareihem, devarkhem, dvareinu, dvareha, devarekh, dvareihen, devarkhen.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 3_Par: 3. You will observe that with the letters b-k-l-m (the servile letters), the first letter is pointed with sheva, except in those forms whose suffix ends with mem or nun, in which case it is pointed with ḥiriq, so that two shevas do not occur at the beginning of the word, as I wrote in the preceding principle. And with b-k-l-m a yod appears before the suffix letter to indicate the plural.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 4_Par: 4. Know that pronominal suffixes attached to nouns always indicate possession, that is, the noun is the property of the one to whom the suffix refers. In the Ashkenazic tongue this is expressed as mein, dein, zain, and the like; and in the vernacular languages as mio, tuo, suo, or di me, di te, di quello, and so forth. Thus ʿavdo (“his servant”) and ʾamato (“his maidservant”) mean “a servant belonging to him” and “a maidservant belonging to him.” But pronominal suffixes attached to verbs indicate the object acted upon, as in peqado, peqadkha, peqadani. In the Ashkenazic tongue: ikh, dikh, mikh; and in the vernacular languages: mi, ti, quello, and the like. That is to say: “he visited him,” “he visited you,” “he visited me,” as I will explain to you clearly in the chapter on pronominal suffixes.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 5_Par: 2. Now, the seven letters that are used at the beginning of nouns have the mnemonic m-sh-h and k-l-b. And since, because of them, the vowel-points of nouns do not change, there is no need to explain them here. Their rules will be explained in the chapter on the servile letters.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 0_Par: The Eighth Principle: On the elucidation of the patterns of feminine nouns.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that nouns that appear in the feminine form are for the most part marked by a final he, with the letter before the he bearing a qamats, and the accent of the word falling on that letter with a qamats, as in: ṣedaqah (“righteousness”), ḥokhmah (“wisdom”), gezela (“robbery”), ʾakhilah (“eating”), simlah (“garment”), ʿavodah (“service”), melukhah (“kingship”), behalah (“terror”). In the construct state, the final he changes to tav, and the qamats changes to a pataḥ; but the other vowels do not change at all, except in those forms that follow the pattern paʿalah, such as ṣedaqah and berakhah (“blessing”). Thus, in the construct state one says ṣidqat Hashem (“the righteousness of the LORD,” Deut. 33:21) and birkat Hashem (“the blessing of the LORD,” Gen. 39:5). The kaf takes a light dagesh, in accordance with the rule of the letters begad kefat after a silent sheva in most cases; but with a pronominal suffix, as in birkato, the kaf is unaspirated (rafuyah), and likewise ṣidqato, and so forth.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 2_Par: 2. The reason for this is that the first qamats changes to a sheva; therefore it is necessary to change the first sheva into a ḥiriq, as I wrote in the Sixth Principle. But the other patterns do not change, as in ḥokhmah → ḥokhmato, gezela → gezalato, ʾakhilah → ʾakhilato, and the like.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 3_Par: 3. The general rule is this: the feminine he at the end of nouns has two identifying signs. The first is that a qamats always appears before it. The second is that the accent must fall on that letter which bears the qamats, that is, the word must be accented on the final syllable (milraʿ). If either of these two signs is lacking, then the he is not feminine, but is merely an added letter or a root letter. Thus in: qara laylah (“He called the light night,” Gen. 1:5), naḥalah Miṣrayim (“the brook of Egypt,” Num. 34:5), ʾarṣah Seʿir (“toward the land of Seir,” Gen. 32:3), and the like— in all of these the accent does not fall on the final syllable, and therefore the he is an added letter, not a feminine ending.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 4_Par: 4. And those cases in which the final he is a root letter belong to the class of roots whose third radical is he (nḥei lamed-he), as I will explain in the Fourth Treatise, Principle Seven, Sections Two and Three. There I will give you rules by which you may distinguish a merely added he from one that is truly part of the root.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 0_Par: The Ninth Principle: On the elucidation of the plural forms of feminine nouns.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 1_Par: a. Know that nouns which appear in the feminine plural are, for the most part, formed with a tav at the end, and the letter before it is pointed with a ḥolam together with a quiescent vav, such as ṣedāqōt, berākhōt, ḥokhmōt, and the like. In the construct state, for example: ṣidqōt Hashem — “the righteous acts of the LORD” (Judges 5:11), birkat avikha — “the blessing of your father” (Genesis 49:26). But in ḥokhmōt śārōtehā — “the wisdom of her princesses” (Judges 5:29), the vowel becomes a pataḥ, because of the presence of a guttural letter.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 2_Par: 2. And sometimes the vav is written, and sometimes it is not written. This is called male (plene) or ḥaser (defective) spelling, according to the Mesorah. Likewise, masculine plurals are sometimes found without a yod. For example, ha-tanninim (“the sea creatures”) occurs three times in Scripture with defective spelling; and tsaddiqim (“the righteous”) is written throughout the entire Torah without an additional yod. And there are very many similar cases. [In the Mantua edition: “as I will explain in my work *Masoret ha-Masoret*, if God wills.”]
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 3_Par: 3. And there are nouns that are feminine in the singular, marked with a final he, yet form their plural with yod–mem at the end, following the pattern of masculine plurals. Thus, for example: from shanah (“year”) comes shanim; from nemalah (“ant”) comes nemalim; and similar cases. Likewise, some masculine nouns occasionally form their plural according to the feminine pattern, such as av → avot, and bor → borot, and others like them. And there are nouns that occur in both ways, that is, sometimes with a masculine plural and sometimes with a feminine plural, such as: from ḥagor come ḥagurim and ḥagurot; from dor come dorim and dorot. All of this will be explained properly in the chapter on measures.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 0_Par: Principle Ten. An explanation of feminine nouns that appear in the singular with a final tav:
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 1_Par: 1. Know that just as, in the participle, the feminine singular form appears in two patterns — poqedah or poqedet, mefaqedah or mefaqedet, and likewise for all similar forms — and although, for the most part, they occur in the pattern poqedet, as I explained earlier (in Treatise Two, Principle One, Section Four), so too nouns in the feminine gender occur in these same two patterns. Nevertheless, in the majority of cases they appear with a final he, as I explained above in Principle Eight. In the following principle I will explain some of the distinctions between these two patterns.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 2_Par: 2. Know now that there are feminine nouns that appear with a final tav, and the letter preceding it is vocalized with a segol, such as qetoret and shibolet. In most cases, two segol vowels appear before it, as in adderet and ʿateret.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 3_Par: 3. Know that these feminine nouns occur only in these two patterns: either with two segol vowels, or with a ḥolam followed by a segol before the feminine tav. The same holds when a prefixed mem is added, as in migʿeret and mishqolet, and likewise when a prefixed tav is added, as in taḥboshet and tifʾeret. In all such cases, the vowel before the ḥolam or the segol never changes, whether or not a dagesh follows it.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 4_Par: 4. Know that their manner of vowel change and pointing—when they occur with guttural letters, or when they appear in pause—may all be learned and understood from three-letter nouns of this same pattern, those with ḥolam and segol, such as qetoret and similar forms. They follow the pattern of ḥadash and qodesh, that is, the ḥolam changes to a ḥaṭaf-qamats, as in qetorto, just as I explained in the Fourth Treatise.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 5_Par: 5. And those nouns whose vowels are two segols, such as ʿateret, follow the same pattern as the nouns with six vowel points. See what I have written about this in the Third and Fourth Principles.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 6_Par: But know that the first segol never changes to a ḥiriq, but only to a pataḥ, as in ʿatarato, tifʾarato, and the like— just as in regel → raglo, and similar forms.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 0_Pa: Principle Eleven. An elucidation of the pronominal suffixes of feminine nouns that end in he or tav, and an explanation of the difference between them.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that nouns whose feminine ending is a final he, when they take pronominal suffixes, change that he into a soft tav. Thus from tsedaqah one says tsidqato, tsidqati, tsidqatam, and so in all cases. But those nouns whose ending is an original tav appear in all singular pronominal suffixes with a dageshed tav. Thus from ateret and tiferet one says aterato, tiferato, ateratam, tiferatam. By this rule you may distinguish the two classes. Accordingly, forms such as milḥamto (“his war”) and mishmarto (“his charge”) show that their absolute forms are milḥemet and mishmeret. For if the absolute forms were milḥamah and mishmerah, their pronominal forms would be milḥamato and mishmerato with a soft tav. And those nouns that have a merely added a final he behave differently in pronominal forms: from miqneh one says miqneka, miqni, and the like; but in the other suffixes the he becomes vocalized, as in miqnehu, miqneha, miqnehem, miqnehon.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Know that feminine nouns in plural, when they take pronominal suffixes, may appear with either of the two plural markers: with yod, the marker of masculine plurality, or with tav, the marker of feminine plurality. Thus one says tsidqotav, tsidqotekha, and the like. Likewise, even those nouns which in the singular take pronominal suffixes with a dageshed tav, as explained above, appear in the plural pronominal forms with a soft tav, such as milḥamotav and mishmerotav. The reason for this is the presence of the ḥolem, after which a dagesh cannot properly occur.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. Know that nouns which are already in the plural, such as shifḥot (“maidservants”) and tsidqot (“righteous deeds”), may take pronominal suffixes for the third person in two different ways. The first way is with a mem of the suffix following the plural ending vav–tav, as in shifḥotam and tsidqotam. The second way is with a he following the plural ending vav–tav, as in shifḥotehem and tsidqotehem. However, forms such as shifḥatam and tsidqatam are pronominal forms of the singular feminine, as I explained above. This is what Rabbi Shelomo Yirḥi (Rashi) explained regarding the verse va-tikhl telunatam (Numbers 17:25). These are his words: “There is a distinction between telunatam and telunotehem: telunatam refers to a single complaint, whereas telunotehem is a noun in the singular form, even if there are many complaints.” Up to here are his words. However, the rabbi did not explicitly explain the grammatical difference between telunatam and telunotehem.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 4_Pa: 4. And I will now explain the difference between them by way of an example. Suppose there are Reʾuven and Shimʿon who together own a single maidservant. Of her we say: “This is their maidservant,” that is, shifḥatam, belonging jointly to Reʾuven and Shimʿon. But if each of them owns one maidservant, we say of them: shifḥotam (“their maidservants”). And if each of them owns two or three maidservants, we say of them: shifḥotehem (“their maidservants” in the fuller plural). I have already resolved to compose a separate book in which I will explain all the grammatical remarks made by Rabbi Shelomo Yirḥi of blessed memory in his commentary on the Torah, if the blessed Name should prolong my life.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 0_Pa: The Twelfth Principle: An elucidation of nouns in which an additional letter is added beyond the three root letters.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that the additional letters found in nouns are six in number, and their mnemonic is ha’emaneti. Sometimes they are added at the beginning, sometimes at the end, and sometimes at both the beginning and the end. However, they are added only to nouns that are derived from verbs, as will be explained in the chapter on categories, in the second category. I will now explain them one by one in the remaining principles, that is, each principle corresponding to one of the three root letters.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. The letter he is not found as an added prefix at the beginning of complete nouns, except in two nouns only, namely ravah and shama. From ravah we find the form harvakhah, and from shama we find lehashma‘at oznayim (Ezekiel 24:26). Aside from these, no other examples occur among complete nouns. However, among nouns that are not complete, additional occurrences are found, as will be explained in their proper places. At the end of nouns, by contrast, three kinds of he are found: some are root letters, some mark the feminine, and some are merely added letters, as I explained in Principle Eight.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. The letter alef is found as an added letter in many places, and for the most part it is vocalized with a segol, as in etsba, esgav, eshkol, egrof. Sometimes it appears with a pataḥ, as in avnet, avrekh, akhziv. After the letters of amanati there is always a resting sheva. Some nouns in which alef appears have it as a root letter; these belong to the class of four-letter nouns, and I will discuss them in the next treatise, Principle Thirteen. Know further that most nouns formed with an added letter from among the letters of amanati do not take the feminine he ending, except in a few rare cases, such as mishmerah, tifarah, and very few others.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 4_Pa: 4. Know further that an added alef does not occur at the end of nouns in the Hebrew language. In the language of the Targum, however, it commonly appears, as in malka, avda. Nevertheless, there are cases where alef is a root letter at the end, such as kise and pele; these belong to the class of roots whose third radical is alef (nḥei lamed-alef), and I will explain them there. There are also cases where alef appears in place of he, as in kematra laḥats and karan li mara.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 5_Pa: 5. The letter mem may be added at the beginning of nouns. For the most part it is pointed with a ḥiriq, followed by a silent sheva, and the final vowel is a qamats, as in mishkan, miqdash. Sometimes it appears with a ḥolam, as in mizmor and mikhlol. When a guttural letter follows the mem, the mem is pointed with a pataḥ, as in maʾakhal and maḥshof. Even without a guttural, such forms may occur, and in those cases they usually appear with doubling in the plural and with suffixes, as in mitʿam, midbar, maḥmad. Thus one says: mitʿamo, midbaro, maḥmადო, mitʿamim, marbadim, maḥmadim. There are also a few doubled forms with a ḥiriq, as from misgav, yielding misgavi. All such doubled forms have pataḥ as their final vowel, but forms ending in a qamats or a ḥolam never take doubling.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 6_Pa: 6. And you already know that nouns whose final vowel is a qamats change to apataḥ in the construct state, as in miqdash Hashem tameʾ, mishkan Hashem, mikol maʾakhal Parʿoh. Some also appear with a feminine he at the end, with the mem pointed with a ḥiriq, a pataḥ, or a segol, as in milḥamah, mamlakhah, memshalah. In the construct state one says milḥemat Kenaʿan, mamlekhet ʿOg, lememshelet ha-yom. This pattern is also found outside the construct, as in misgeret ṭofaḥ, et ha-migʿeret, or with a ḥolam, as in mishqoleth and maḥagoreth. I have already written their rules in Principle Ten. There are also nouns that appear with an added mem at the end, such as pitʾom and shilshom, though these are few. But the mem that appears at the end of nouns to indicate the plural, as in devarim and zekharim, is not called an added letter but a functional one. It is preceded by a full ḥiriq, that is, with a yod. When such a noun enters the construct state, the mem drops away and the yod remains by itself, and the preceding letter is pointed with a tsere, as in zeqenei and divrei.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 0_Pa: 13. The Thirteenth Principle. On the explanation of the vowel patterns of nouns that contain an added nun, tav, or yod, whether at the beginning or at the end.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that the letter nun is not added at the beginning of nouns, except in a few cases that are proper names, such as Naftali, Nimrod, and the like.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Know that at the end of nouns the letter nun is very often added. Most commonly, the first radical is pointed with a ḥiriq, as in zikaron (“remembrance”) and shilton (“rule”), and the final syllable takes a qamats, as in pishtan (“flax”) and ḥartzan (“grape-stone”). There are also a few cases in which the first syllable has a ḥaṭaf-qamats or a qubbuts, such as qorban (“offering”) and shulḥan (“table”). These form their feminine plural with -ot, for example qorbanot and shulḥanot. Many nouns, however, have a final nun that is part of the root itself; these belong to the class of four-letter nouns, such as hashman and darban, and I will discuss them in the following treatise, in the Thirteenth Principle. There are also many nouns of this type that are geminated, such as zikaron and shibaron, and likewise some in which the middle radical has a sheva, for example kalshon and qamshon, though such geminated forms are relatively few.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. The letter tav is added at the beginning of nouns. In most cases it is pointed with a pataḥ, even without the presence of a guttural, and it is followed by a sheva naḥ. The final vowel is most often shuruq, as in tamrud, tamruq, and taʿanug. A few forms are found with ḥiriq or tsere, such as talmid, tavrik, tarshish, and tashbits. There are also cases in which the tav is pointed with a ḥiriq, as in tidhar. In addition, there are nouns that have tav both at the beginning and at the end, such as talbushet and tifʾeret. All of these forms are accented on the penultimate syllable (milʿel).
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 4_Pa: 4. There are also nouns in which a tav is added at the end but not at the beginning. In these, the letter immediately before the tav is pointed with a shuruq, and the first radical has pataḥ, as in malkhut, gevahut, mardut, and shaḥrut. There are also cases in which the first radical has a ḥiriq, such as refuʾut, shiflut, and ʿiqshut. Others have a sheva on the first radical followed by a ḥiriq, as in yedidut and meridut. The proper plural of all these forms should be made with a mobile yod, that is, with the masculine-style plural ending. Thus, just as from malkhut we find the plural malkhuyot, so too one should say kilyot, ʿiqshuyot, and gevahuyot.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 5_Pa: 5. There are also nouns in which a tav is added at the end and the vowel before it is a ḥiriq, such as gofrit, sheʾerit, reʾshit, ḥamishit, and the like. These too form their plural with a mobile yod, following the pattern found in the Talmud, such as ḥamishiyyot, and accordingly one should say reʾshiyyot. This is especially the case for those whose third radical is he, as I will explain in the Fourth Treatise, Principle Seven.
text.7_Third Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 6_Pa: 6. The letter yod is most often found added at the beginning of proper nouns, such as Yitsḥaq, Yaʿaqov, Yitshar, and the like. It is also found in words such as yalqut and yanshuf, and sometimes with a ḥolam, as in yanshuf and ʿorev, following the pattern of sappir and yahalom. At the end of proper nouns it is found only rarely, as in nahari and naʿari and a few similar cases. However, in words such as yehudi, mitsri, and ʿivri, the final yod is not an added letter, but rather a marker of relation or attribution, as will be explained in the chapter on categories.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 0_Subject, 0_Paragrap: On the elucidation of the patterns of nouns that are not complete, and it is also divided into thirteen principles:
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 0_Pa: The first principle. An elucidation of nouns whose first radical nun is deficient (ḥaserei peʾah-nun).
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that all nouns whose first radical nun is deficient (ḥaserei peʾah-nun) appear with an added mem at the beginning. This mem is always vocalized with a pataḥ, and a dagesh follows it, in order to indicate the missing nun. Thus, for example: mattaʿ (“planting”), whose root is nataʿ, and massaʿ (“journey”), whose root is nasaʿ. Likewise mabboʿa (“spring”) and mabbul (“flood”), whose roots are navaʿ and naval. These nouns also occur with the feminine he ending, such as mappēla (“downfall”) and mattara (“target”), and with a tsere, such as maggēfa (“plague”) and massēkha (“molten image”), and the like. The same rule applies to nouns deficient in an initial yod, for their grammatical treatment is identical to that of nouns deficient in an initial nun, as explained in the Second Treatise, Principle Six, Section Six.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Know that nouns which are geminated (i.e., marked by a dagesh) do not undergo vowel change, as explained in the Third Treatise, Principle Five, Section One. Accordingly, nouns deficient in the first radical that pattern with quiescent lamed behave in the same way, such as makkeh and matsah, whose roots are nakah and natsah, and whose final he marks the feminine. By contrast, qatsar ha-matsah (“the covering is too short”) has the root yatsaʿ. Some nouns have a final he that is truly part of the root, such as matteh; the proof that the he is radical is that it is preceded by a segol. This will be explained further in this Treatise, Principle Six. Likewise, among nouns deficient at the end we find mattan, and among those deficient at both ends mattet.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 0_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. Know that every noun you find with an initial mem bearing a pataḥ and followed by a dagesh is a noun deficient in an initial nun. There are also two such nouns with an added he at the beginning and a dagesh following it, such as ruaḥ ve-hatsalah (“relief and deliverance”) and hakkarat penehem (“the recognition of their faces”), whose roots are natsal and nakhar. There are also two nouns of this class that appear without any added letter at the beginning, namely si and sig, as in ya‘aleh la-shamayim si’o (“his height rises to the heavens”) and ve-khi sig lo (“and when he mocks him”), whose roots are nasa and nasag. However, no general rule can be derived from these, for they are very few.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 0_Pa: The second principle. On the elucidation of nouns with a quiescent first radical aleph or yod.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that a letter can never be quiescent at the beginning of a word. Therefore, nouns of this class appear at the beginning of a word in the same manner as complete roots, for example: from *amar* comes *omer*; and from *akhal* come *okhel* or *akhilah*. They are also found with an added mem at the beginning, such as *ma’amar* and *ma’akhal*, with the aleph remaining sounded. Likewise, in the middle of a word the letter does not become quiescent, as in: from *sha’al* come *she’elah* or *mish’al*.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Nouns whose first radical is a quiescent yod are, for the most part, formed with an added mem or tav at the beginning, and are vocalized with a ḥolam, as in motsa and moshav, with a qamats at the end. They are also found with a tsere at the end, such as mo‘ed and moqesh. Know that those which have a qamats in the singular will also retain a qamats in the plural, for example: from moshav and motsa one says moshavim and motsa’ot. But those which have a tsere will take a sheva in the plural, such as mofet and moqesh, yielding mofetim and moqshim. All of these are accented on the final syllable (milra‘).
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 3_Pa: Know that you already understand the alternation of a qamats and a tsere at the end of words. Such nouns are also found with an added tav, for example toshav → toshavim. However, for the most part, those which have tav at the beginning appear with a feminine he at the end, such as toledah and tokhaḥah. Likewise, among nouns with quiescent final radicals one says torah and todah, derived from the roots yarah and yadah. There are also forms with tav both at the beginning and at the end, such as to‘elet and tokhelet. A few are found with a mem at the beginning and a he at the end, such as mo‘etsah and morashah. The rule is: any noun that you find with a mem or a tav at the beginning and vocalized with a ḥolam belongs to the class of nouns whose first radical is a quiescent yod. There are two exceptions to this rule, namely morakh (“faintness”) and ma‘al (“trespass”), which belong to the class of doubled roots.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 1_Principle, 4_Pa: And only a few are found in which the mem is vocalized with a shuruq, such as musar and mutsaq. There are also forms found without any added letter and with a feminine he, such as shanah, ‘etsah, de‘ah, and ledah. In the construct state, the tsere in these forms changes to a sheva, and the qamats changes to a pataḥ, as explained in the First Treatise, Second Principle. There are also two forms found without the feminine he, namely tse (as in “say to him, go out”) and bul (as in “the produce of the mountains”). Their roots are yatsa and yakhol.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 0_Pa: The third principle. An elucidation of nouns with a quiescent middle letter (ayin) that occur with an added letter:
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that most nouns with a quiescent middle letter (ayin) occur with an added mem, vocalized with a qamats, such as maqom, malon, manos. In the construct state and with pronominal suffixes, this qamats properly changes to a sheva, as in maqom → meqomo, malono, menusi, in accordance with the rule for complete forms. For this reason, those who recite in the hymn Adon Olam the phrase “hu nissi u-menusi” with the mem of menusi in qamats are mistaken, for its correct vocalization is menusi with a sheva, as required by the transformation of a qamats to a sheva in pronominal forms. Indeed, we similarly find misgavi and menusi. However, in the metrical structure of that poem this form cannot stand, since a yated (metrical peg) is required there, and a shuruq followed by sheva does not constitute a yated. Therefore, the correct reading must be u-menos li. Yet cantors have grown accustomed to saying “hu nissi u-menusi, manat kosi” in order to preserve the rhyme. When such nouns occur with a feminine he ending, the mem always takes a sheva and is followed by a shuruq, as in meshuva, melukha, mevukha. Likewise, this pattern appears with an added tav at the beginning, as in tequma, teluna. But without a feminine he ending, this pattern never appears with an added mem or tav.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 2_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. And the general rule is this: any noun of this class that you find with an added mem at the beginning, vocalized with a qamats, and which in its four inflectional forms takes either a mem or a tav with sheva, belongs to the class of nouns with a quiescent middle letter (nḥei ʿayin). There are two such nouns that appear with an added tav at the end, namely nofet and bōshet. I have already informed you, in the Third Treatise, Principle Eleven, Section Five, that a tav of this kind appears with a dagesh when pronominal suffixes are attached, as in levashtakha and levōshet. Accordingly, one should likewise say nofeti, noftekha from nofet. There is also one example with an added mem at the end, namely reqem.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 0_Pa: The fourth principle. An elucidation of nouns whose middle radical is quiescent ʿayin, which occur without the addition of any extra letter:
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that there are nouns belonging to this class that occur without any added letter, and these consist of only two letters. In all of them, the first radical is pointed with one of the five “major” vowels: • with a qamats, as in: zar, tsar, raʿ; • with a tsere, as in: ger, tsad, ʿed; • with a ḥiriq, as in: sir, qir, ʿir; • with a ḥolam, as in: ʾor, yom, tov; • and with a shuruq, as in: shur, dor.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. But they are not found with the minor vowels. Most of them do not undergo any change, and those that do change do so in different ways. For example, from yom (“day”) the plural and its pronominal forms come with a qamats, as in yamim, yamav, and so forth. Likewise from rosh (“head”) come rashim, rashav. Apart from these, there are no others.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 3_Pa: And tov (“good”) comes in the construct state and with pronominal suffixes in shuruq, as in tov, tovo, and the like—this is when it is a noun. But when it is an adjective, it does not change. See the roots in the work of Rabbi David Kimhi.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 4_Pa: 3. And those with a qamats or a tsere do not change at all, and the reason for this will be explained to you in this treatise, Principle Eight. Likewise, those with a ḥiriq or a shuruq mostly do not change. The exceptions are as follows: ʿir (“city”) forms its plural with a mobile yod, as in ʿirim and ʿirot; shoq (“leg” or “thigh”) forms its plural with a mobile vav, shoqim; and from qots (“lock of hair”) comes qotsotav. Likewise, from dud (“pot”) we find the forms sirōt and dudim.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 5_Pa: 4. There are also cases in which a mobile yod appears in singular, such as bayit (“house”), ʿayin (“eye”), zayit (“olive”), layil (“night”), ḥayil (“strength”), and ʿir (“city”). All of these are accented on the penultimate syllable; were this not so, the yod would have to be doubled, as is the rule after a short vowel. In all four types of inflection, the yod becomes quiescent with a tsere, as in bayit, bayto; zayit, zayto, zaytim; layil, laylo, leilot; ayil, ayilim; ḥayil, ḥaylo. The plural with a mobile yod also appears in the plural form ḥayilim. Likewise, from ʿir comes ʿirim, and the pronominal form is ʿiro, with ḥiriq. The word batim (“houses”) is very exceptional, in that it has a doubled consonant after a long vowel and is accented on the final syllable.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 3_Principle, 6_Pa: 5. There are also cases in which a mobile vav appears in singular, such as ʾon (“iniquity”), ʿol (“yoke”), mot (“death”), and tokh (“midst”), with a qamats or a segol. These have no parallel among the regular (complete) patterns, as I mentioned in the Third Treatise, Principle Two, Section Seven. In the construct state and with pronominal suffixes, the vav becomes quiescent in most of them, as in betokh ha-ʿir (“in the midst of the city”) and mot yesharim (“the death of the upright”). Likewise with suffixes: lifnei moto (“before his death”), el tokho (“into its midst”), mehashivat ʾonakh (“from turning away your iniquity”). When a he is added at the end, the vav remains mobile, as in mota and ʿola. We also find a mobile vav before a suffix, as in be-ʿavla asher ʿasa (“in the wrongdoing that he committed”). This sheva belongs to the same pattern, but it has been lightened and the segol has changed to a sheva because of the quiescence of the aleph, whose proper vowel is a sheva.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 0_Pa: The fifth principle. An elucidation of nouns whose third radical is quiescent aleph (naḥei lamed-aleph):
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that most of these nouns have three full vowels, such as kela, pela, geva, and tena. They follow the pattern of the regular (complete) nouns, sometimes taking a ḥiriq with pronominal suffixes, as in kelao and pelao, and sometimes a pataḥ, as in tenaʾkha.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Some are found on the pattern paʿal, such as tsama and tsava, and some on the pattern poʿal, such as guma and sova. There is one that appears with a doubled consonant, namely kisse (“throne”). It does not change in the construct state, but with pronominal suffixes the tsere changes to a sheva and the doubling falls away, as in kiso and kisakha. In the plural it appears in the feminine form, as in kisaʾot.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 4_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. ḥeṭʾ (“sin”) also belongs to this pattern. It would properly have been ḥaṭaʾ, but it has been lightened, just as a sheva is lightened from the pattern paʿal, as I explained earlier. Now the ḥet of ḥeṭʾ has a tsere, following the pattern of those nouns with five vowels. Therefore, with pronominal suffixes the ḥet comes with a segol, as in ḥeṭo and ḥeṭam, as explained in the Third Principle of the First Treatise, Section Six; and in the plural ḥeṭaʾim. But in the phrase derekh ḥaṭaʾim (“the way of sinners”), it is an adjective belonging to the class of doubled forms, which do not change. Accordingly, in the construct state and with plural suffixes one says ḥaṭaʾei, as in ḥaṭaʾei (“sinners of”) and ʿami u-ḥaṭaʾeha yashmid (“He will destroy my people and its sins”).
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 0_Pa: The sixth principle. An elucidation of nouns whose third radical is quiescent he (naḥei lamed-he):
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that nouns whose third radical is quiescent he usually occur with an added mem or tav at the beginning. They are vowelled with a ḥiriq, followed by a quiescent sheva, as in mitsvah, minḥah, tiqvah, and tikhlah. When a guttural letter follows, the vowel is a pataḥ, as in maḥatsah, maḥtah, and taʾavah.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Know that all of these final he letters mark the feminine form. The proof is that they are accented on the final syllable, and furthermore that the he changes to a soft tav in the construct state and with pronominal suffixes, as is the rule for a feminine he, for example: mitsvot Hashem (“the commandments of the Lord”), minḥat Yehudah (“the offering of Judah”), mitsvato (“his commandment”), taʾavato (“his desire”). A few cases are found in which the he is merely an added letter, such as from ʿalah (“to go up”), maʿalah (“ascent”), and similar forms. These are accented on the penultimate syllable, as I explained in the Third Treatise, Principle Eight, Section Two.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 5_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. However, many cases are found in which the final he is a root letter. In such cases it is always preceded by a segol, as in miqneh, miqreh, and mishneh. If the first radical is a guttural, as in maḥaneh (“camp”) or maʿaseh (“deed”), the same rule applies. By this they are distinguished from the feminine he and from an added he, for those always have qamats before them. Moreover, these forms do not change in the construct state or with pronominal suffixes, except that the segol changes to a tsere, as in maḥaneh Dan (“the camp of Dan”) and mirʿeh ʿadarim (“a pasture of flocks”). However, when a tav is added at the beginning, a root he is never found. And with pronominal suffixes the he always drops away, as in miqnehu, mishnehu, maʿasehu. Likewise with suffixes using vav for the masculine, as in yadehu (“his hand”) and raglehu (“his foot”). In forms such as miqni, miqnekha, miqnam, and the like, the he is absent in all of them.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 0_Pa: The seventh principle. An elucidation of nouns whose third radical is quiescent he, which occur with an added tav or mem at the beginning, and with a tav at the end:
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that there are nouns from this class that occur with an added mem at the beginning and a tav at the end, such as maskit and marbit; and others with a tav both at the beginning and at the end, such as tavnit and takhlit.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Know that these forms ought properly to be marbiyyit and tavniyyit, with three yods. One yod is the connective yod, like the one that appears after the third radical in the participle of the hifʿil pattern (as in mafqid → mafqidah). The second yod stands in place of the final he of the root, since their roots are ravah and banah. The third is the yod of relation, as in ʿivrit (“Hebrew”) and mitsrit (“Egyptian”). All of these form their plurals with a mobile yod, following the pattern ḥamishiyyot, as I wrote in the Third Treatise, Principle Thirteen. I will speak of these further in my book on composition, under the word mavligiti.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. There are also forms on this pattern in which the final vowel is shuruq. This occurs specifically when there is a tav at the beginning, as in tarbut (“increase”) and taznut (“licentiousness”). A parallel case is found with an initial mem, as in matsotekha (“those who contend with you”), whose singular form is matsah. The expected form would have been mintsah, since its root is natsah. A similar formation is found in the language of the Mishnah, malkot (“lashes”), derived from the root laqah.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 6_Principle, 4_Pa: 4. And remember that the mem and the tav that appear at the beginning of these forms are always vocalized with pataḥ, even without the presence of a guttural letter. One additional case is found with an added alef at the beginning, as in aḥoti be-ozneikhem (“my utterance in your ears”), whose root is ḥavah. The general rule is this: any noun that you find with an initial mem or tav vocalized with ḥiriq or pataḥ, and with the following letter bearing a sheva, and which is not from the class of complete roots (that is, it does not contain three fully vocalized radicals), belongs to the class of roots whose third radical is he (naḥei lamed-he). Only two exceptions are found with an initial tav bearing sheva, namely ta‘alah and tela’ah.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 0_Pa: The eighth principle. An elucidation of nouns from the class whose third radical is he (naḥei lamed-he) that come without any additional letter at the beginning, and that end with a feminine he.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that there are additional nouns from this class that appear with a feminine he at the end. Some of them have the first radical with a qamats, such as safah, manah; and some with a tsere, such as me’ah, pe’ah. All of them change to a sheva at the beginning, according to their rule.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 7_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. However, nouns of the class with a quiescent middle letter ayin that come on these two patterns do not change at all. Thus, from qamah and tsarah, in the construct state qamat, tsarat, and in the plural qamim, tsarim, the qamats does not change. Likewise, those with a tsere from quiescent ayin roots: one says tsid, shiv, tsidah, shivah; and in the construct tsadat. Likewise shivath avdekha (“the life of your servant”), where the tsere does not change. The reason for this is that roots with a quiescent ayin always require a full (long) vowel to indicate the quiescent root vav that follows the qamats; therefore they do not undergo change. But in safah, manah, pe’ah, me’ah, where the long vowel at the first radical does not serve to indicate quiescence, they do change, and one says sefat, pe’at, and the like. Remember this well, for it is a great general rule. I will speak further about this in the class of doubled roots in the Eleventh Principle, Section Four. Those that come with a root he at the end I will explain in the following principle.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 0_Pa: 9. The ninth principle. An elucidation of nouns from roots with a quiescent final he that come with a root he at the end:
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that the nouns which come with a he as an essential root letter are few, such as gaʾeh (“proud”) and ram (“exalted”), as in “the proud and exalted” (Isaiah 2:12), and goh, as in “it went out from his body” (Job 20:25). They also occur with a segol, as in gaʾeh meʾod (“very proud,” Jeremiah 48:29), and reʿeh David (“David’s companion,” 2 Samuel 15:37). In the plural one says geʾim (“the proud”) and reʿim. From gaʾeh with a qamats comes geʾe yonim (“the pride of the oppressors,” Psalms 123:4), with a mobile yod. Likewise, from goh the waw is transformed into a mobile yod in construct forms, as in begviyyat ha-aryeh (“in the carcass of the lion,” Judges 14:8), and the plural is gviyyot (“corpses,” Psalms 110:6).
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Know that there are many nouns of this class in which the final he is transformed into a quiescent yod at the end of the word, with a ḥiriq before it. They fall into four types. The first type has an initial qamats, such as tsali and qali. In the construct state the vowel reduces to sheva, as tsli and qli, and in the plural one says aniyyim, neqiyyim. The second type has an initial sheva, such as shevi, peri, meri, and keli. Sometimes these shift to a segol in pause, as meri, keli, or to a tsere, as in ḥatsi. With suffixes one says shivkha, merkha, telikha, or with ḥiriq shivyo, neshikha, and in the plural shivhem, shivkhem, perim or perhem. See Radak under the pattern paʿi. The third type has an initial ḥolam, such as ḥoli, ʿoni, tsori, and ḥeri. In the construct state and with suffixes they revert to a ḥataf-qamats, as ḥolyo, even though the final vowel is not a segol, as I explained in the Third Treatise, Fourth Principle, Section Two. They are also found with a ḥataf-qamats even without construction, as in “all sickness” and “what burning.” The fourth type has an initial segol, such as meshi, peti, and qeri. With suffixes the yod becomes mobile, as kerim. Rabbi Solomon ibn Gabirol also said in one of his poems “garments of meshim,” meaning “their silk.”
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 8_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. The patterns just mentioned sometimes also appear with an added tav at the end, such as ʿamit and tsofit. Some occur with a final ḥolam, such as aḥot and ḥamot. In the construct state and with suffixes they revert to sheva, as ʿamitkha, aḥotkha, ḥamotkha, and the like. There are also forms with sheva at the beginning even without construction, such as ḥanit and shevit. At times they appear with a final shuruq, such as galut and ḥazut, and with an initial sheva, as shevut and pedut. I have already explained the method of their pluralization in the Third Treatise, Thirteenth Principle, Section Five. There are also forms with an added nun at the end, such as ratson and qalon. In these, the quiescent vav stands in place of the final radical he, and the nun is an addition. Others are found with an added nun and a mobile yod in place of the final he, such as binyan, inyan, and qinyan.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 0_Pa: The tenth principle. An elucidation of nouns from the class of roots with a quiescent final he (naḥei lamed-he) that consist of two letters:
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 1_Pa: 1. Know that there are nouns of this class that appear without any additional letter, and in them the final he of the root is lacking. As a result, they consist of only two letters. Some of them always take a qamats, some always take a pataḥ, and some are sometimes with a qamats and sometimes with a pataḥ. These are determined by tradition, such as: av (father), yad (hand), dag (fish), qav la-qav (“line upon line”), tsav la-tsav (“command upon command”). All of these intermingle with the classes of roots with a quiescent middle letter (naḥei ʿayin) and with doubled roots. In the following principle I will give you signs and rules by which you may distinguish these from one another. There are also some that are pointed with a ḥiriq and a quiescent yod. These are nouns derived from roots whose middle radical is one of the letters vav or yod. Thus, from the root ravah comes ri, as in “even the pure ones” (af beri); from naḥah comes ni, as in “a lament from among their sons” (min benehem qinah); from tsiyah comes tsi, as in “a mighty fleet” (tsi adir); and from kavah comes ki, as in “instead of beauty” (taḥat yofi). In all of these cases, the yod stands in place of the root he, and the middle radical is absent.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 2_Pa: 2. Know that pi (“mouth of”) does not belong to this class, for its root is peh, which consists of only two letters, on the pattern of seh. It is one and the same form both in the construct state and with a pronominal suffix referring to the speaker himself. That is to say, there is no difference between pi Hashem (“the mouth of the Lord”) and pi ha-medabber aleikhem (“the mouth of the one speaking to you”). Strictly speaking, it ought to have been piy, but because of the heaviness of two yods, one of them was dropped. According to the context, you will recognize in each place whether it is a construct form or a pronominal suffix.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 9_Principle, 3_Pa: 3. And the general rule is this: everything I have stated in this principle and in the preceding one—that any noun of two letters which has an added tav at the end, preceded by a ḥiriq or a shuruq, or which has a quiescent yod at the end, whether it consists of two moving letters, or of one, or whether it has a moving yod after two root letters—belongs to the class of roots whose third radical is he (nḥei lamed-he). Examine this carefully and you will find it to be so. What I said—specifically “after two root letters”—was meant to exclude the sound (i.e., complete/regular) roots and the nḥei ʿayin roots. For when a yod appears in sound roots, it comes after three root letters, as in ḥamishiyyot and the like; and in nḥei ʿayin roots it comes after the first letter, as in bayit, zayit, and so on. I also did not include in this rule every noun that has a final nun preceded by a ḥolam, such as ratzon, kalon, lest you be misled by nouns in which the nun is a root letter, such as aron, adon, and likewise madon, which is from the nḥei ʿayin class, with root letters d-w-n.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 0_P: 11. The eleventh principle. In explanation of nouns from doubled roots that occur with the loss of a letter:
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 1_P: 1. Know that most nouns derived from doubled roots come with the loss of one of the doubled letters, in the same manner as verbs of doubled roots. As a result, only two letters remain, such as dal, tal, sal, taf. Most of these are vocalized with pataḥ, while some are vocalized with a qamats, as determined by tradition. Many are also found with a ḥolam, such as oz, ḥom, ol, qor, and others with a tsere, such as ḥen, shen, tsel. All those with a qamats and a tsere follow the same patterns of inflection as nouns with a quiescent middle letter (nḥei ayin) and those with a quiescent final letter (nḥei lamed), as I have already shown you in their respective weights and governing principles.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 2_P: 2. And I will give you a sign by which you may recognize which nouns belong to the class of those with a quiescent middle letter (nḥei ayin), which to those with a quiescent final letter (nḥei lamed), and which to the doubled roots. This is the rule: nouns of doubled roots ought, by their nature, to appear with a dagesh, in order to indicate the doubling of the two identical letters. However, it is impossible to place a dagesh forte on one of them when it stands at the beginning of a word, since a dagesh forte never occurs at the beginning of a word. This will be explained to you in the chapter on Shirah, in Song Eight.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 3_P: And at the end of a word a dagesh can never occur. Therefore, when you encounter a noun consisting of only two letters and you do not know to which class it belongs, you may test it in the following way: If it is capable of receiving a dagesh in its pronominal suffixes, or in its plural forms, or when combined with the feminine he, then it belongs to the class of doubled roots.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 4_P: 3. And the example is from zakh. If you wish to know from which class it comes, place at its end a letter of plurality, or of a pronominal suffix, or the feminine he, and you will find: zakkim, zakkav, zakkah. All of these take a dagesh; therefore they belong to the class of doubled roots. And from ḥag you say ḥaggim, ḥaggo; all with a dagesh, so they too are from the doubled class. But from dag you say dagim, dagah, with the gimel remaining soft. Therefore it is from the class of quiescent roots. And I have already given you a sign in this treatise, in the Eighth Principle, by which you may distinguish quiescent middle-letter roots from quiescent final-letter roots. I explained there that quiescent middle-letter roots never change their vowel. Thus, since you say dagim, dege ha-yam (“the fish of the sea”), where the qamats changes to a sheva, it follows that it is from the class of quiescent final-letter roots, and its root is gadah. But from ger you say gerim, garu, and the tsere does not change. Therefore it belongs to the class of quiescent middle-letter roots, and its root is gur.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 10_Principle, 5_P: 5. And the general rule is this: Every noun that you find consisting of two root letters, where the second letter appears in the plural, in pronominal suffixes, and in the feminine form, belongs to the class of doubled roots. Such nouns always have one of the short vowels at the beginning. Even those that are pointed with a qamats according to the tradition—such as yam (“sea”) in “the Salt Sea” (Genesis 14:3), or tam (“perfect”) in “perfect and upright” (Job 1:1), and the like—when they appear in the plural, with suffixes, or with the feminine ending, they become a pataḥ-vocalized, as in temimim, temah. Those with a tsere appear with a ḥiriq, such as shen → shino, ḥen → ḥano. Those with a ḥolem appear with three vowels, as from ḥoq: ḥuqqo, ḥuqqai, ḥuqqam. And when the middle radical is pointed with a sheva, then the first radical takes a ḥatef-qamats, as in “You guided them in Your strength” (Exodus 15:13), and likewise ḥuqqekha, ḥuqqekhem, as Rashi explained on “my strength and song is Yah” (Exodus 15:2). However, Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra rightly challenged him there—see his commentary.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 0_P: 12. The twelfth principle. An elucidation of nouns derived from doubled roots that occur with an added mem or tav at the beginning.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 1_P: 1. Know that nouns which occur with an added mem at the beginning are, for the most part, vocalized with a qamats on the first letter, following the pattern of nouns with a quiescent middle letter (naḥei ʿayin). However, there is a distinction between them: Those nouns of the naḥei ʿayin class typically have ḥolam in the final syllable, such as maqom, makhon, malon. By contrast, these nouns take either a qamats or a tsere in the final syllable, such as masakh and magen.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 2_P: 2. There is a further difference: just as nouns with a quiescent middle letter (naḥei ʿayin) normally change from a qamats to a sheva, as you already know, these do not undergo such a change. For example, from nagan one says magen, magenim, mageney. The qamats does not change. The reason is that it stands in the place of a dagesh; therefore it cannot change, just as I have said repeatedly, that forms which function as if they were dagush do not change.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 3_P: 3. There are also a few nouns with an initial mem and a ḥolam, following the pattern of roots with a quiescent first yod. Here too there is a distinction: those have a final qamats or a tsere, such as moshav and moqesh, whereas these have a final pataḥ, for example forms derived from roots like radad or rakhakh. These cases are very few.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 11_Principle, 4_P: 4. However, with feminine forms they are numerous, and they are useful for identification, since they are dageshed in the middle radical (ayin), such as megillah and meḥittah; and with an added tav, such as tefillah and taḥannah. There is also a single example with an added mem at the end, namely ḥinnam, derived from the root ḥanan.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 0_P: The thirteenth principle. An elucidation of nouns consisting of four or five letters.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 1_P: 1. Know that there are doubled nouns of four letters—meaning that between the two doubled final radicals, the first radical of the root appears again. Thus, from barar comes barburim; from baqaq comes baqbuq; from tsalal comes tsaltsel; from qadad comes qodqod, and similar forms.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 2_P: 2. There are also doubled nouns of four letters in which the lamed (the third radical) is doubled, such as ra‘anan, sha’anan, ḥakhlil, and similar forms. Some of these also appear with a feminine he, for example sha‘arurah, and with an added yod, as in sha‘aruriyah.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 3_P: 3. There are also doubled nouns of five letters, that is, forms in which both the ‘ayin and the lamed of the root are doubled. Examples are: from yaraq comes yeraqraq; from adom comes adamdām; and from asaf comes asafsuf, and similar forms.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 4_P: 4. There are also nouns of five letters in which no letter is doubled, such as shaʿatnez and tsefarʿadeaʿ and similar forms. Some say that these are compound words: shaʿatnez = shaʿuʿ, taʿui, and nuz (as taught in Torat Kohanim, Kedoshim 4:18, and Yevamot 5b); tsefarʿadeaʿ = “one who knows the frog,” meaning one who knows the croak. Likewise, there are four-letter words such as pilegesh and pelag, and ishah. But it is more correct to say that these are words borrowed from Egyptian, Babylonian, or Persian. As a general rule, I tell you: every word of five letters is not originally from the holy language. Thus also patshagen, adarkemonim, achashteranim, achashdarpanim, and similar words, as I will explain in the introduction to the Book of Composition.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 5_P: 4. There are also nouns that contain an alef at the beginning or a nun at the end, concerning which there is disagreement as to whether these letters are root letters or merely added. Examples include avnet and chashman, and likewise argaman. There are many such cases. Some say that the alef and the nun in these words are added letters, the alef as in ezroaʿ, and the nun as in zikaron.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 6_P: 5. And those nouns that consist of four distinct letters (i.e., without any letter being doubled) are very numerous, such as kaftor, sefarad, garzen, barzel, gizbar, serafad, tifsar, and the like. You already know that final qamats and tsere vowels undergo change, and you will observe—by studying the regular roots and learning from those nouns of three letters—that for the most part they all follow the same pattern.
text.8_Fourth Treatise, 1_, 12_Principle, 7_P: 6. There are also quadriliteral nouns whose plurals appear with a dagesh. These are those whose final vowel is a pataḥ. For example, from ḥashmal the plural is ḥashmalim, and likewise “like the appearance of ḥashmal” (Ezekiel 8:2), where the lamed is doubled. Similarly, from genaz (storehouse, treasury) we say genazkha, genazkim. Likewise from saraʿaf (as in “my anxious thoughts”), all are open-vowel forms. And from “princes shall come out of Egypt” (Psalms 68:32), we derive ḥashman. This is the word after which I named this book, which I composed in Rome, in the year of Rome, as explained in the introduction.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 0_Paragraph: This song I made in Rome at the end of the first edition:
text.9_Concluding Poem, 1_Paragraph: Two syllables and a peg; and two syllables; two syllables and a peg, and two syllables.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 2_Paragraph: O master of words, what need have you today of the seventy elders, or of Aaron and Hur?
text.9_Concluding Poem, 3_Paragraph: Turn to your discourse, to the foundation of grammar; behold, this book is called Ha-Bachur.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 4_Paragraph: With it comes a tongue of pure gold and a mantle; speech upon the lips, pleasant all around, without flaw or breach.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 5_Paragraph: Any matter that proves difficult for you—ask it; it will tell you an answer at once, without delay.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 6_Paragraph: To those who ask the book, ‘To whom do you belong?’ it will reply: ‘To Elijah—Bachur is his byname.’
text.9_Concluding Poem, 7_Paragraph: And this is the poem that I composed for the second edition (added in the printed version):
text.9_Concluding Poem, 8_Paragraph: I cry out and call to all people— to youths, to elders, and to the aged as well.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 9_Paragraph: Come to me, and I will teach you the rules of the holy tongue, set forth with new clarity.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 10_Paragraph: The foundation of grammar is surely examined in my book, for those who know religion and law, the sages of the new age.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 11_Paragraph: Behold, in it I will bring hidden things to light, and I will reveal the secrets treasured by the commentators.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 12_Paragraph: Into four principal treatises I shall divide it, to clarify and explain the matters under discussion.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 13_Paragraph: And thirteen principles to each one— that is, fifty-two in total.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 14_Paragraph: Let my book be called by the name Bachur; may it gladden both God and humankind.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 16_Paragraph: In ten pleasant languages this poem is spoken:
text.9_Concluding Poem, 17_Paragraph: So I replied: do not despise it.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 18_Paragraph: [A peg and two movements; and a peg and two movements in the opening and the closing.]
text.9_Concluding Poem, 19_Paragraph: I praise the Lord God and bow down, to the Creator of light and the One who brings on evenings.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 20_Paragraph: He granted me understanding to compose a book on grammar; its words are sweet nectar, pleasant as honey.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 21_Paragraph: I gathered within it concise rules, both new and old, pleasing and clear.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 22_Paragraph: Within it are proofs strong as lions, and sharp against the wolves of confusion.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 23_Paragraph: All the books of grammarians before it are like barren fields, without sweetness.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 24_Paragraph: It is better than fine gold, than gold of Ophir, and than all the merchandise of traders.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 25_Paragraph: Acquire it, David, and labor within it, and you will prosper— like a tree planted by waters, with pleasant roots.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 26_Paragraph: And even if you lack silver for its price, take it—give a pledge instead.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 27_Paragraph: Thus we shall merit to gather what is scattered, when He who rides the clouds gathers us in.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 28_Paragraph: And the Redeemer of Israel will rejoice in God, with Michael and Ishmael, the pleasant ones.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 29_Paragraph: And whoever wishes to know the time and its details— let him take this into his hand.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 30_Paragraph: completed and completed—praise to the eternal God.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 31_Paragraph: On Tuesday, the 23rd of Marḥeshvan, year 317 according to the minor count, in the house of Messer Venturin Rofenileio, by the scribe, our teacher Rabbi Meir, son of Rabbi Ephraim of blessed memory, of Padua.
text.9_Concluding Poem, 32_Paragraph: May He grant us merit to compose many books without end, and may He magnify Torah and make it glorious.
